Sports.title: Crystal Palace v Nottingham Forest, Hull v Everton, Southampton 1-0 Portsmouth: football – live
Sports.content:
3m ago 10.08 EDT Back underway in the Premier League There’s a delay as an officials’ communication check takes place at Hull. The referee has to call over the captains, and the game can resume. Share

7m ago 10.03 EDT The Premier League match centre says this about that disallowed Everton goal at Hull: “After VAR review, the referee overturned the original decision of goal to Everton – with Johnson in an offside position and deemed to be challenging an opponent for the ball. “REF: ‘Everton No.22 is in an offside position and challenges Hull No.3. Final decision is offside.’” Share

16m ago 09.54 EDT Half-time: Crystal Palace 2-1 Nottingham Forest How the hell did that happen? Palace were all over the shop, Pierre Sage headed down the dumper and now Selhurst is rocking. Forest did not score the many goals they might have scored, Walter Benitez standing tall in the Palace nets. And so that’s why that’s where we are. Share

18m ago 09.52 EDT Half-time: Hull 0-0 Everton The story of the half was the disallowed goal, Brennan Johnson in an offside position. Everton had struggled to break the deadlock, and once they had their “goal” ruled out, started to come under Hull pressure. Share

20m ago 09.51 EDT Goal! Crystal Palace 2-1 Nottingham Forest (Lerma, 45+4) Palace somehow rampant. Wharton’s corner comes in, and Lerna bundles home. Disaster for Forest, all those missed chances now rued. Matz Sels had just made a brilliant save from Tyrick Mitchell. Here’s VAR, but no, given. View image in fullscreen Jefferson Lerma puts Palace in front. What a turnaround. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters Share Updated at 09.53 EDT

22m ago 09.48 EDT Niall Fogarty gets in touch: “It seems that VAR wants to find reasons to punish Everton. This is the second time in three games VAR has disallowed an EFC goal for incredibly petty reasons… happened last season too.” Share

24m ago 09.47 EDT Hull 0-0 Everton: Two chances for Hull, first for Joe Gelhardt, firing just wide, and then Nobel Mendy heading wide from a corner. Hull have pushed onwards since that disallowed goal. Share

25m ago 09.45 EDT Crystal Palace 1-1 Nottingham Forest: Palace had been battered, and had not had a shot for 30 minutes. And yet here we are. It’s been a tough season so far for Glasner at Forest though he took time at Palace, with historic results following by the end. Share

28m ago 09.43 EDT Goal! Crystal Palace 1-1 Nottingham Forest (Kamada, 41) Where did that come from? Palace put together a passing move, and Kamada slots in, so coolly. Strand Larsen’s flick finds the Japan player, and then Quinten Timber finds the final assist. and Oliver Glasner is aghast. Here’s VAR…and it stands…. View image in fullscreen Daichi Kamada levels for Palace! Photograph: Justin Setterfield/Getty Images Share Updated at 09.46 EDT

30m ago 09.41 EDT Norrie gets in touch: “Incredibly annoying to see the continued trend today of pundits, players and managers dead-batting with “let’s wait for the appeal.” Let’s not. A three-year process concluded with an emphatic result of overwhelming guilt. If any of these people have any reason as to why an appeal will overturn that - let alone for why City should be allowed to further delay - they should say so.” Share

31m ago 09.40 EDT Crystal Palace 0-1 Nottingham Forest: While all that VAR was rolling on in Hull, Forest should have had another goal. Morgan Gibbs-White hit the crossbar and Liam Delap cannot beat Walter Benitez when he might have done better. Palace living very dangerously. Share

33m ago 09.38 EDT On-field review from referee - Everton goal ruled out The goal does not stand… Tzolakis dropped the ball … and was Johnson behind him? “Everton no 22 is in an offside position,” says the ref. And that gets huge cheers. Share Updated at 09.38 EDT

35m ago 09.35 EDT Goal! Hull 0-1 Everton (Johnson, 34) - but VAR on the case Grealish and Branthwaite get the ball into the Hull box and following a ricochet, Johnson stabs home. Was the keeper impeded? Hull are raging. View image in fullscreen Hull City's Konstantinos Tzolakis drops the ball in the box as Brennan Johnson pounces to put the ball in the back of the net. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters View image in fullscreen Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters Share Updated at 09.40 EDT

39m ago 09.32 EDT Crystal Palace 0-1 Nottingham Forest: Forest may be disappointed they do not have a greater advantage. Can Palace be this organised for the full 90? Perhaps they can … Gibbs-White smashes the latest decent Forest chance wide. There are great spaces in the Palace half to exploit. Share Updated at 09.33 EDT

42m ago 09.29 EDT Hull 0-0 Everton: Garner, who spent the international break with England, flashes over a corner that Branthwaite smashes back into the area. Hull are doing well enough, holding off the threat of their visitors. Share

46m ago 09.25 EDT Crystal Palace 0-1 Nottingham Forest: Ndoye has a header saved by Walter Benitez, and then there’s one hell of a scramble in the Palace box. All problems caused by playing out from the back. Pierre Sage would seem to employ that Russell Martin ideal. Steve Parish, in the stand, looks unimpressed. Palace perhaps lucky to be only a goal behind. Share

48m ago 09.22 EDT Hull 0-0 Everton: Some afters in Hull, where Tarkowski and McBurnie fight out a running battle, the Hull striker getting booked. VAR looked at the Tarkowski challenge that set off the rancour. View image in fullscreen Oli McBurnie tangles with James Tarkowski. Photograph: Daniel Hambury/Focus Images Ltd/Shutterstock Share Updated at 09.27 EDT

51m ago 09.20 EDT Hull 0-0 Everton: Branthwaite, the auxialiary left-back, looks to be walking slowly. He’s had his injury problems, some of which possibly prevented him from being sold off. Share

53m ago 09.18 EDT Crystal Palace 0-1 Nottingham Forest: Gibbs-White is doing the usual, given the free role he likes by his manager, and looking for openings. James McAtee almost finds one, only to be fouled by Jefferson Lerna, who is booked. Not a red, as there was cover between McAtee and goal. Share

1h ago 09.14 EDT Hull 0-0 Everton: Jack Grealish is fouled by Matt Crooks after a poor first touch from the Hull player. That’s his fourth booking of the season. What’s that joke? His second touch is a tackle. View image in fullscreen Jack Grealish is tripped by Matt Crooks. Photograph: Anna Gowthorpe/Shutterstock Share Updated at 09.18 EDT

1h ago 09.13 EDT Crystal Palace 0-1 Nottingham Forest: Quinten Timber fires a shot wide. Palace have looked capable of creating chances. Share

1h ago 09.10 EDT Crystal Palace 0-1 Nottingham Forest: Palace might have pulled level, though Strand Larsen might have done better to have hit the ball at Matz Sels, the Forest keeper. Share

1h ago 09.08 EDT Hull 0-0 Everton: Branthwaite goes on the overlap as he receives a pass from Dewsbury-Hall. Everton are dominating possession, which is all part of Sergej Jakirovic’s plan. Share

1h ago 09.06 EDT Crystal Palace 0-1 Nottingham Forest: Ndoye did well for Switzerland in the Nations League and has taken his confidence into club football. Forest’s away form continues to look better than at the City Ground. Share

1h ago 09.05 EDT Goal! Crystal Palace 0-1 Nottingham Forest (Ndoye, 3) What a goal. Palace concede possession and Ndoye makes hay, Khalali the guilty party, and the Forest fans can sing for Oliver Glasner. View image in fullscreen First blood to Forest. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters Share Updated at 09.10 EDT

1h ago 09.03 EDT Hull 0-0 Everton: Jarrad Branthwaite is lining up at left-back for Everton; the latest example of the club’s failings in the summer transfer window. Good player, but he’s a centre-back by design. Share

1h ago 09.00 EDT To the Premier League we revert, with Hull v Everton, and Crystal Palace v Nottingham Forest. And we are underway in both. Share Updated at 09.01 EDT

1h ago 08.56 EDT What does that mean for the Championship table? Report and reaction to follow. Share

1h ago 08.55 EDT Full-time: Southampton 1-0 Portsmouth This was a case of Saints toughing it out. Portsmouth have not proved capable of finding a way back from James Bree’s goal, and even after Cameron Bragg’s first-half red card. The Portsmouth fans will be kept back for a while yet and they do so in disappointment. View image in fullscreen A huge win for Southampton! Photograph: Adam Davy/PA Share Updated at 09.08 EDT

1h ago 08.53 EDT Southampton 1-0 Portsmouth Marko Milovanovic fires a late chance wide for Portsmouth but he was at the wrong angle in any case. Share

1h ago 08.51 EDT Southampton 1-0 Portsmouth Daniel Peretz climbs up to claim a Bailey cross to loud cheers from the home fans. Portsmouth look to have run out of ideas. Share

1h ago 08.49 EDT Southampton 1-0 Portsmouth Nothing much being created by Pompey, for all their efforts, with the ball falling to Abou Kamara in the box, though he loses the flight of it. Saints clear their lines. As they have done all afternoon. Big cheers when Azaz buys a foul, and Portsmouth’s Poole takes a chunk out of the Ireland player. There’s five minutes to be added on here. Share

1h ago 08.41 EDT Southampton 1-0 Portsmouth Having threatened to boil over further following the dismissal of Cameron Bragg, Saints have been tighter, more controlled, but as soon as that is said, Nico Schlotterbeck is booked. James Bree is in a bandage, having taken a bang to the head. He then concedes a soft corner that is cleared away after a couple of swings and misses from both sides. Share Updated at 08.42 EDT

2h ago 08.39 EDT Niall Mullen gets in touch: “It’s funny how having let a bull into the china shop in 2008 the Premier League has finally determined that the bull did in fact, contrary to the rules, break all of the china. Meanwhile the bull has evidence (dare I say, irrefutable evidence) that the china remains intact and that they are not even a bull but a porcelain enthusiast who has been excluded from the trade by big Delft. Meanwhile, pending a check to make sure the china was actually broken, the bull continues to terrorise the high street.” Share

2h ago 08.38 EDT Southampton 1-0 Portsmouth Down on the south coast, Pompey are going at it but Saints can see the finishing line. Caspar Jander has replaced Cyle Larin with Finn Azaz asked to lead the line in the Canadian’s stead. Share

2h ago 08.34 EDT Oliver Glasner spoke to Ben Fisher ahead of his return to Crystal Palace. double quotation mark Glasner was on holiday in the serene Austrian lakes with his wife, Bettina, the sun beating down on the water, when the interest from Forest ramped up. “She said: ‘Why are you always looking at your phone?’ [I said:] ‘I’m going to Athens tomorrow.’ She said: ‘Are you crazy? We are here on vacation.’ There were many, many different options in the summer. The one I thought I would do is staying at home, which is why my family was not really pleased with my early decision to leave again … but in that moment when I looked in detail, into the [Forest] squad, and [gathered] my thoughts, I started to get butterflies.” Oliver Glasner: ‘There was no plan for me to be Nottingham Forest manager’ Read more View image in fullscreen Oliver Glasner is back in south London. Photograph: Sebastian Frej/Getty Images Share Updated at 08.36 EDT

2h ago 08.30 EDT The prelims to Palace v Forest saw Oliver Glasner and Daniel Munoz get a warm reception when returning to Selhurst Park. Forest’s better performances have come away from home, including their sole win, at Aston Villa. That’s very Glasner, as Palace fans would recognise. Share

Sports.title: Liverpool v Manchester City: Premier League – live
Sports.content:
Key events 41m ago Preamble

27m ago 09.43 EDT John Brewin A four-match international break has presented a stress test. “The intensity of the squad, the athleticism of it, really, I think it’s designed for the elite,” said the Wales head coach, Craig Bellamy, on the completion of four matches in 11 days. Elite club coaches would disagree. The Nations League and the wider set of international games staged across the globe have been accompanied by a daily list of casualties, club officials viewing matches through their fingers as players pull up and gesture to the bench. Almost certainly to the disquiet of Enzo Maresca, City’s Elliot Anderson and Marc Guéhi were, alongside Harry Kane, the only England players to start all four Nations League matches, with Nico O’Reilly withdrawing halfway through. Liverpool’s problems appear to run deeper, with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo, early successes for the Andoni Iraola regime, sustaining injuries with Sweden and the Netherlands respectively. Jérémy Jacquet, another bright spark this season, reportedly strained a hamstring with France. Havertz, Isak, Dorgu … spate of injuries with national teams leaves sour taste for top clubs Read more Share

35m ago 09.36 EDT Will Unwin It was quiet around Anfield three hours before kick-off but there is a sense of what is to come. For £15 you can buy a ‘Guilty’ flag, depicting the City squad in jail or a ‘Cheats’ banner riffing off Oasis’s own style. What larks. View image in fullscreen The merch scene outside Anfield before Liverpool’s game against City. Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images Share Updated at 09.40 EDT

36m ago 09.35 EDT Barney Ronay The internet: an apology. It turns out you were right. It was actually a simulation all along. Now, talk to me about chemtrails again. And yes, maybe Vinícius Júnior has been replaced by a handsome, baffled-looking waxwork. Welcome to the weirdest weekend of them all. We are now post-judgment, post-statement, postlapsarian. As the Premier League prepares to snap back into what must be described, out of habit, as reality, armed with the knowledge its serial champions have been the authors of a 10-year sham supremacy, the first question is fairly simple. How is it going to feel? There is no precedent for this. Even the state of total confusion feels brittle given City maintain their complete state of innocence and deny all charges. We await the release of Irrefutable Body of Evidence, the great lost Madonna erotic thriller sequel, presumably recast around a steamy three-year regulatory tribunal scenario. The Premier League is back: welcome to the new era of post-verdict unreality | Barney Ronay Read more Share Updated at 09.38 EDT

Sports.title: Ten-man Southampton hold on to beat rivals Portsmouth in feisty derby
Sports.content:
Relief will surely be the overriding emotion for Tonda Eckert when he reflects on his last few days as Southampton’s head coach. After avoiding an immediate ban after Wednesday’s ruling on his part in the Spygate scandal that rocked the Championship last season, he oversaw victory in his first south coast derby in the St Mary’s dugout as his 10 men held firm in the face of Portsmouth’s second-half onslaught following Cam Bragg’s red card.

There was widespread surprise at the leniency of Eckert’s punishment after Southampton admitted to spying on three of their opponents last season – a six-week ban that is suspended until the end of the 2027-28 campaign and a £28,000 fine – meaning he was able to take his place on the touchline on Sunday. An FA independent disciplinary commission noted Eckert’s “genuine contrition” at what had happened. At Southampton, there is a sense that their expulsion from the playoffs in May and four-point deduction was punishment enough, and Eckert is keen to move on from a period of uncertainty that he admitted this week had changed his life.

The Portsmouth head coach, John Mousinho, had also welcomed a resolution to the case before Sunday so that the football could be the focus. James Bree was the author of the winning goal, turning the ball home after 20 minutes, but the pattern of a fiercely contested game shifted with Bragg’s first-half dismissal for two yellow cards. Southampton held on to move into the top half – they would be third without the points deduction – with Eckert now able to approach a promotion push with a clear conscience.

Mousinho’s big selection call came in goal, with Nicolas Schmid getting the nod ahead of Daniel Bielica for the first time in five games. The Austrian rose to the occasion within the first two minutes, spreading himself to block Cyle Larin’s bobbling shot after the Canada striker had taken down Ryan Manning’s diagonal long ball. The first flare-up came moments later when a smirking Manning bumped chests with Ebou Adams after a Portsmouth free-kick came to nothing.

The Portsmouth full-back Jayden Meghoma, who made his professional debut for Southampton as a 17-year-old, was a magnet for Saints ire. He was a threat down the left, firing wide at the near post in a promising opening, but he lost Bree for Southampton’s opener. Finn Azaz was given too much space in midfield and clipped a ball in behind a static Meghoma for Bree, forward from right-back, to guide a left-footed finish into the far corner.

View image in fullscreen Southampton’s James Bree coolly opens the scoring, his goal turning out to be the winner. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

The Portsmouth midfielder Adams was a central figure, just as he had been in scoring his team’s first goal in this fixture in 14 years last January. He twice picked Bragg’s pocket in the Southampton half and drew yellow cards on both occasions. The 20-year-old Bragg, a lifelong Saints fan from Winchester, was consoled by his teammates after receiving his second yellow and marching orders for an instinctive tug of Adams’s shirt after being caught on the ball. Colby Bishop and Ryan Kavuma-McQueen went close to equalising before Eckert could try to plug the gaps at half-time.

View image in fullscreen Cam Bragg is consoled as he walks off the pitch. Photograph: Robin Jones/Getty Images

After Leo Scienza spurned a chance on the counterattack after the restart, Southampton were perhaps fortunate not to be reduced to nine players when Azaz, frustrated at not being given a free-kick under Adams’s challenge, then lunged in on him on the touchline. The busy referee, Adam Herczeg, flashed his yellow card and Eckert allowed himself a smile with the fourth official. More relief.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

When Bree was treated for a battle scar around his eye, Eckert was able to hold council with his remaining midfielders James Ward-Prowse and Flynn Downes after a flurry of Portsmouth chances. The substitute Adrian Segecic was drifting into spaces and had fizzed a couple of low efforts wide in the minutes before, while the right-back Zak Swanson saw his cut-back cleared by Jack Stephens from under the Southampton crossbar.

View image in fullscreen Tempers fray at St Mary’s but the hosts held on for victory. Photograph: Warren Little/Getty Images

While Eckert gradually reduced his side’s attacking presence, Mousinho emptied his bench in an attempt to find a way through a resilient Southampton defence marshalled by Stephens and Keven Schlotterbeck, who laid their bodies on the line more than once in front of Daniel Peretz in goal. Their clean sheet was a priceless end to a week where their manager was given a clean slate.

Sports.title: Scottish Premiership: Celtic end losing skid and take top spot back from Rangers
Sports.content:
Jota made his long-awaited return to action as Celtic claimed a much-needed 2-0 victory at Motherwell to move top of the Premiership again and ease the sense of gloom and tension that had engulfed the club during the international break.

Five months on from a dramatic late win that helped them on their way to last season’s title, Martin O’Neill’s side enjoyed another big result at Fir Park to stem a three-game losing streak and climb back ahead of Rangers, who had leapfrogged them at the summit on Saturday.

After a renewal of hostilities between supporters and the Celtic board as well as uncertainty about O’Neill’s future as manager during the three-week break since their home defeat by their bitter rivals, an early strike from Camilo Durán helped restore a semblance of calm for the Hoops.

The champions had control of proceedings thereafter and – despite an inspired display from the home goalkeeper Alex Paulsen – Celtic added to their lead through Benjamin Nygren in the 58th minute as they made it seven wins in eight league matches this term.

The huge Hoops support sporadically unfurled banners and chanted against major shareholder Dermot Desmond, who was the subject of a tennis-ball protest by a group of balaclava-clad supporters at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship in St Andrews last weekend. Long before the end of a largely one-sided encounter, however, it was Motherwell’s fans who were displaying their frustration by making for the exits as their insipid side slid to a fourth consecutive defeat.

Derek McInnes praised his Rangers players and blamed the extended international break for some disjointed play in Saturday’s 3-1 win over Kilmarnock.

Rangers went into the break three up at Ibrox after Ryan Naderi twice headed home either side of a Kevin Kelsy strike. But Killie had chances throughout, especially after the interval, before finally getting their reward when substitute Nicky Clescenco struck on a last-minute counterattack. The visitors ended the game with six efforts on target to Rangers’ four, but the home goalkeeper, Ivor Pandur, was seriously troubled once before being beaten.

View image in fullscreen Ryan Naderi celebrates after opening the scoring for Rangers against Killie. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

“I was really pleased with how clinical we were in the first half,” said McInnes. “We put the ball in the box, we scored goals. We just didn’t do it enough for whatever reason. But we have to be honest, for long spells we looked like a team that hadn’t been together for the last three weeks. There’s a bit of understanding for me where the players have been. Whoever came up with this idea, it’s such a long time for your players to be away. We pay their wages, we look after our players and for them to be away for nearly three weeks is too long. But we’ve got the job done and credit the players for digging deep and getting three points.”

Hearts eased to their biggest home win in the league for three-and-a-half years as they dismantled St Mirren 5-0 to remain on the coattails of Rangers and Celtic.

The third-placed Jambos dominated from the start and Laurent Mendy fired them ahead in the 20th minute. Calvin Miller scored two penalties, either side of half-time, before goals from Cláudio Braga and Josh McPake ensured a smooth afternoon for Hearts.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Hearts’ Calvin Miller scores his side’s second from the spot against St Mirren. Photograph: Zak Mauger/Getty Images

It was Hearts’ biggest league win at Tynecastle since they defeated Ross County 6-1 under Steven Naismith in April 2023 and they are now comfortably the top scorers in the league. Hearts manager, Wouter Vrancken, said: “We try to play a kind of football that is positive and constructive and proactive, and not a reaction. I think people come to the stadium to see nice football, to see goals from your side.”

Ashley Hay scrambled in a stoppage-time winner to secure Dundee a 2-1 victory at Falkirk. The striker, out since early August with a ligament sprain, converted from close range after latching on to Ethan Hamilton’s free-kick in the first minute of added time. His goal completed the turnaround after Owen Bevan’s second goal for the Dark Blues had cancelled out Jacob Murrell’s first-half penalty at Falkirk Stadium.

Marink Reedijk endured a disappointing first game as Hibernian’s manager as his side suffered a 1-0 defeat against Dundee United at Tannadice. The hosts scored in the first half through winger Daniel Bennie, on loan from QPR, and the visitors finished the game with 10 men after Jacob Devaney was sent off.

This story will be updated

Sports.title: Robbie Savage the panto villain puts scepticism aside to leave Leicester reeling
Sports.content:
It felt as though the stars had aligned when Robbie Savage’s first League One match in charge of Peterborough – his first EFL managerial role – happened to be at Leicester. He made his name here and forged a divisive and enduring reputation that has kept him a permanent fixture in English football.

Savage has long been a joker figure – an image born in his playing days, when he hurtled around midfields with long blond hair bouncing, launching into challenges that at one point made him the most booked player in Premier League history. A pantomime villain, a prankster and an eccentric who was once fined £10,000 by the Football Association – and two weeks’ wages by Leicester – for using referee Graham Poll’s toilet before a match (Savage blamed an upset stomach brought on by antibiotics.)

That persona followed him into the media after retirement and it hardly screams management material, yet Savage has quietly built a more serious reputation on the touchline in recent years.

At the phoenix club Macclesfield, he was handed his first chance in the dugout by his mate Rob Smethurst, the owner, and won promotion to the National League North with a mammoth 109 points – winning 35 of 42 games. Last season, he guided Forest Green Rovers to the National League playoffs, losing to Boreham Wood.

Perhaps because of his personality, scepticism has shadowed the 51-year-old throughout his fledgling managerial career. In a lengthy interview with the Peterborough board, he won them over with his passion and ideas for restoring confidence in a young, talented, but struggling squad. Darragh MacAnthony, the club’s chair, suggested Savage’s character and work rate were required from “top to bottom” at the club.

Even so, when Savage took the Posh job he immediately addressed “the doubters” before anyone had really expressed any doubt. He pointed out he was told he was not good enough when he was released by Manchester United – one of the forgotten members of the Class of ’92 FA Youth Cup winners – and that he had battled his way into the Leicester team.

At the King Power Stadium on Saturday, he was so animated on the touchline it bordered on parody. He approached the travelling Peterborough fans and pumped his fist towards them – a gesture most managers save for after a victory, but Savage performed before kick-off. He was equally lively when the game started, dressed in baggy dark grey trousers and jacket, if not crouching on the edge of his technical area then shouting instructions, clapping his hands, pointing his fingers. There was a lot of pointing on his way to an impressive 3-1 win away.

View image in fullscreen Robbie Savage gees up the Peterborough fans before kick-off with a few fist pumps (top left), then runs through a gamut of emotions during the match. Composite: James Holyoak/Shutterstock; Michael Zemanek/Shutterstock; Jez Tighe/Prosports/Shutterstock

His exertions were so energetic the jacket came off within 10 minutes. “I’m exhausted,” he said. “I think I’ve done 10k in the technical area, kicking every ball for my team.”

It is no surprise he was handed a two-match ban last season for yellow cards received for over-exuberant celebrations and overexuberant discussions with officials. When Lucca Mendonça crunched Bobby De Cordova-Reid, Savage leapt and punched the air with as much enthusiasm as he celebrated Owura Edwards’s opening goal.

Quick Guide League One: Plymouth on top; dream start for Savage Show Plymouth came from behind to beat Wimbledon 2-1 with a stoppage-time goal from substitute Xavier Amaechi which put them clear at the top of League One. Jayden Stockley had put the Dons ahead in the 16th minute, with Caleb Watts equalising ahead of the break. It looked like the points would be shared before Amaechi swept the ball home in the fifth minute of added time. New Peterborough manager Robbie Savage had a dream start with a 3-1 win at Leicester, to pile more pressure on Foxes’ manager Russell Martin. Posh took an early lead through Owura Edwards and Harry Leonard before an own goal from Warren O’Hora made it 3-0 just before the break. Emil Riis scored a second-half consolation for the hosts. Mark Harris and Cameron Brannagan scored as high-flying Oxford secured a 2-1 win over Notts County at Meadow Lane. Bradford were held to a goalless draw by Leyton Orient at Valley Parade, slipping two points behind Plymouth. Huddersfield missed the chance to go second after Sheffield Wednesday fought back with two late goals to snatch a 2-2 draw at the Accu Stadium after Jamal Lowe scored a penalty deep into stoppage-time. Kyle Wootton scored twice as Stockport came from behind to beat Barnsley 3-1 at Edgeley Park to sit third. Gassan Ahadme’s late goal gave fifth-placed Cambridge a 1-0 win over 10-man Blackpool at the Abbey Stadium, where there had been a 15 minute delay to kick-off because of issues affecting supporters entering the ground. Reading are sixth after a 5-1 away win at strugglers MK Dons while Luton were comprehensive victors at Wycombe with a dominant 4-1 display to spoil a day of celebration for Tom Hounsell. Efforts from Kasey Palmer, Nahki Wells, Jamie Donley and Devante Cole were more than enough against a home side who announced Hounsell as permanent head coach before the game. Leon Ayinde’s first EFL goal was enough to move Doncaster out of the bottom four with a 1-0 home win over Burton. Mansfield edged home 2-1 in their first ever game against Bromley to halt a run of four games without a victory. Wigan remain adrift at the bottom of the table after a 1-0 defeat at Stevenage. Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

As at Macclesfield and Forest Green, his football was fast and direct. A ball over the top allowed Bolu Shofowoke to round the Leicester goalkeeper before Harry Leonard tapped in.

The Posh fans started chanting Savage’s name just before half-time, then called for him to give them a wave. But he was so engrossed in the Peterborough attack that led to their third goal that he didn’t hear them.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

That marauding style does leave them exposed at the back, but Savage doesn’t care. “My philosophy is: the best players are at the top of the pitch,” he said. “If I can get it there as quick as we can, by limiting the passes, but on the floor, through the lines, you can push the full-backs out. At times we were 2-1-1-6. That’s how we play. We are open. But let’s be brave.”

Even then, Emil Riis’s back-post tap-in – Savage, held his head in his hands as though the world was ending after conceding – took only a lick of gloss off the occasion. It was a stunning result for a side that in the league had won once all season, scored four times and gone seven weeks without a victory.

View image in fullscreen Robbie Savage offers a theatrical response to Peterborough’s victory at his former club Leicester in his first game in charge. Photograph: Jez Tighe/ProSports/Shutterstock

“I’m just humble to come up against somebody like Russell Martin, who’s managed in the Premier League,” Savage said. “Two and a half years ago I was up at Hebburn and Stockton, playing in front of 200-300 people. My team have come to the King Power and put in a performance like that. I’m so proud of them.”

At the final whistle, Savage hurried around the pitch, where he must have shaken the hand or slapped the back or hugged every player, coach and staff member from both teams. The Peterborough fans stood and chanted his name long before and well after he returned to pump his fist in celebration.

Savage will be entertaining this season. And he might just surprise a few people with his football, too.

Sports.title: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Football, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. The Premier League is the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game.

What the Manchester City case has exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it’s perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales.

Football clubs in England and Wales still represent their communities, a relationship that may be strained in certain cases by the pressures of a globalised entertainment economy, but remains broadly true. Arsenal can feel like the club of choice for the nouveau fan from across the world, but the scenes of celebration when they ended their 22-year wait for the league title last season were an undeniable expression of local pride.

The idea that there was ever an idyll when clubs were run by benevolent potentates for the good of those communities is romantic nonsense. But just because there was no golden age is not to say that the situation has always been as bleak as this.

How did we get into a situation in which clubs are flotsam on the swirling currents of geopolitics and the world economy? Chelsea alone in the past four years have had a Russian oligarch forced to sell the club after falling under UK government sanctions, while a subsequent American co-owner has been forced to sell his minority stake after his insurance business came under federal investigation in the US. It’s a curious world in which the professional gamblers feel like a welcome breath of fresh air.

View image in fullscreen Chelsea fans hold banner during a peaceful, fan-led protest calling for accountability and structural change at Chelsea Football Club in January. Fans criticised the club’s ownership model, recruitment strategy, and overall leadership since the takeover, urging an end to micromanagement and a return to long-term ambition at the top level of English and European football. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images

The days of the local businessmen, the owners of mines, shipyards and factories, the hauliers and scrap-metal dealers, are gone. Some invested because they genuinely wanted to give back to their communities or liked the sport. Others did so because it was easier to fund a local football club than to improve working conditions or pay a proper wage. And some did so because, wrongly in most cases, they thought there may be money to be made.

But nobody should think those were days of purity. The decrepitude of English stadiums in the 1980s should caution anybody who thinks football was uncomplicatedly better then.

The contradiction has always lain at the heart of English football. Clubs represent their communities and for fans support becomes an aspect of identity, a link to family and place and past, a role that has only become more significant as the influence of traditional institutions – the church, the workplace, the social club – has faded. Yet fans in England have almost never owned their club, which in part underlies the present crisis.

That is not to say fan ownership is a panacea. There is much to be admired about the German 50+1 model which, to oversimplify, ensures outside investors can never own a majority of the club. But it has not prevented Bayern Munich from winning 13 of the past 14 Bundesliga titles. Some sort of recognition that a club is not just a business, that it has a community function might, though, have prevented the free-for-all that has led to this mess.

At least when most owners were local, there was some understanding of what the club meant to its area, and a recognition that exploitation or neglect could have direct consequences. No owner wanted demonstrations at the directors’ entrance, or to be jeered as he drove the streets in his Rolls-Royce, or to have his car showroom boycotted because he put up ticket prices then sold a popular centre-forward at a knockdown price. The distant majority shareholder in his boardroom in Los Angeles, his penthouse in Monte Carlo or his luxury villa on the Gulf feels the sting less keenly.

Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League, who did more to shape the modern competition, for good and for ill, than any other individual always spoke of being “neutral about ownership models”. Essentially that meant taking the money without worrying too much about where it came from. The current Premier League is the consequence: a gleaming, world-leading edifice, but built on what?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Perhaps it’s not fair to be too harsh on the Premier League. This is not just modern football; it is modern Britain. As Miguel Delaney and Jack Pitt-Brooke argued on the Libero podcast this week, the Premier League is a direct outcome of Blairite economic policy, a point made clear in Oliver Bullough’s Butler to the World In the book he described the classic New Labour approach as “allowing something, making money from it and attempting to solve the problems it causes after they’ve occurred”.

But how do you solve those problems in football? How can football extricate itself from the clutches of the mega-rich? Regulation, up to a point, helps – and there may at least now be a sense that there can be enforcement. Whatever the flaws of the profitability and sustainability rules, or the squad cost ratio that has replaced them, it may be useful if football could accept the basic premise that the game shouldn’t just be about how rich your owner happens to be. But that can only go so far; a door open to the world has admitted a world of problems.

Short of some sort of financial crash in football, the sort of apocalyptic event that would make the sport unappealing to big finance and require the game to be built anew, with a fresh spirit that might recategorise football clubs as community assets rather than simple businesses, we’re probably stuck with it.

How, after all, could football ever escape the society that produced it?

Sports.title: Manchester United and Spurs come back to reality as City saga offers brief distraction | John Brewin
Sports.content:
Turning back the clock is impossible. Up in the Stretford End’s middle tier, the ticker had returned, a retouching job to “51 years” invoiced for the pertinent sum of £114. The Manchester City that existed before the Abu Dhabi project won their last trophy in 1976. Questionable maths is perhaps not confined to the Etihad’s accounts department, though Manchester United’s support must get their kicks where they can.

Should City’s fall from grace be fully confirmed by the appeals and sanctions process, there is nothing in the way of irrefutable evidence of United’s former supremacy being restored. How United fans would love to return to 2008, when Michael Carrick was a key cog in Sir Alex Ferguson’s team of European champions. Instead, the autumn of 2026 brings a familiar swell of doubt, another manager dragged towards the meat grinder. It will be 40 years next month since Ferguson was appointed. A draw made United’s start to their league campaign the worst since then. The Carrick bounce has come to a standstill.

Sweet succour for City fans caught in legal limbo while railing against a “red cartel”. Should such a thing exist, United are a poor relation. Only Ipswich have been defeated by United this season in the Premier League, the latest disappointment to follow many years of corners being turned, only for culs-de-sac to be found. As the club who previously had the financial muscle to match the disguised funding of City, United have become the model for frittering away financial advantages. That the Glazer debt repayments since 2005 are a sum higher than City’s £900m-plus injection of petrodollars represents bitter irony. The cash has been flushed down a hole as deep as the Ship canal. That won’t be coming back either.

View image in fullscreen Bryan Mbeumo put Manchester United in front, but they could not hold on against 10 men. Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty Images

It can be readily argued that Tottenham have been more disadvantaged by City’s breaches. As with United, their lawyers have laid a legal marker against City for the compensation that could follow the completion of the Premier League process. Champions League revenue, extra Premier League prize money and attendant endorsements would have been helpful for a club that built a new stadium during those disputed years.

As with United, Tottenham’s self-inflicted wounds have been heavy. Whatever happens to the pariahs in blue, neither club can act as if the last 18 years were all a nasty dream. The City saga has been a welcome distraction when the international break might otherwise have been flush with speculation over the latest crises. Over close to 100 minutes, both teams personified the wastage and chaos that has reigned in north London and Stretford. A ragged affair, usually shapeless, full of errors forced and unforced, eventually boiled over. Rodrigo Bentancur was sent off, with Luke Shaw fortunate not to accompany the Uruguayan on a walk of shame. Both the goals scored owed much to defensive losses of concentration.

If Tottenham still lack a first Premier League win, they had their successes, and soon quietened the home support. Instead of rejoicing in City’s downfall with a flourish of vindication, as against Hull, as in the second half against Brighton, and three weeks ago, as against Fulham, United players were second to challenges, sluggish, space left achingly open.

Howls of anguish followed a chance that should have been buried by Mohammed Kudus. Further Tottenham chances followed. Boos accompanied Senne Lammens clearing his lines by belting the ball into the stands. Had Tottenham possessed anything like nerve in front of goal, they could have been beyond reach within an opening half hour that reduced Old Trafford to an anguished hush. Instead, the familiar path of beginning brightly to little avail was followed. If Spurs can start scoring goals they might be seriously dangerous. And yet they lie third-bottom of a Premier League table awaiting asterisks and appendices.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Dominic Solanke (right) celebrates his goal with Tottenham teammate Archie Gray. Photograph: Dave Thompson/AP

As prescribed by Roberto De Zerbi, Spurs counter-pressed with vigour, taking control of a midfield area where their opponents’ energy deficit was glaring. Carlos Baleba, signed for £70m, one of De Zerbi’s players at Brighton, arrived on the hour. The answer to a problem unsolved since Carrick’s retirement does not appear to be Youri Tielemans, who the debutant replaced. The Belgian, with significant miles on the clock, appears the latest example of United falling foul of buying cheap and probably needing to buy twice.

A marked increase in output that followed Baleba’s arrival pushed the game into United’s hands as Tottenham dropped off. De Zerbi-ball heavies the legs, particularly when rewards are scarce. Injustice, Bentancur’s red card, replenished them. Dominic Solanke’s goal, via unconventional means, came when the 10 men pushed onwards as United failed to press home their advantage, a pattern all too familiar this season. The anti-City chants were brought to a halt. Wallowing in others’ plight is little comfort when you are yourself stuck in the mud.

Sports.title: Real Madrid’s Vinícius Júnior sent off for hair-pulling in victory over Villarreal
Sports.content:
Yan Diomandé earned Real Madrid a tight 1-0 victory over Villarreal to keep them six points behind La Liga leaders Barcelona, even though winger Vinícius Júnior was sent off for hair pulling.

Vinícius, on as a substitute, scored but his goal was disallowed and then he was dismissed after a VAR review showed he had pulled the hair of Villarreal’s Nathan Saliba.

José Mourinho’s side battled through the final stages with 10 men, holding on to win and provisionally going third. But the red card left a bitter taste for Real, with Vinícius running the risk of a potential ban which could keep him out of El Clásico on 25 October.

“I don’t know what’s going on with the referees, with this red card, I don’t understand,” said the Madrid midfielder Aurélien Tchouaméni. “But the most important thing is the victory.”

Kylian Mbappé was fit to start the match for Madrid after suffering a knee problem playing for France during the international break. There were a smattering of whistles for the superstar forward, with some fans believing he has been unprofessional in recent weeks, but also applause from others.

Mbappé, a candidate for the Ballon d’Or trophy later this month, was Madrid’s most threatening player in the first half, although he had little competition.

View image in fullscreen Players react as the referee, Isidro Díaz de Mera Escuderos, sends off Vinícius Júnior. Photograph: Denis Doyle/Getty Images

Mourinho started with out-of-form Vinícius on the bench, following his trips to Australia and India with Brazil during the international break.

Madrid improved defensively, giving Villarreal few chances of note, but struggled to build much in attack themselves in a drab opening half.

Mbappé struck the post from Álvaro Carreras’s lay-off as Madrid pushed Villarreal back early on. Villarreal soon gained a foothold and restricted Madrid’s opportunities, until Mbappé forced a good save from Peter Gulacsi.

There was some more mild whistling for Madrid’s display from their fans at half-time, but soon they were able to celebrate summer arrival Diomandé’s first goal for the club. The Ivorian winger, Madrid’s record signing, produced a sharp low finish into the far corner after good work from Federico Valverde to play him in.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Yan Diomandé scores the only goal of the game at the Bernabéu. Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images

Vinícius thought he had doubled Madrid’s lead after Jude Bellingham charged in down the left and cut the ball back for him. However the winger’s joy turned to anger after the referee, Isidro Díaz de Mera Escuderos, was called to watch Vinícius’s hair pull on Saliba in the buildup by VAR and sent off the Brazilian, disallowing his goal.

Madrid’s Belgian goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois, who had made a couple of smart saves earlier in the half, then produced an acrobatic stop to thwart Carlos Romero.

Mbappé was denied again by the Hungarian goalkeeper Gulasci as the forward left the Bernabéu frustrated in his hunt for goals, although his team were able to clinch three important points to stay on Barcelona’s trail.
