World.title: Silent inflammation could be damaging your body — and 5 habits may help keep it in check
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Inflammation is a natural immune response that helps protect the body from injury and infection, but when it becomes chronic, it can pose a health threat, according to the National Institutes of Health.

Over time, chronic inflammation can contribute to rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease and cardiovascular disease.

Keeping the condition in check can help protect healthy tissues and support overall health, experts say.

POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS

Jim LaValle, a clinical pharmacist and metabolic medicine expert based in Texas, told Fox News Digital that inflammation can be influenced by a variety of factors beyond injury or infection.

LaValle first pointed to the gut-immune-brain connection — the communication between gut microbes, the immune system and the central nervous system — as one pathway that can influence the body's inflammatory response.

Beyond gut health, he said several everyday lifestyle factors can play a role in preventing chronic inflammation.

DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE

No. 1: Manage stress

Managing stress and anxiety can help support the gut-brain connection and keep inflammation in check, according to LaValle.

He pointed to cortisol, a hormone released in response to stress, which he said can "wreak havoc on your chemistry" when levels remain elevated.

Chronic stress can also affect the intestinal barrier, potentially allowing substances that would normally remain inside the gut to pass through more easily, LaValle said.

This increased intestinal permeability is sometimes called "leaky gut."

ZERO SUGAR, MORE PROBLEMS? STUDY REVEALS SURPRISING GUT HEALTH EFFECTS

"So, it turns out that if I'm stressed out a lot, I can be more prone to irritable bowel," LaValle said, as stress can trigger or worsen digestive symptoms in some people.

No. 2: Watch for food triggers

Diets high in sugar, fat and ultraprocessed foods can also affect gut health.

Paying attention to which foods trigger certain symptoms may help identify potential food sensitivities or intolerances, LaValle noted.

Symptoms such as bloating, rashes or discomfort after eating certain foods may signal a food-related reaction, although they can have other causes.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Certain medications, including antibiotics, may also alter the gut microbiome, but their effects vary depending on the drug and the individual, the expert said.

No. 3: Keep blood sugar in check

Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is another important factor in managing inflammation, according to LaValle.

LaValle noted that conditions such as diabetes and insulin resistance are often associated with chronic inflammation.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Research suggests that GLP-1 medications, commonly prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity, may have anti-inflammatory effects, while scientists are investigating other potential benefits beyond weight loss and blood sugar control.

No. 4: Be aware of environmental exposures

The "exposome," or the environmental exposures people experience throughout their lives, can influence inflammation and the risk of chronic disease, according to the National Institutes of Health.

LaValle pointed to emerging research on how environmental exposures — including "forever chemicals," microplastics, metals and pesticides — may affect weight, blood sugar regulation and other aspects of health.

CLICK HERE TO 

"A lot of us don't think about that kind of impact on our health and how that could trigger inflammation signaling," he added.

No. 5: Don’t over-train

Regular exercise supports overall health, but intense workouts without adequate recovery time can put additional stress on the body, LaValle cautioned.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"You’re not getting a good enough recovery," he said. "You’re training hard. And, in fact, you might be training hard every day to lower that cortisol, but you're not getting good recovery. And that could lead to silent inflammatory signaling as well."

Anyone who is concerned about chronic inflammation or is experiencing persistent symptoms should consult a doctor to determine the underlying cause and appropriate treatment.

World.title: Major attack on Saudi airport kills 12 and leads Trump to weigh joining fight
World.content:
The deadliest attack on a Gulf Arab state since the start of the Iran war raised new questions Sunday about whether the United States might be about to join another conflict in the region.

The missile strike on Saudi Arabia’s main international airport drew widespread condemnation and intensified pressure on the kingdom and its allies to respond to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The attack was the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade and marked a sharp escalation in the Yemen-based Houthis’ campaign against the leading oil exporter, which has already rattled the global economy.

President Donald Trump indicated it could now prompt America to join the fight, weeks after the conflict between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition reignited alongside the unresolved clash between Washington and Tehran.

At least 12 people were killed and 309 injured when the missile hit King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh on Saturday, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. The victims included one American as well as four citizens of Saudi Arabia, two Bangladeshi nationals, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Palestinian, a Syrian and one Sudanese.

Some of the wounded were in critical condition, authorities said, while airport operations remained suspended Sunday.

Saudi Arabia’s government and its allies blamed the Houthis for Saturday’s strike. The group did not immediately claim responsibility for the latest attack, although it renewed a warning to stay away from Saudi airports.

Washington also blamed the Houthis for Saturday’s assault, the latest of several on the busy facility in the past week. Three people were killed there in an attack on Thursday.

The aftermath of an explosion at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on Oct. 8. via Reuters

The attack has put fresh scrutiny on Washington’s response to the widening conflict, in which the Houthis have hit Saudi energy infrastructure and seize territory that gives them leverage over shipping in the Red Sea.

Trump said Saturday that the U.S. was considering joining Saudi military operations against the Houthis, leaving open the possibility of direct American involvement.

“We may. We’re gonna look at it,” Trump told reporters. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

00:16 Trump responds to potential U.S. involvement after Saudi attack 00:00 00:00

The U.S. launched a three-month bombing campaign against the Houthis last year to stop them from targeting shipping through the critical waterway, an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

The Saudis will be looking to allies like Pakistan, Turkey, Syria, Egypt and the U.S. for help, said Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics.

“But I doubt very much whether there is an answer or even a military solution to the Yemeni conflict,” he told NBC News.

“The Houthis are determined to fight to the end,” Gerges said. “I suspect that the reason why the U.S. has been reluctant is not only because of the Iran war, but also because the U.S tried for several months to force the Houthis to stand down, and they did not succeed.”

At the same time, the Houthis are becoming “more nimble, more resourceful, more deadly by the day, and I think what we have seen in the past few weeks is that the targeting system of the Houthis has become much more effective,” he said.

Egypt said Sunday that it “stands firmly” with Saudi Arabia, expressing “strong condemnation” for the attacks.” Qatar called the missile strike “a grave violation of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and a direct threat to regional security.”

Germany and Canada also condemned the attacks, with Prime Minister Mark Carney describing them as “abhorrent.”

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres blamed the Houthis, calling the attack “a violation of international law.” The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis called the attack a “fully-fledged war crime” and vowed a strong response.

00:13 Houthi strikes on Riyadh airport kill 3 Saudi nationals 00:00 00:00

The renewed fighting has developed alongside the broader war involving Iran, with the Houthis stepping up attacks on Saudi territory as Saudi-backed forces battle the group inside Yemen. The latest violence follows the collapse of a truce in July and a renewed Saudi-backed offensive against Houthi positions.

The Houthis have expanded their operations along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the Bab el Mandeb strait, a critical shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Disruption there threatens international trade and energy shipments, raising fuel prices and adding another source of instability to global markets.

Trump has focused intensely on energy prices ahead of the midterm elections, including a diesel deal with the Kremlin that stunned Ukraine. But he has so far resisted deeper involvement in the Middle East.

After sweeping gains by Houthi forces last month, Trump said the group had contacted the U.S. to stress that they “don’t want to fight with us” and would “much prefer not having us involved.”

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman urged Trump in September to take military action against the Houthis, a person familiar with the matter told NBC News.

“There is a whole lot that America can deliver,” said Abdulkhaleq Abdulla, a retired professor of political science from the United Arab Emirates.

“It doesn’t have to be in the form of going all out against the Houthis, but American sharing of intelligence, America providing the best of defense systems against Houthis’ drones and missiles is needed, and I think if that is delivered, Saudi Arabia and the rest can defend themselves,” he said.

Abdulla also called on Turkey and Pakistan to come to Saudi Arabia’s defense. The three nations signed a joint defense agreement in Mecca in August, a pact of Sunni Muslim U.S. allies alarmed at growing regional conflict.

“Now it’s the time to activate what this alliance treaty involves,” added Abdulla. “That an attack on one is an attack against all.”

World.title: Pope Leo says he will undergo surgery to remove a nodule on his lung
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he will undergo surgery to remove an early-stage nodule on his lung.

The Vatican said the procedure was planned for this week.

“Recently, during some medical tests, doctors discovered a localized nodule in my lung,” the American pontiff, 71, said during his noon prayer at St. Peter’s Square.

“It was detected at a very early stage and is well localized,” Leo said from the window of the Apostolic Palace. “The doctors believe it is best to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to have it removed.”

The pontiff said that surgery had already been scheduled “for the coming days,” and thanked onlookers for their support.

“I entrust myself to your prayers,” he said.

The news drew applause from the thousands gathered in the square, before he wished the crowd a “happy Sunday.”

Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said in a statement that “the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week.”

Leo announced the surgery at the end of his regular address, in which he appealed for an end to the war in Ukraine and the safe transport of grain across the Black Sea.

“The daily bread of millions of people cannot be held hostage by war,” he said.

Leo has no previously known health problems and is known to be physically active, including weekly games of tennis.

The pontiff has a major trip scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November. It’s unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wished Leo well.

“I would like to express to the Holy Father my personal support, and that of the Italian government, as he faces this challenge in the coming days,” she said in a statement.

“The serenity and composure with which he spoke about it (today) ...are reassuring,” Meloni added.

Born Robert Francis Prevost, he became the first American pope when he was appointed in 2025.

Originally from the South Side of Chicago, he spent much of his career ministering in Peru and leading the Vatican’s powerful office of bishops.

Leo’s father, Louis Prevost, served in the Navy during World War II and worked as a superintendent of schools in the south suburbs of Chicago. His mother, Mildred Martinez Prevost, was a librarian with a master’s degree in education and two sisters who were nuns.

Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, died of a stroke last April at age 88 after a long hospitalization following a number of health issues.

World.title: Bracing for the midterms, Trump says he will be blamed if Republicans lose
World.content:
CLARKSVILLE, Tenn. — Even as he makes a case that Republicans should win the midterm congressional elections, President Donald Trump is bracing for the fallout should they lose.

Someone is bound to get blamed, and Trump said at a rally in Tennessee on Saturday that he expects it will be him.

“If we don’t win the midterms, they’re going to blame me,” Trump said. “You know that. And if we do win them, I will get no credit whatsoever. It’s true. I won’t get any.”

“But I’m working my ass off,” he added. “You better get out there and vote.”

Trump is in “grind it out mode” ahead of the midterms, a person familiar with the matter said, and is prepared for the worst-case election outcome.

Midterm elections often punish the sitting president’s party, and Trump’s popularity isn’t helping the GOP’s cause. Only 38% approve of his performance in office, compared with 59% who disapprove, according to an NBC News average of polls.

Trump is looking to defy historical trends by motivating core supporters who might be inclined to sit out the elections, and by offering voters an unusual sweetener if they preserve the Republican majority in the House and Senate.

He closed his hour-and-a-half-long speech with a reminder that “with your vote on Nov. 3, you’ll get $5,000.”

That’s the size of the payment he’s promising to send adults if Republicans win the midterms. The total price tag is estimated at $1.3 trillion.

Trump is indeed pushing himself as the elections approach, keeping up a frenetic schedule. Tennessee was the seventh state he has visited since the start of October. He had planned to fly to an eighth, Alabama, later in the day to attend the Georgia-Alabama football game, but canceled the trip with Hurricane Isaias bearing down.

Trump used part of the rally to debunk the idea that his popularity has dropped. In a social media post Saturday, he wrote that the notion that he’s in disfavor is a “false narrative.” Onstage, he played a CNN clip showing that his support among his MAGA supporters is nearly unanimous and has shown no slippage since the 2024 elections. (CNN was one of three news outlets that the Trump administration last month banned from White House grounds.)

“I’m very popular, I really am,” Trump told the crowd.

For Trump, traveling to a deep-red congressional district in a deep-red state like Tennessee might seem like time wasted in the few weeks left before the midterms. Republicans are expected to sweep the state’s House and Senate races.

Trump’s rally took place in an indoor arena in a northern Tennessee county that he won by 18 percentage points in the 2024 presidential race.

Trump himself suggested the state’s congressional candidates are already on a glide path to victory, with or without him.

“These guys are all going to win,” he said. “These congressmen are phenomenal. So, I’m saying, ‘What the hell am I doing in Tennessee?’”

Answering his own question, he said he wanted to “reward the places that have automatically treated you well.”

Trump won Tennessee in all three of his presidential campaigns.

Other Republicans said Trump is hewing to a sensible strategy: mobilizing his supporters and making sure they vote on Nov. 3 even though he’s not on the ballot.

“It rallies the base,” Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., said in an interview before Trump took the stage. “And that’s really what we’ve got to see in a midterm election. That’s what you’ve got to have: the base.”

Much of Trump’s address was a recitation of what he considers his chief accomplishments. He cited a rise in the median household income in his first year in office and a drop in the nation’s poverty rate.

Never shy about rebranding American landmarks, he also mused about renaming the Atlantic or Pacific oceans in ways that would ensure he’s not forgotten.

Presumably in jest, he said, “We call it, ‘Trump Ocean.’ Or, ‘Ocean of the Americas,’ something like that. No, we have to. We should have before I get out, I think we should have an ocean and we need a great river.”

World.title: One month into the NFL season, referees are the biggest story
World.content:
When New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel cursed out an official last week for a defensive holding penalty he described as a “terrible ... effing call,” it was hardly the first time he’d complained to that level.

“I’ve said that 87 times since I’ve been a head coach,” Vrabel said. “It was nothing derogatory.”

It earned Vrabel an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty all the same and led him to call the official “a little sensitive.”

Tension between officials and those who must abide by their rules has existed since sports began and is so commonplace as to go mostly unremarked. But five weeks into the new NFL season, that’s no longer the case. Rare public suspensions, numerous flags and rescinded fines have made those who set and enforce the rules as much of a discussion topic as the league’s more visible stars.

Games have averaged 15 penalties, the third-highest leaguewide average through Week 4 since the 1970 merger, according to research by NBC Sports. The number of total fouls called per game, 16.86, is down from the 17.44 that were called at the same point of last season, according to a league spokesman. That still is higher than the number of fouls called through Week 4 in 2024 (15.52), 2023 (15.34) and 2022 (14.38).

Penalties are only one reason officials are in the spotlight.

The NFL this week took the rare public step of announcing suspensions of two officials after line judge Jeff Seeman was shown on camera cursing multiple times toward Arizona tight end Trey McBride, leading to a two-game suspension. Referee Adrian Hill also was suspended, for one game, for his contentious reaction to Minnesota’s Eric Wilson after accidental contact knocked Hill to the ground. The NFL said the instances reflected “unprofessional conduct,” while the union that represents NFL officials vowed to challenge the discipline, calling it “excessive and inconsistent with past precedent.”

Coaches including Minnesota’s Kevin O’Connell and Arizona’s Mike LaFleur complimented the work of Seeman and Hill.

Seeman returns the challenge flag to New York Giants coach John Harbaugh during a game against the Arizona Cardinals in East Rutherford, N.J., on Sunday. Caleb Bowlin / Getty

“There’s a lot of verbal back-and-forth, or really one-way traffic, from the coaches, players to the officials, but we’ve always told the officials you cannot respond in kind,” former NFL referee Dean Blandino said this week.

Though the union disagreed with the level of punishment handed down, it did acknowledge that such verbal back-and-forth was not necessarily an outlier. In a statement, the referees’ union said it wanted to meet with the players’ union “to address on-field conduct and the growing levels of confrontation between players and officials.”

“It’s about time,” Super Bowl-winning former coach Bruce Arians said this week about the discipline. “You know, there’s finally some accountability in that department.”

The NFL does not exempt officials from accountability. It just rarely publicizes it. Referees’ performances are judged using internal grades for which high performers are rewarded with high-profile postseason assignments, while consistently low scorers can lose their jobs.

A new and more visible accountability measure exists, as well. As part of a new, seven-year collective bargaining agreement between the league and its referees that was established in May, the NFL has created a “bench” of referees who can step in for in-game switches.

“They’re going to start working this weekend,” Blandino said. “So if you have an underperforming official on a crew, that official will sit down and you’ll have a bench official that will come in like that backup, that No. 2, that will come in and work for them.”

Referee Alan Eck, center, and umpire Paul King, left, talk things over with Seeman, right, during a wild-card playoff game between the San Francisco 49ers and the Philadelphia Eagles in Philadelphia on Jan. 11. Chris Szagola / AP

The NFL this week also walked back fines — ranging from $8,847 to $14,926 — it had issued multiple players for celebrations the league initially said showed them imitating chugging a beer, which it deemed an offensive demonstration. In one case, San Francisco’s Kyle Juszczyk said he was imitating drinking from a juice box, a play on his last name’s pronunciation and his “Juice” nickname.

“Even if it was beer, I don’t think that should be a problem with all the beer endorsements that we have in the NFL,” Juszczyk told reporters after the fine was issued. “We have everything. So even if it was beer, which it wasn’t, I still felt like it wasn’t an infraction.”

Confusion about what celebrations are allowed and which are not led the league and its players union this week to issue a joint statement clarifying the line that should not be crossed. Violations include gestures that are sexual or depict smoking, violence and using drugs, gang-related signs or weapons.

“Conversely, recent celebrations imitating drinking a beverage will not be considered violations or result in discipline,” the joint statement read. It added that “individual and team celebrations are part of the game.”

So, too, this season is the focus on the flags and the officials who throw them.

World.title: Justice Department investigating major TV networks over suspending pool coverage of Trump
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department said it is investigating five major TV broadcast networks for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of President Donald Trump, a department spokesperson said.

The investigation into the networks that make up the White House TV press pool — NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — is underway, and the department sent out “civil investigative demands” on Friday, according to a Justice Department official.

“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” department spokeswoman Emily Covington said Saturday.

The pool is a rotating group of networks that share the duties of recording the president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The network performing pool duty then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets.

The New York Times first reported the investigation.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

ABC News said it has not received any notification from the Justice Department but expects to. Representatives for NBC, CBS and CNN declined to comment. Fox did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The investigation appears to be the latest move from the White House in its escalating feud against the press corps.

Last month, Trump barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds, citing what he said was “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” The other networks in the TV pool briefly declined to participate in pool duties after CNN was removed from its spot in the rotation.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued to block the ban, claiming it was a violation of the First Amendment. They were reinstated about a week later after a judge ruled that the administration had to temporarily restore their access for 14 days. A federal judge this week extended the order to Tuesday.

The five major networks released a joint statement at the time, saying: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”

The pool system has been recognized by administrations from both parties for decades, and the coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which include outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets.

During the time the outlets declined to provide pool coverage, individual TV networks, including NBC News, continued to provide coverage of White House events that were open to the press, outside of the pool.

Bruce D. Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, said in a statement that the First Amendment protects the decisions news organizations make about coverage and called the investigation “another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists.”

Kelly O’Donnell reported from Washington, and Marlene Lenthang from Los Angeles.

World.title: In new Elon Musk documentary, his lieutenants are the most damning voices
World.content:
SAN RAFAEL, Calif. — It’s easy to find people with bad things to say about tech magnate Elon Musk, and plenty of those people show up in “Musk,” a new documentary about his rise to political and corporate power. What’s more surprising in the film are the unflattering statements by some of his own employees, including ones who still work for him.

Some of the harshest scenes in the film, which opens Friday in Los Angeles and New York, are ones in which Musk’s lieutenants were recorded on video or in audio as they wielded power on his behalf or discussed what they had already done for him.

Warning: This article includes spoilers for the documentary “Musk.”

There are clips of Ashok Elluswamy, a high-ranking Tesla engineer, acknowledging in a videotaped deposition that an infamous hype video he helped put together in 2016 about the company’s self-driving capabilities was not an accurate representation of Tesla’s technology at the time.

There are also audio snippets from Jared Birchall, who handles Musk’s personal matters. He is heard on a recording of a phone call with online influencer Ashley St. Clair, shortly after she had given birth to a child she and Musk conceived, in which he plays hardball on child support arrangements.

Both incidents were documented in the media: Reuters reported in 2023 on the transcript of Elluswamy’s deposition, and The Wall Street Journal reported last year on Birchall’s phone call with St. Clair.

But the video and the audio appear to be newly public, giving the documentary a mix of voices beyond the usual critics and creating moments of surprise even for a viewer who is familiar with the ins and outs of Musk’s complicated story.

Filmmaker Alex Gibney says in the documentary that he and his team spent more than three years researching Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, pulling together not only archival interviews and hard-to-find footage but also a database of quotes from Musk that are peppered throughout the film.

Musk, 55, did not participate in the documentary, and he has panned it, saying on X that it is a “hit piece” and that Gibney has “zero integrity.” Musk, Tesla, SpaceX, Elluswamy and Birchall did not respond to requests for comment.

The nearly four-hour film is a comprehensive tour through Musk’s life story, with deep dives into the growth of SpaceX and Tesla, his fathering of 14 known children and his on-again, off-again alliance with President Donald Trump, including his becoming the biggest donor to Trump’s 2024 campaign.

The film is a reminder of how often Musk has put himself at the center of public discourse and pop culture, and it moves swiftly through the highlights and lowlights: from his 2021 hosting gig on “Saturday Night Live” and his chaotic purchase of Twitter the next year to his Grok chatbot’s embracing the identity “MechaHitler” and his wielding of a chain saw early in Trump’s second term.

“I like to call it a ‘svelte’ four-hour film,” producer Jessie Deeter said at a screening Wednesday at the Mill Valley Film Festival in Marin County, California. (The film has a 10-minute intermission, but it is still roughly the length of the 1962 epic “Lawrence of Arabia.”)

At the screening, which was about 90% full, the biggest applause came during a moment of anti-Musk defiance, as a former career federal employee explained why they quit the Trump administration last year rather than cooperate with Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency.

The film lands at another potentially pivotal moment for Musk, amid speculation that Democrats may investigate him if they take control of Congress after the midterm elections. Polling shows that Musk remains deeply divisive, with a majority of Americans holding unfavorable views of him even as Trump honored him at the White House on Thursday.

The documentary demonstrates that Musk’s dabbling in politics is nothing new: Archival videos show that, years before he endorsed Trump in 2024, Musk was rubbing elbows with politicians such as former California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, and the late Sen. Dianne Feinstein, D-Calif., and getting benefits in return, such as low-emission credits for Tesla.

Part of what drives the documentary forward is how it crosses genres: Parts of it feel like a political thriller or a legal whodunit, while others are like a video game simulation, a science fiction fantasy or a celebrity tabloid drama.

Other moments are closer to a horror film, especially as Gibney narrates some of the graphic details of collisions involving Tesla’s driver-assistance software. He includes, for example, dashcam video from a 2019 crash in which a Tesla on “Autopilot” ran a stop sign in Florida and killed a pedestrian — a crash for which a jury found Tesla 33% at fault and ordered it to pay $243 million in damages.

One of the people interviewed in the film, science fiction author and tech activist Cory Doctorow, adds to the grim feeling by wearing a guillotine pin on his lapel.

Later, the documentary lingers again on death, as Gibney tries to tally the human cost of Musk’s drive last year to dismantle the U.S. Agency for International Development. Between shots of malnourished children in Africa and elsewhere, Samantha Power, who was a USAID administrator during the Biden administration, says the cuts froze some food programs for the world’s poor and blames the cuts for 14 million potential deaths. (The number is based on a projection published last year estimating possible deaths over the following five years.)

In the film’s rendering, the horror of those statistics and images stands in stark contrast with Musk’s ongoing obsession: traveling deeper into space, including to Mars, for the potential benefit of future, unborn generations.

A few parts of the film are presented without evidence or explanation. Gibney boosts a conspiracy theory that Musk used his Starlink constellation of internet satellites to meddle in the 2024 election — an unfounded idea that independent fact-checkers have long criticized. He also raises concerns about potential data collection by Starlink satellites and by Tesla vehicles but does not go beyond vague theories.

A more pressing question the film wrestles with is whether or how much Musk has changed over his years in the public spotlight. The film repeatedly shows a younger Musk who is not only physically different, with thinner hair and a slighter build, but also speaking about different issues from those he addresses now — including “oil addiction,” an old motivation behind growing Tesla.

Another of Musk’s associates, former SpaceX engineer Jim Cantrell, says in the film that Musk has changed less than some people may imagine.

“Success has allowed him to take the lid off what he’s really thinking,” he says.

World.title: Food pantries overwhelmed by Trump cuts
World.content:
“There’s a decent chance we could run out,” said Likens, who runs the food pantry in Dunlow as director of community outreach for Cabwaylingo Presbyterian Chapel, a small brick church he attended growing up.

“I don’t want them to sit in that line and not get anything,” he said. “But I don’t have a lot of extra food these days.”

Increasingly, the job of feeding the nation’s hungry is falling on the shoulders of everyday Americans like Likens, who have become the last bulwark against hunger in a land of plenty.

Likens and others on the front lines of feeding their neighbors say they face unprecedented challenges brought on by Washington. Food distribution programs are getting less food from federal programs to feed the hungry after cuts by the Trump administration. At the same time, restrictions on food stamps from the Republicans’ “big, beautiful bill” have driven up demand, while rising gas prices because of the Iran war have cut into the budgets of households and food banks alike.

Bill Likens, director of community outreach for Cabwaylingo Presbyterian Chapel, grew up hungry in Dunlow. Now he works to make sure that doesn't happen to other kids. Mike Belleme for NBC News

The challenges extend far beyond Appalachia. An NBC News survey of 48 of the largest food banks across 35 states and Washington, D.C., found that nearly three-quarters said more people are showing up at their doors over the past year, from workers on their lunch breaks to older adults overwhelmed with medical expenses. At the same time, more than 80% said the food and funding they received through the U.S. Department of Agriculture had dropped and they were struggling with higher fuel costs for transporting food.

In Maine, Good Shepherd Food Bank said the USDA cut the amount of food it received from 13 million pounds to 9 million pounds in one year. A Michigan food bank, Forgotten Harvest, said it’s handing out less food to make sure there is enough to go around: one bag of potatoes instead of two, two tubs of yogurt as opposed to six.

“People are facing multiple hits to their budgets,” said Poonam Gupta, a senior research associate at the Urban Institute, a think tank that researches social and economic issues. “It is really difficult to find a way to continue affording a healthy and nutritious and balanced diet when you just have these constant hits.”

Food banks’ struggles started in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term when officials cut a $400 million Covid-era program to supply food banks with food from local farmers and paused an estimated $500 million in other planned food purchases by the USDA. Funding from Congress for a separate decades-old program to supply food banks with emergency food assistance has increased over the past several years, but many food bank leaders said they’re still getting less overall than during the Biden administration.

We want to hear from you Have you been affected by changes to the SNAP/food stamp program? Share your story here.

Trump also signed into law the new restrictions on who can receive Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, or food stamps, requiring nearly all able-bodied adults not caring for young children to work, volunteer or go to school at least 80 hours a month. Since the law was enacted, more than 5 million people, including at least 1 million children, have lost their food benefits.

White House spokesperson Anna Kelly defended the administration’s policies, saying Trump is “uplifting every American’s financial situation” through tax cuts and efforts to increase jobs and business investments.

“President Trump is strengthening SNAP for the Americans who need it by ensuring these programs are sustainable for future generations,” Kelly said, including measures to “crack down on waste, fraud and abuse.”

World.title: Transcript: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 11, 2026
World.content:
The following is the transcript of the interview with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 11, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation. We've got a lot of politics ahead, but we want to start with a quick update on the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias, which made landfall Friday night and resulted in the deaths of four people. For that update, we turn to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Good morning to you, Mr. Secretary. This is the first Atlantic hurricane of the year. Hundreds of thousands of people left without power. I know the president approves some federal support. What is needed?

SECRETARY OF HOMELAND SECURITY MARKWAYNE MULLIN: Well, we were in touch with the- with all the governors that are affected and might be affected by the continuing storm moving across the nation. The president has been very involved in this from the get-go. Cam Hamilton, who is our director of FEMA, we started pre-positioning assets into every state and working closely with their emergency responders. Right now, from the conversation I've had with each governor, they're in good shape. We're- we have good partnership. What's interesting about this area is they're- while they may not have been hit with storms real bad the last two years, they work really, really good together. When I was talking to Governor Kemp from, you know, from Georgia, he was talking about his relationship with Ron DeSantis. When we're dealing with the other governors, they were talking about how they're cooperating with sending assets to the areas that are affected without power to get the- the power restored. FEMA is standing by responding with- with life-saving responses. The Coast Guard is out in the inner waters and the Mississippi, the mouth of Mississippi, out in the- our shores, and we are still doing some boat rescues, but really it's more recovery of the boats, not of the individuals. So we're working together well as a team. We were, you know, you never can be fully prepared for- for a storm like this, but I can tell you that the coordination from- from the Oval Office with President Trump's leadership to the- to the governors to the county first responders, we're all working very closely together.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, we hope everyone in that pathway is safe. I want to ask you about something else on the enforcement side of things. There have been at least 30 DHS officer-involved shootings under the Trump administration, according to CBS's tally of events here. There was this incident last week in New York City, and the NYPD did release security video that shows a man dressed as a civilian with a gun drawn approaching a car and then punching in the window. I know you have said there were other DHS ICE officers in the area who were put at risk by the driver, but just to clarify events, when are you going to release the body cameras worn by those officers?

SEC. MULLIN: Well, Margaret, what you're seeing is a pole cam. What you're not seeing is actual- the audio footage or a different angle where you have multiple officers that are actually approaching this- this individual named Oscar with a long, very long, extensive rap sheet. He's only been in the country for- for three years, and he has a rap sheet of four charges of felony robbery, two charges of felony assault, felony larceny, misdemeanor assault, possession of- of weapons, possession of stolen property, two felony charges of drugless- of dangerous drugs, and strong gang affiliation that- that has direct or indirect knowledge of- of a CBP officer that was shot last year. And this guy evaded officers last month when we tried to get to him. We knew he was armed. We knew he was dangerous. We knew, or there was a possibility in being armed. We knew he was dangerous, and we knew he was going to evade. So when we approached his vehicle, we were giving lawful commands. We had approached him just like any other undercover agency that's out there, from local, state, federal, or- or county that has undercover officers. We had our badges out. Once again, giving lawful demands. He decided that he was going to accelerate and try to evade again. We had taken every precaution to try to keep that from happening, and- and unfortunately, this took place. We would have loved for him to exit the vehicle like we asked him to. He decided not to, and unfortunately, because of the selfish behavior, he put his five-year-old at danger. But as far as--

(CROSSTALK)

MARGARET BRENNAN: You said they were wearing body cameras. Will–

SEC. MULLIN:--the information being released--

MARGARET BRENNAN: When will you release that footage?

(END CROSSTALK)

SEC. MULLIN: As far- Margaret, as far as the information being released, FBI and HSI is going to do the investigation. Continue to do the investigation. When it's completed, we'll release all the information.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay. There was that five-year-old you just mentioned. Given that rap sheet and how long you'd been monitoring, how come those officers didn't notice that a child was put in that car?

SEC. MULLIN: Well, what- our understanding is- is he drove into the neighborhood. We knew his pattern of life, but we didn't know the five-year-old was in the vehicle. Who did know who the five- who was in the vehicle was Oscar. Now, as a father of six individuals, or six kids I mean, no way would I ever put my kids in danger. If I was getting lawful commands- and he knew he was being sought after. He knew the police was looking for him because, like I said, he just evaded a month ago. I would have immediately got out of my vehicle to protect my- my- my child. There's no way I would have been selfish enough to put my child in danger, he was absolutely selfish enough to put his child in danger. He's the one that decided to accelerate and- and ram into another vehicle with his five-year-old in the vehicle, and then tried to accelerate towards other police officers. That's- that is that tells you the type of character that Oscar is, and yet somehow the mayor is out there protesting about this, but yet seven days ago, when NYPD officer got stabbed in the same neighborhood by- by criminals that they released, by the way, Oscar had been released multiple times back onto the streets. Not one time did the governor, not one time did the mayor have a press conference or talk about--

(CROSSTALK)

MARGARET BRENNAN: They did release a statement and visit the officer in the hospital.

SEC. MULLIN: --how awful it was that these criminals are stabbing NYPD officers.

(END CROSSTALK)

SEC. MULLIN: That's right.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But I think we're all thankful, as I'm sure you are, that that five-year-old was not harmed. Let me ask you about something--

SEC. MULLIN: -- Absolutely--

MARGARET BRENNAN: -- about this, though. Okay, let me ask you--

SEC. MULLIN: -- It's frustrating, though, Margaret, because this guy should have never been on the streets because we had asked- we had had a detainer on him and asked the New York City to hand him over to us when they had him on in- in their possession, he was on probation. He's an illegal. He should have never been on the streets to begin with.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Let me ask you about another concern. Secretary Hegseth said that he plans to livestream the upcoming execution by firing squad of convicted murderer Nidal Hassan, who killed 13 service members in 2009. Hassan's in a wheelchair. Doesn't the administration risk livestreaming this and making him a martyr to his cause? Couldn't this be a risk to the homeland?

SEC. MULLIN: First of all, no one- no one has to watch it--

MARGARET BRENNAN: -- Well then why are you livestreaming it?--

SEC. MULLIN: -- But for me to have sympathy for anybody that killed 13 service members and a scumbag like this, it's a psycho who was supposed to be a psychiatrist--

MARGARET BRENNAN: -- I'm not asking about him. I'm asking about the livestreaming and the risk that could be created by it.

SEC. MULLIN: Listen, once again, no one has to watch it if they don't choose to--

MARGARET BRENNAN: -- Why livestream it?--

SEC. MULLIN: -- I follow President Trump. He's a commander- he's a commander in- in chief of the- of the country, and he does a phenomenal job. He leads this country with a very, very, very direct, forward, straight hand, and he's restoring America values and bringing us and bringing- where America should be back in line--

MARGARET BRENNAN: -- Your Republican colleagues Lisa Murkowski and Kevin Cramer have both said that this provides exactly what terrorists crave, an audience. It risks martyrdom. Have you weighed the risk here of radicalization of just creating a risk?

SEC. MULLIN: Margaret, we weigh- we weigh the risk every single day in this country. The Department of Homeland Security, that's what we do: is we protect the homeland. But I don't see an elevated risk at this point at all because of this. I think people need to understand if you attack- if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the- that the punishment fits the crime. And in this case, he killed 13 individuals on Fort Hood. I have no sympathy for him, and I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies. My job as Secretary of Homeland Security is to protect the homeland, and that's what we do. And all 270,000 employees we do that work in DHS do every single day.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes, that's why I was asking about the homeland. I want to ask you about another issue. Money that was allocated by Congress to Customs and Border Protection was used to purchase roughly $20 million in ads that have run on networks. One of the ads will be on this program as well. It's touting President Trump's accomplishments and also him personally. There has been outcry from some Republican senators, including on this program last week. The president has since said his political action committee will pay for future ads. That's taken care of. Okay. What about the past spending? Will U.S. taxpayers be reimbursed for the money that was spent on this?

SEC. MULLIN: Anytime we can do a public service announcement and brag about America, I'm all about it. You have so much negative media that's out there by fake media that's constantly controversy. That if it bleeds, it leads. I think 99% of the coverage on President Trump is negative. The majority of it is negative about our country and supposedly the direction that we're headed--

MARGARET BRENNAN: -- So no reimbursement of the $20 million?--

SEC. MULLIN: --But yet, murder rates are down to 126-year low. We have- we have most secure borders in probably our nation's history, fentanyl- fentanyl deaths are dropping. Drug seizures are dropping every- or drug apprehension is- is- is gaining speed every single day, and we should be bragging about what's happening inside America. I- I commend the opportunity to have the- I commend the opportunity. Of President Trump to give us the opportunity to brag about America.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, so no reimbursement. Secretary Mullin, thank you.

World.title: Billy Crystal on finding humor in the darkest of times
World.content:
If Billy Crystal is one of the kings of comedy, his family home in L.A.'s Pacific Palisades neighborhood was definitely his castle. "Sunday Morning" was invited there a few times for interviews, and I'd usually end up getting schooled on his backyard basketball court.

It was, he acknowledged, a magical place: "Yeah, it kept me young, that place," he said.

Correspondent Tracy Smith and Billy Crystal shooting hoops at the comedian's home in 2021. CBS News

It was his family's forever home, but things don't always last forever. In January 2025, a massive, wind-driven inferno tore through the Crystals' Pacific Palisades neighborhood, devouring more than 5,000 homes, including the Crystals'. The fire took everything, but in the smoldering ruins of what was once their family home, Billy Crystal and his wife Janice found inspiration.

Crystal is taking the story of his home, and his life, to Broadway, in his new one-person show, "860," talking about what he lost, and what he learned.

"Oh God, what a morning. Helicopters and sirens woke us up to the news that there was a big brush fire in the Highlands."

He describes the disaster moment by moment, and it's a harrowing tale. But he's still Billy Crystal.

"Janice is the more practical of the two of us. She's thinking about medicines and prescriptions. I'm thinking about that half a veal parmesan sandwich that's in the refrigerator."

"860" is now in previews, and opens October 21. Crystal wanted the audience to feel like they're really inside his house, so the "860" set is an exact replica of his home office, with everything just as it was. "Yes, we're fortunate to have this and have that, but that doesn't take away the hurt. That doesn't take away the loss," he said.

Smith and Crystal on the stage set of his one-man Broadway show, "860." CBS News

According to Crystal, nothing survived.

But there are some things that no fire could ever touch. The memories are all intact, and funny as ever.

The name of the show, "860," is actually the street address of the house he lost. Truth is, Crystal wasn't sure what to call it, until his dear friend Rob Reiner weighed in. "He said, 'What are you going to call it?' I had these other titles, and the third one was '860.' He went, 'That's the one. I love that. I like that.'"

And then, in a year that was already traumatic beyond belief, the unimaginable happened, In December 2025, Rob Reiner and his wife Michelle were killed in their home. For Crystal, it's all still too hard to process: "No, it's too big," he said. "It's so insane, because we were together the night before. We said goodbye, like, late that night, 10:30 or something, at the party we were at together for the holidays, and then … what?!?"

But Crystal has found a way to process his grief, and maybe ours, too, sharing stories and laughter.

Asked how he can find humor in the darkest of times, Crystal laughed, "That's what I do! You have to, man. You got to, you got to … It's a healer. It always has been that way. You know, we say when life gets tough, all you can do is laugh."

Billy Crystal in the Broadway show "860." CBS News

Twenty-two years ago, Crystal did another one-man show: "700 Sundays," named for the approximately 700 Sundays he had with his father before he died. It was a major hit, and a ticket to a Tony Award. And for Crystal, it was a cathartic experience, which he said healed him. Asked if he thinks "860" will as well, Crystal replied, "It already has, 'cause I'm doing it, and I've been doing it. If I didn't get to perform it even, I'm OK. I've absorbed the biggest pains that people couldn't go through, the loss of home, dearest of friends. And I'm OK."

Still, he says the body blows of 2025 have changed his outlook a bit.

In "700 Sundays," he describes conversations with God. Asked if he has been talking to God over these past couple of years," he said, "No, 'cause I don't trust Him. Too many bad things have happened. The Earth is in bad shape. This is a weird, scary time. So no, not anymore."

Billy Crystal, star of the one-man Broadway show "860." CBS News

"860" is a one-man show, but Crystal leaned on some Broadway heavyweights to bring it all to life: director Scott Ellis, and legendary composer Marc Shaiman, who remarked on Crystal's ability to extract humor from dark memories. "He can't help but find the humor," Shaiman said. "That's just who Billy is, and that's why he is who he is."

"But it is family," added Ellis. "That's the thing that is the core of it, is how do you move forward? You move forward with friends and you move forward with family. And that's what you want and need, and he's lucky to have it. Not a lot of people do."

CBS News

The show is in a limited run in New York just until January. After that, Crystal says he hopes to bring it to the city where it all happened, Los Angeles.

The house might be gone, but the heart that built it is still there, strong as ever. "I'm 78 now, and I feel really good," he said, "and I'm optimistic for what life is going to bring. And if we've gotten through this in the way that we've gotten through it, we're doing OK."

World.title: Zelenskyy claps back after Trump calls for new Ukrainian president
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday vowed to continue striking Russian oil refineries, pushing back against recent comments from President Trump, who took aim at Zelenskyy's leadership.

After Mr. Trump suggested Zelenskyy should be replaced and blamed him for high diesel prices, the Ukrainian president said Russia alone was responsible for the war in Ukraine.

"Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure," Zelenskyy wrote on X.

"It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not want to do so," he said, adding that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees.

The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company's facilities in four days. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion.

Speaking to ABC News' "This Week" on Sunday morning, Zelenskyy said Ukrainians "want peace."

"About energy, I said it to President Trump ... to his team and to his people several times. We want peace," Zelenskyy said. "We are ready for ceasefire. We are ready to begin from any kind of steps of de-escalation."

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has also pushed back on Mr. Trump's comments, writing on X late Saturday that Zelenskyy was leading the country through a war for its independence.

"He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well," Sybiha wrote.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks to the media after a German-Ukrainian business forum in Kyiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. AP Photo/Dan Bashakov

Mr. Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.

"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Mr. Trump said.

According to an announcement from Mr. Trump on Friday, the U.S. has made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy more than 300,000 tons of diesel from Russia right away, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons after that. Amid the deal, which attempts to address high fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, Mr. Trump has also urged Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy criticized the deal and said it would help fund Russia's war in Ukraine.



Mr. Trump has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war effort.

The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.

"As a result of the drone attack, the infrastructure of Yandex's data center in Vladimir was damaged. Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries," said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which provides operational updates on service availability.

A Yandex food delivery courier rides his scooter in Moscow, Russia, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. AP Photo/Alexander Zemlianichenko

In Moscow, residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and that on several rides he had to cancel after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger.

"I'd press the 'call' button to contact them, but nothing happens," he said. "There's nothing I can do, so I'm just forced to cancel."

Igor Mann said he went to check the status of an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a VPN did not help. "Nothing worked," he said.

Another Moscow resident, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had "direct impact" and weren't just about "convenience."

"It's also about work," he said, adding that they also affected "healthcare, and everything else."

On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. A day later, Ukrainian drones hit the company's major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, partly putting it out of action, Yandex said.

Yandex, often described as Russia's Google, runs the country's most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia's artificial intelligence development.

Elsewhere, Zelenskyy said search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday.

Zelenskyy said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, eight of whom remain hospitalized.

A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday.

World.title: Steve Bannon on the GOP and the midterms: "We can't afford to lose"
World.content:
There he was, in February 2017, on the cover of Time Magazine: Steve Bannon, chief White House strategist. They called him "The Great Manipulator." He threatened at times to overshadow the president himself – not the best career move – and for a while he visibly fell out of favor.

Steven Bannon, dubbed "The Great Manipulator" less than one month into President Trump's first term. Time Magazine

To this day, though, Bannon remains a passionate Trump supporter. "When Trump decides to leave the stage actively, he can't be replaced," he said. "Like Washington or Lincoln, these are people that they name the age of."

Yes, Bannon mentions Trump in the same breath as Washington and Lincoln. "Oh, I am," he said. "I think he's at that level. Because I think General Washington was there at the birth of the nation; Lincoln was the rebirth of the nation; and I absolutely believe (and I think 99% of MAGA believes) that Trump was there for the salvation of the nation."

Bannon is a man of unwavering commitment. He did four months in prison for contempt of Congress, for refusing to testify about his role in the events leading up to the January 6 assault on the U.S. Capitol (including telling podcast listeners on Jan. 5, 2021, "All hell is going to break loose tomorrow").

He set up an influential podcast, "War Room": Two hours in the morning, two hours in the evening. It was in his studio where, on September 29, we sat down for an interview.

Bannon clearly has a taste for the right wing. "Definitely, it's no doubt," he said. "I am right wing; I'm not conservative. I'm a right-winger and proud of it."

The Great Manipulator is, by most accounts, once again in regular and amicable communication with the president. But Bannon has no illusions. If Democrats gain control of the House in a couple of weeks, the "Age of MAGA" is in jeopardy. On his podcast he announced, "If we lose the House, it's going to turn the White House into Fort Apache."

Bannon told us what he sees as the repercussions of a Democratic victory: "I think you'll see Bobby Kennedy impeached, I'll think you see Pete Hegseth impeached. I think you'll see subpoenas flying every day. They will look to destroy President Trump, and we'll be bogged down for two years."

He believes that is a compelling argument to vote Republican this year – though polls show it may not be so compelling to the majority of American voters. "But you don't need the majority," Bannon argues. "Here's my point on the midterm: Remember, midterm elections are always driven by base getting out, and the base's ability to get more of their low-propensity voters out."

Bannon has few, if any, illusions about the agenda of old-line Republicans who are "all set for getting beyond Trump." But he disagrees that his own future lies beyond Trumpism. "First off, President Trump, I would say I'm the leader of trying to get President Trump to run for a third term," Bannon said. "It appears that he's not interested or it just won't happen."

He does not admit that the idea of a third term for Mr. Trump runs counter to the 22nd Amendment of the Constitution limiting a president to two terms. "Oh, I think you could drive a truck through that amendment," he said. "I talked to constitutional lawyers, and there were, I think, a number of different alternatives. Would it be contested? Yeah, it'd be contested, because everything [Trump] does is contested in the courts."

The war with Iran

The president is also confronting the same nemesis as his predecessor: old age. But Bannon does not see President Trump, who turned 80 this year, as having lost a step or two. "Oh, I don't agree with that," he said, claiming that the president works 20 hours a day. Nor does he dismiss the president's rambling speeches (such as his recent suggestion that Iran "take out" Los Angeles or San Diego).

"I would not call them 'drivel,'" Bannon said. "President Trump has been known to go off-script."

Steve Bannon. CBS News

Any suggestion that Americans are embarrassed by Mr. Trump leads Bannon to draw accusations of media bias. "Ted, if you're part of the media elite, if you're a part of the East Coast elite, if you a Atlanticist, what President Trump has done, yes, you're not going to like it and probably you're going to hate it," he said. "I understand this war is a huge issue. But I think working-class Americans are not embarrassed. They're supportive of President Trump and how he presents the United States."

Despite polls that show a majority of Americans oppose the war with Iran, Bannon said, "Let's bifurcate the war. If you look at the first part, the 12-day war, and President Trump, the total obliteration of their nuclear program …"

Interrupted with the knowledge that Iran's nuclear capabilities have not been "totally" obliterated, Bannon replied, "I believe it's obliterated enough. What we're doing is tearing down their economy through economic warfare of Scott Bessant, given what he's doing with their currency, given the blockade on the oil."

The power of film

Interviewing Steve Bannon still offers the occasional surprise. If the Democratic Socialists sometimes offer positions that make more traditional Democratic candidate wince, count on Bannon to find hidden advantage for Republicans, while seeming to praise the opposition. "These people are very focused," he said. "Some of the candidates may stay way outside the mainstream, but they have a ground game that people have to understand that they have dedicated people and they're going to turn out their vote."

Bannon reminded me that he got into politics making films for the Tea Party: "I had a very particular take on it," he said. "It was very populist, very nationalistic. Critics came and said, 'Hey, this is fascist filmmaking.' And I said, 'Look, Leni Riefenstahl was one of the most powerful filmmakers ever.'"

Indeed, she was. Riefenstahl made the Nazis look mythical. Her coverage of military parades and the Berlin Olympics of 1936, in films such as "Triumph of the Will," has influenced filmmakers for decades, among them Bannon. In Alison Klayman's 2019 documentary "The Brink," Bannon was heard asking, "What would Leni Riefenstahl do? How would Leni cut that scene?

But most of all, Riefenstahl was known as Hitler's image-maker. "She was amoral, and she was a filmmaker for the Nazis, but her films were very powerful," said Bannon. "And what I was trying to do is to try to recreate the power of those films to make sure that people, particularly the little guy, understood that they could have a voice."

Over the past nine years Steve Bannon has cultivated ties with far-right movements across Europe. In March 2018, he spoke before the French National Front party's annual congress, telling Marine Le Pen and her followers, "You're part of a worldwide movement that is bigger than France, bigger than Italy, bigger than Hungary, bigger than all of it."

He is also close to Germany's fiercely anti-immigrant party, the AfD, which recently won a state election in a landslide. "Alternative for Deutschland is now here to teach us," he said. "They went to ground, and what they did is they went door-to-door, and they convinced people with no campaign money, that our way, our policies is to re-industrialize Germany, stop this mass immigration, re-migration, are policies you should vote for. I think we can learn a lot from them.

A question of fascism

Asked if the United States is moving toward fascism today, Bannon replied, "It's not fascism. It's actually more inclusionary, it's more entrepreneurial. It's not fascism at all. Remember if you go back, we win at the ballot box. The MAGA movement has only lost the Pelosi election of '18. The core belief of the MAGA movement is we won the 2020 election."

Except President Trump lost the 2020 election. "That's not true. We won!" Bannon exclaimed.

Actually, Joe Biden won. "It's not true," Bannon contested.

"War Room" host Steve Bannon with "Sunday Morning" senior contributor Ted Koppel. CBS News

When faced with more than 60 court cases, all of which Mr. Trump lost while alleging election fraud, Bannon replied, "We can go debate this another time, but we didn't have standing. We never even got into court."

Bannon's technically correct; they didn't have standing. They couldn't find a judge who thought they had a significant case worth hearing. So, for six years they've just kept saying the same thing over and over.

But with the midterms upon us, Bannon was asked how he would bet on the outcome. "I would push all our chips in the middle of the table and say, 'Guys, there's no retreat, and there's no substitute for victory. Let's fight like hell,'" he said.

Is he suggesting that Republicans can't afford to lose? "Oh, we can't afford to lose. I don't think there's any doubt about that," he said – affirming that he will do whatever it takes to win the fight. "Exactly."

World.title: Pope Leo XIV to undergo lung surgery this week
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV to undergo lung surgery this week

toggle caption i Gregorio Borgia/AP

Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he would have surgery this week to remove a "localized nodule" in his lung.

Leo said the nodule was found at a "very early stage" with doctors recommending surgery.

"Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it," Leo said during his weekly Sunday noon blessing in St. Peter's Square.

The surgery is due to occur at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, which is the primary location for popes to receive medical attention.

Leo has had no known previous health problems.

"I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers," Leo said to the crowds on Sunday.

According to the American Cancer Society, a lung nodule is a small abnormal area, less than or equal to 3 cm, found during a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. These tests are often conducted as routine screenings for "trauma, heart disease, non-cancer related lung disease, or lung infection."

Sponsor Message

Most lung nodules are benign. The American Cancer Society said these nodules are "more often the result of old infections, scar tissue, or other causes" and that tests are needed to confirm it is not cancerous. He later posted the message about his surgery on social media.

The Vatican did not disclose whether the nodule was cancerous.

Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said in a statement that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week."

Leo's next major international trip is scheduled for early November to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear if the surgery would affect his travels.

During his papacy, Leo has been outspoken about peace throughout the world. He spent part of his Sunday address renewing calls for peace in Ukraine.

"I make a heartfelt appeal to the parties to the conflict to allow the safe transport of grain across the Black Sea," Leo said. "The daily bread of millions of people cannot be held hostage by war."

On Saturday, the Pope also called for the death penalty to be abolished, saying on X that it is "inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person."

Sponsor Message

"The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption," Leo said.

World.title: Hurricane Simon nears Mexico with 155 mph winds and flooding fears
World.content:
Hurricane Simon nears Mexico with 155 mph winds and flooding fears

toggle caption i Fernando Llano/AP

PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico — The eye of Hurricane Simon was just off the Pacific coast of Mexico early Sunday and was expected to move inland later in the day as an extremely powerful storm.

Simon has strengthened to 155 mph (250 kph), only just below the threshold for becoming a Category 5 storm, the highest on the Saffir Simpson scale. It was about 60 miles (100 kilometers) west-southwest of Manzanilla and moving north-northwest at 6 mph (9 kph).

The hurricane could bring 10 to 20 inches (25-50 cm) of rain over parts of southwestern Mexico, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 30 inches (76 centimeters).

Sponsor Message

"This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the center warned.

Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas. It also asked the tourism sector in Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for U.S. tourists, to ensure that both workers and visitors were fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.

Convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows Saturday, and few were walking the streets under overcast skies.

"Let's hope it doesn't hit us, right? That it doesn't affect us," Jesús Gómez said as he stood outside a shop and handed out free samples of candied peanuts to passersby. "We'll be working as usual throughout the day, but when Civil Protection officials come and tell us we need to close, then we'll close and take shelter until the storm passes."

The hurricane center expected a dangerous storm surge along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall. The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.

Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who along with his wife still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.

Sponsor Message

"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do. "I just don't know what to expect."

World.title: Don't be scared: Being afraid is outright fun, and maybe useful
World.content:
Don't be scared: Being afraid is outright fun, and maybe useful

toggle caption i Ryan Benk/NPR News

It's October and that can only mean one thing – the spooky season is in full swing.

Americans are expected to spend more than $13 billion dollars on celebrating this season, whether that's on horror films, costumes, candy or attractions, according to the National Retail Federation.

As much as $300 - $500 million of that spending comes from attending a haunt, where people willingly give up their hard-earned cash to be frightened. And tens of millions of people take part in this kind of activity every year.

But why do people like getting scared? The search for that answer starts with one of the largest haunted attractions in the country, Markoff's Haunted Forest in Dickerson, Maryland. Markoff's has more than a mile of haunted trails and dozens of themed haunted houses. It employs hundreds of engineers, retail attendants, makeup artists and actors.

Sponsor Message

Open since 1992, the attraction starts with towering skull-emblazoned wooden gates reminiscent of folk horror movies like "The Wicker Man."

Just inside, director of operations Paul Brubacher stands in between two huge bonfires.

"Some of our designers, including myself, have done some music festivals before. So yeah, that's the inspiration… from kind-of [a] Van Helsing vampire village aspect of things," Brubacher says.

There is hardly a thing that happens in this haunt without him knowing.

"This is an emergency radio that we have in each one of our scenes. In case an actor has a problem or somebody falls down and needs to be evacuated," Brubacher says. Before hitting the trail, he takes us behind the scenes to a barn where scare-actors are getting finishing touches of makeup.

Art director and makeup manager Chris Knowles and his team are using a bevy of pressurized airbrushes to quickly creep-ify all kinds of ghouls, vampires and aliens.

"It's great because you can get color on really finely or cover areas. [It] swaps colors really quickly as well, which is essential because we've only got like about seven minutes to do the makeup because we got like 100 odd people and two hours to do it," Knowles says.

toggle caption i Ryan Benk/NPR News

Robert Doyle, 38, is in Knowles' chair at the moment.

Sponsor Message

"I love Halloween. I love going out and interacting with people, entertaining them, making them laugh. Giving them a good scare, you know, giving them a good dopamine rush," Doyle says.

Doyle has played all kinds of frightening characters in his five years at Markoff's. He's been a killer clown, a demon and tonight he's a Nosferatu-style vampire with sharp fangs, a bloody mouth and pupils as dark as coal.

toggle caption i Ryan Benk/NPR News

Doyle thinks people keep coming back to places like Markoff's to face down their fears safely.

"People want to challenge themselves and they can say they accomplished something," Doyle says.

Another scare-actor, wearing a black top hat and looking like a cross between a straw and hair covered zombie, and hoodoo shaman is ready for his opening night.

His day-walker name is Jermaine Hoes.

"I am something that you see when you wake up at 3 o'clock in the morning," Hoes says.

toggle caption i Ryan Benk/NPR News.

Hoes has been a scare actor at different haunts around Maryland for years, and he says his reason for moonlighting as a horrific beast is pretty simple.

"I like scaring people. I like to make you run and scream and holler everywhere," Hoes says.

Leaving the actors so they can get into character, it's time to take to the trail, which begins with an ominous, steady heartbeat pumping through hidden speakers.

The trail is dark, foggy and winding. It's constructed in such a way that you can't escape the scares. Even trying to escape signals to the actors that you're ripe for a fright.

There are snakes, zombified pumpkin heads, ghosts, vampires, ghouls, aliens and even cannibals.

The trail is barely a mile, but between the terrain and its twists, it can take more than an hour to get through.

Voices cry out in pain and shriek in fear. Many seem menacing.

Sponsor Message

"You can join us," one voice in the shadows snickers.

"Don't you want your face on one of these pumpkins?," another cackles. "It just takes a little bit of a beating!"

Anything that could scare you is here, and it didn't take much in this secluded, murky environment.

The science of screams

"Fear is extremely fast," says Harvard Medical School associate professor of radiology Nouchine Hadjikhani.

For much of her career, Hadjikhani has studied what happens in the brain when someone is afraid. She uses computer screens and brain monitoring equipment to show subjects frightening images and measure their brain's reaction.

"If I show you very briefly, so for, you know, 30 milliseconds or something, snakes and spiders, I will see that your amygdala gets activated," Hadjikhani says.

She says it's this activation that makes a jump scare so effective.

"Your heart goes faster. You go a little further back and you start sweating. Your pupils get high for a stupid image on the screen," she says.

According to Hadjikhani, we get scared when something – usually visual – sets off the fear center of the brain. And she says she can elicit that same brain reaction in people just by showing them pictures of other folks who are scared. But she says it's difficult to know why some people derive pleasure from fear.

You have to talk to them.

Fear is fun

For that we need the scientists at the Recreational Fear Lab at Aarhaus University in Denmark.

YouTube

Co-directors Matthias Clausen and Marc Andersen have created all kinds of studies into what keeps people coming back for frights.

Over the years, what they've found is that there is more than one type of recreational fear.

"We did an early study where we tried to see if we could identify the personality profile of the horror fan and what we found was a god-forsaken mess," Clausen says.

A rollercoaster enthusiast, for example, may detest horror films. And a scary movie scream queen might lose her lunch at a theme park.

Sponsor Message

But Clausen says survey after survey at the Fear Lab shows fear-for-fun is surprisingly universal.

"When you engage in recreational activities, you're essentially administering a fear vaccine," Clausen says. Seeking out fear is our way of preparing our bodies for the sometimes scary real world.

And this vaccine is actually fun for most people. "It doesn't hurt," Clausen says.

The duo has called this a "fear inoculation."
