World.title: Uganda’s Army Rejects New York Times Report on Muhoozi
World.content:
UGANDA · MILITARY AND MEDIA

Key Facts — What happened Uganda’s army rejected a US newspaper feature on its chief.

— When Statement issued on Saturday, 10 October, by Col Chris Magezi.

— The target A Megan K. Stack feature published on Thursday, 8 October.

— The person Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, army chief and President Museveni’s son.

— Army’s line Claims are unfounded; foreign interference “will not be tolerated.”

— Still open No public reply yet from the newspaper or Washington.

Uganda’s military has turned a US newspaper feature into a fight over who shapes the country’s post-Museveni future.

The Uganda army on Saturday, 10 October, rejected a New York Times feature on its commander, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba. The feature links him to alleged human rights abuses.

The Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) called the report unfounded and part of a sustained character assassination campaign, the Daily Monitor reported.

The dispute matters beyond Kampala because Muhoozi is President Yoweri Museveni’s son and widely seen as a possible successor. Uganda is also a long-standing US security partner, with troops deployed against al-Shabaab in Somalia.

What the Uganda Army Said

The statement came from Col Chris Magezi, Acting Director of Defence Public Information, the army’s chief spokesman. He said the article “regurgitates long held, twisted opposition and activist narratives” against the government, according to the Daily Monitor.

Magezi defended Muhoozi as a decorated officer with decades of military service. He said the UPDF works within Uganda’s constitution and that serious accusations require serious evidence, not anecdotal or politically motivated sources.

Muhoozi, 52, has been Chief of Defence Forces since March 2024. He is also Senior Presidential Advisor for Special Operations, according to the army.

Museveni has ruled Uganda since 1986. The question of who follows him dominates the country’s politics, and Muhoozi’s rise has made the army central to that debate.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Uganda Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the US Newspaper Reported

The feature, written by Megan K. Stack and published on Thursday, 8 October, is titled “The Authoritarian Future Is Already Here.” The Daily Monitor said it describes a growing state surveillance system in Uganda, including facial recognition and digital tracking tools.

According to the same summary, the piece links Muhoozi to the detention and suppression of opposition figures. It names singer-turned-politician Robert Kyagulanyi, known as Bobi Wine, and Kizza Besigye, a veteran opposition leader on trial for alleged treason.

Kyagulanyi leads the National Unity Platform, Uganda’s main opposition party. Besigye, a former Museveni physician, ran for president four times before founding his own movement.

The feature also draws on the account of Kakwenza Rukirabashaija, an exiled Ugandan novelist. He alleges that Muhoozi visited him in detention, ordered him to undress and later offered him a bribe.

The Army’s Answer to Kakwenza

Magezi said Muhoozi and Kakwenza have “never met.” He called the writer “a known fiction teller” and his account “a fine figment of his imagination,” the Daily Monitor reported.

The spokesman also pointed to what he called contradictions in the story.

He said the account had Kakwenza bending over to look shorter, yet too injured at the ankles to stand. He called this “quite laughable.”

Kakwenza was arrested in December 2021 after social media posts about Muhoozi and Museveni. He left Uganda in 2022 and has since lived in exile, from where he continues to write about his detention.

A Wider Charge Against Foreign Media

The statement went beyond one article. Magezi accused The Telegraph, The Wall Street Journal and The Economist of bias against Muhoozi as well.

He said Muhoozi “is not their preferred successor of choice to a post-Museveni Uganda.” Uganda’s political future, he added, belongs only to its voters, and external interference “will not be tolerated.”

On the same Saturday, the army’s own website reported Muhoozi meeting the Commonwealth Secretary-General and a Malian military delegation. It also welcomed a new battle group to its Somalia mission area.

What It Means for US Readers

The row puts a major American newspaper at the centre of Uganda’s succession politics. Kampala’s sharp tone suggests the government sees Western coverage of Muhoozi as a political threat, not only a press matter.

For Washington, Uganda is a difficult partner. Its soldiers have formed a core part of African Union forces fighting al-Shabaab in Somalia, a long-running US counter-terrorism priority.

Yet Washington removed Uganda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act trade programme from January 2024, citing human rights. On Saturday, the Daily Monitor also reported that Uganda remains on Tier 2 in the 2026 US Trafficking in Persons report.

Investors watching Uganda’s oil projects on Lake Albert, led by France’s TotalEnergies and China’s CNOOC, track succession risk closely. A more confrontational tone from the army towards Western media adds to that picture, though it changes no policy by itself.

What Is Not Known

The full army statement could not be independently reviewed. Its content here rests on reports by the Daily Monitor and Nile Post.

It is not clear whether it was released as a press statement or on social media.

No public response from the newspaper to the army’s criticism had been reported by Sunday morning. Nor had any comment from Muhoozi himself or the US Embassy in Kampala.

Kakwenza’s allegations have not been tested in any court. The army’s account of his claims has not been tested either.

What Comes Next

Watch for any reply from the newspaper, the writer or the opposition.

Remarks by Muhoozi, who often posts on social media, are also likely. Any comment from the US State Department would raise the stakes.

The statement does not mean any legal action against the newspaper or its reporter. No such step has been announced.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who Is Muhoozi Kainerugaba?

He is Uganda’s Chief of Defence Forces and the son of President Yoweri Museveni. Many Ugandans see him as a possible successor to his father.

What Did the US Newspaper Report?

According to the Daily Monitor, the 8 October feature describes growing state surveillance and links Muhoozi to the suppression of opposition figures. It also carries a writer’s allegations of abuse in detention.

How Did the Uganda Army Respond?

Spokesman Col Chris Magezi called the claims unfounded and part of a character assassination campaign. He said foreign interference in Uganda’s politics “will not be tolerated.”

Who Is Kakwenza Rukirabashaija?

He is a Ugandan novelist who was detained in December 2021 and now lives in exile. The army says he has never met Muhoozi.

Why Does This Matter to the United States?

Uganda is a key US security partner in Somalia but faces US pressure over human rights. The dispute touches both issues at once.

Sources: Uganda People’s Defence Forces; Daily Monitor, army statement on Muhoozi; Nile Post, army statement on Kakwenza; Daily Monitor, US trafficking report (all accessed 11 October 2026).

World.title: Senegal Arrests 6 Over US$1.9 Million in Fake Banknotes
World.content:
SENEGAL · CRIME

Key Facts — What happened Senegal’s gendarmerie arrested six people over fake dollar and euro notes.

— The numbers Seized notes valued at 1.1 billion CFA francs, about US$1.9 million.

— Where Operations in Dakar, Thiès, Mbour and Louga followed a 5 October tip.

— US link The haul included 6,600 fake US$100 bills, US$660,000 at face value.

— Also seized A 9 mm pistol, a dagger, a bulletproof vest and suspected mercury.

— Still open Charges, suspects’ identities and the notes’ origin have not been disclosed.

Raids in four Senegalese towns turned up 17,800 fake US and European banknotes valued at about US$1.9 million.

Senegal’s national gendarmerie has arrested six people in Dakar, Thiès, Mbour and Louga and seized fake banknotes in US dollars and euros. It put their equivalent value at 1,104,914,840 CFA francs (about US$1.9 million).

The haul, mostly fake US$100 and €100 bills, matters to foreigners because those are the notes visitors, traders and investors carry. Investigators also found a pistol, a dagger, a bulletproof vest and bottles believed to contain mercury.

What the Gendarmerie Seized

The Brigade de recherches de Dakar, the gendarmerie’s criminal investigation unit for the capital, announced the case on Saturday, 10 October. The Agence de Presse Sénégalaise (APS), the state news agency, carried the statement that evening, as did the Dakar news site Seneweb.

According to the statement, investigators acted on intelligence received on Monday, 5 October. The tip pointed to a suspected network holding foreign-currency notes for chemical washing and use as fraudulent payment.

The largest batch was 10,000 notes made to look like €100 bills, €1 million (about US$1.12 million) at face value. The gendarmerie valued them at 650 million CFA francs (about US$1.1 million).

Investigators also found 6,600 notes made to look like US$100 bills in a briefcase, or US$660,000 at face value. The gendarmerie valued them at 376.2 million CFA francs (about US$643,000).

A third batch held 1,200 so-called black notes in €100 denominations, €120,000 at face value (about US$134,000). Their stated value of 78,714,840 CFA francs (about US$134,000) matches the fixed rate of 655.957 CFA francs per euro.

Conversions use a market rate of 585.40 CFA francs per US$1 on 11 October 2026.

Beyond the notes, investigators seized a Taurus 9 mm automatic pistol, 20 blank 9 mm cartridges and 15 further cartridges. The list also includes two forgers’ stamps, a bulletproof vest, a dagger and bottles believed to contain mercury.

Seneweb headlined the case as “one billion in fake notes, pistol, dagger” and called it a big gendarmerie seizure. APS described it as trafficking in fake foreign currency worth more than one billion CFA francs (about US$1.7 million).

How the Washing Scheme Is Said to Work

The gendarmerie did not describe the scheme beyond the chemical washing process. Blackened notes and chemical cleaning are, however, hallmarks of what is widely known as the “black money” or “wash-wash” scam.

In the typical version, victims are shown stained paper and told it is real currency disguised for transport. They are then asked to pay for an expensive chemical that will supposedly restore the notes.

A few genuine notes are often “cleaned” in front of the victim to win trust. The rest proves worthless once the money for the chemicals has changed hands.

The gendarmerie said only that the bottles were believed to contain mercury, a toxic metal. It did not say how the substance was used, and the statement does not explain the two forgers’ stamps either.

A Four-Town Operation

Dakar, the capital, is home to Senegal’s main port, airport and banks. Thiès lies about 70 kilometres east, Mbour about 80 kilometres south-east on the coast, and Louga about 200 kilometres north-east.

Mbour sits next to the Saly beach resorts, which draw many European visitors. The gendarmerie did not say which arrests took place in which town.

Senegal’s gendarmerie is a military force that carries out police and criminal investigation work alongside the national police. Its Dakar research brigade investigates serious crime in the capital region.

Senegal is a West African country of about 18 million people. One US$ buys about 585 CFA francs, the currency it shares with seven other West African states.

What It Means for US Readers

The seized haul included 6,600 notes made to look like US$100 bills. The US Secret Service protects the dollar against counterfeiting worldwide, but the gendarmerie did not mention any US role in this case.

For American travellers, the practical lesson is to change money only at banks, ATMs and licensed exchange offices. Offers to swap, “clean” or multiply foreign cash are a clear warning sign.

Business visitors and investors should be wary of cash deals presented as discreet or urgent. Fraud schemes of this kind can reach foreigners through personal contacts, social media or email.

The case also shows police action against financial crime in a country courting foreign investors, including in oil and gas. There is no sign it affects Senegal’s currency or its banks.

What Is Not Known

The gendarmerie did not name the six suspects, give their nationalities or say what charges they may face. It is also not known whether they remain in custody or have been brought before a prosecutor.

Where the fake banknotes were printed, and whether any victims paid money, is unclear. The statement also does not say whether any genuine notes were among the seized bundles.

The gendarmerie did not say whether the pistol was registered or whether foreign authorities have been informed. All six are suspects, and none has been convicted of any offence.

What Comes Next

The gendarmerie said its investigation is continuing, which could lead to further arrests. In Senegal, suspects held by the gendarmerie are normally handed to a prosecutor, who decides on charges.

It asked the public to share information on its free lines, 800 00 20 20 and 123. The seizure does not mean fake banknotes are common in Senegal’s shops or banks.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Senegal’s gendarmerie seize?

It seized 6,600 fake US$100 notes and 11,200 fake 100-euro notes, some of them blackened. It also found a pistol, a dagger, a bulletproof vest and suspected mercury.

How much were the fake banknotes worth?

The gendarmerie put their equivalent value at about 1.1 billion CFA francs, or about US$1.9 million. As fakes, the notes have no real value.

What is a black money scam?

Fraudsters show victims blackened paper, claim it is real currency and sell them a costly chemical to clean it. The gendarmerie said the seized notes could be put through a chemical washing process.

Have the suspects been charged?

The gendarmerie has not announced charges or named the six people arrested. They are suspects, and the investigation is continuing.

Is it safe to use cash in Senegal?

Yes, with normal care: use banks, ATMs and licensed exchange offices. Refuse anyone who offers to exchange, clean or multiply currency.

Sources: Gendarmerie nationale du Sénégal; Agence de Presse Sénégalaise (APS); Seneweb (all accessed 11 October 2026).

World.title: Guinea-Bissau Party Loses 33 Members Over Poll Boycott
World.content:
GUINEA-BISSAU · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country West African state of two million, run by a junta since 2025.

— What happened 33 APU-PDGB officials and members resigned in one collective letter.

— When The letter is dated and stamped received on Friday, 9 October.

— Most senior signatory Party vice-president Samuel Dinis Manuel.

— The grievance Leader Nuno Nabiam kept the party out of the November 2025 elections.

— Still open Nabiam and the party leadership have not formally responded.

A former prime minister’s party is splitting as Guinea-Bissau’s military rulers search for a new election date.

Thirty-three officials and APU-PDGB members have quit the party of former prime minister Nuno Nabiam in Guinea-Bissau. Their collective letter, dated Friday, 9 October, says he took key decisions alone, above all sitting out the November 2025 elections.

The split matters beyond one party because Guinea-Bissau, a small West African state under military rule, has no date for civilian rule. APU-PDGB has just lost its vice-president and several regional leaders before any new vote.

What the Resignation Letter Says

APU-PDGB stands for the alliance of Assembleia do Povo Unido (United People’s Assembly) and Partido Democrático da Guiné-Bissau (Democratic Party of Guinea-Bissau). Nabiam founded it and still leads it.

The two-page letter is addressed to him and signed by a “Group of Leaders and Members Resigning from APU-PDGB”. A stamp from the office of the party’s secretary-general shows it was received on 9 October.

The signatories say they are giving up both their posts and their membership. They blame “the deep leadership crisis” for what they call the weakening and gradual breakdown of the party (translated from Portuguese).

The letter lists three grounds. First, it says decisions of major political weight have been taken unilaterally, without consulting members.

Second, it rejects Nabiam’s decision not to run for president and to stop the party from contesting the legislative election. Both votes were held in November 2025, and the signatories say such a choice needed a full debate in the party’s bodies.

Third, it cites “constant violations” of the party statutes, including political agreements the leader signed alone. It names APU-PDGB’s entry into the Plataforma Republicana Nô Kumpu Guiné as one example.

Who Is Leaving APU-PDGB

An attached list names 33 people with their membership card numbers, posts and signatures. The Bissau weekly O Democrata, which saw the letter, reported the resignations on Friday evening.

The most senior is Samuel Dinis Manuel, a vice-president and member of the party’s Standing Committee. He also coordinated youth, economic affairs, vocational training and employment.

Beto Infande, president of the party’s Forum of Cadres, signed, as did its secretary-general, Buo Manuel. Garcia Biifa Bedeta, a deputy national secretary, and Rosalia da Costa, listed as president of the party body ONAMA, also signed.

The list also includes local political committee leaders from Biombo region, the Bária section and the Prabis sector. Two signatories are listed simply as rank-and-file members.

The group says the “political and ethical conditions” no longer exist for it to stay under the current leadership. It does not say whether its members will join another party.

The 2025 Vote and the Embaló Alliance

Guinea-Bissau held presidential and legislative elections on Sunday, 23 November 2025. Three days later, on 26 November 2025, the army seized power before provisional results were released.

General Horta Inta-A, an army officer, now leads the transition as president. The deposed president, Umaro Sissoco Embaló, had been seeking a second term.

Nô Kumpu Guiné, Creole for roughly “Let’s Build Guinea”, was a 16-party alliance formed in September 2025 to back Embaló’s re-election. Le360, a Moroccan news site, reported its launch on 3 September 2025.

The dissidents’ complaint is therefore about a party that sat out the ballot itself while signing up to the incumbent’s camp. With the vote voided by the coup, that bet left APU-PDGB with no seats to defend and no clear role.

The letter arrives during a busy week for the transition. Officials said on Thursday that the planned 6 December election cannot go ahead, and no replacement date has been set.

What It Means for US Readers

Guinea-Bissau has long been a transit point for South American cocaine bound for Europe. A fragmented party system and an open-ended military transition make stable, accountable government harder to rebuild.

Washington has had no resident embassy in Bissau since 1998 and handles the country from its embassy in Dakar, Senegal. Embaló was among five West African leaders hosted at the White House in July 2025.

For travellers and businesses, the split itself changes little on the ground. It is a signal, though, that the civilian parties a future election depends on are weakening while the army sets the timetable.

What Is Not Known

Nabiam and APU-PDGB’s leadership had not issued a formal response by Sunday morning, 11 October.

On Saturday, the Bissau news blog Conosaba posted a short message under his name: “the struggle does not end here”. It did not name the defectors.

It is not known how many members APU-PDGB has in total, so the share of the party leaving cannot be measured. It is also unclear whether the signatories plan a new party or will join an existing one.

What Comes Next

The transitional president must now set a new election calendar after being told the December date is not possible. Parties that want to compete will have to renew their internal bodies first.

The resignations do not dissolve APU-PDGB, and Nabiam remains its leader. Whether more members follow will show how much of the party survives into the next vote.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is APU-PDGB?

APU-PDGB is a Guinea-Bissau political party founded and led by former prime minister Nuno Nabiam. Its full name means United People Assembly, Democratic Party of Guinea-Bissau.

How many people resigned?

The collective letter carries a list of 33 named officials and members. The most senior is vice-president Samuel Dinis Manuel.

Why did they leave?

They say Nabiam took major decisions alone, including keeping the party out of the November 2025 elections. They also object to his joining an alliance backing the former president without consulting party bodies.

Who runs Guinea-Bissau now?

A military-led transition under General Horta Inta-A has ruled since the coup of 26 November 2025. No date for a new election has been set.

Is Guinea-Bissau safe for American travellers?

The party split has no direct effect on security. Travellers should check the current US State Department advisory before going.

Sources: Collective resignation letter and list of signatories, APU-PDGB dissidents (published by Conosaba); O Democrata, Bissau; Conosaba, message attributed to Nuno Nabiam; O Democrata, transitional council on the December vote; Le360 Afrique (all accessed 11 October 2026).

World.title: Panama Earthquake Aftershocks Continue as Residents Survey Widespread Damage
World.content:
Residents near the epicenter of a major earthquake in southern Panama began cleaning up on Saturday, traumatized by the previous day’s heavy shaking that left widespread damage but so far no reported deaths. “This is something we’ve never seen before. We weren’t prepared for this kind of event,” said Aldulfo Quintero as he cleared debris from a store in Chitre, about 250 kilometers (155 miles) southwest of Panama City.

The 41-year-old said he has a “great fear” that a new earthquake could strike any moment. After the initial 7.7-magnitude quake around midday Friday, over 100 aftershocks have been recorded, some as strong as magnitude 6.0. Like many others in Chitre, the capital of hard-hit Herrera province, 28-year-old Yakshuri Castillo chose to sleep outdoors due to fears of another quake.

She said she “went into shock” when the first quake struck. Dozens of homes were damaged in the city, whose 66,000 residents were still without electricity on Saturday. The epicenter of the initial quake was registered by the US Geological Survey (USGS) about 60 kilometers away, near the border of Herrera, Los Santos, Veraguas provinces.

Earthquakes are rare in Panama and usually occur in western Chiriqui province, bordering Costa Rica. Strong shaking in Panama City, over 200 kilometers from the epicenter, sent panicked people pouring into the streets from the capital’s numerous high-rise buildings. While no deaths have been reported from the quake, about 30 people have been treated for minor injuries.

Authorities are still assessing the damage in remote areas. Several communities have been cut off due to roadways damaged by the quake. “The disaster we are facing is massive,” President Jose Raul Mulino said upon arriving in one of the affected areas. The United States, which counts Panama among the members of President Donald Trump’s new “Shield of the Americas” initiative, has pledged rapid support.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that he was “closely monitoring” the situation, with his office “rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist.” The top US military commander in the region, Francis Donovan, has “directed immediate support to help the people of Panama, including on-the-ground support from rotary-wing aircraft… and the airlift of key personnel and supplies into the country,” US Southern Command said in a statement on Saturday.

The Panamanian quake is at least the fourth quake this year in Latin America surpassing 7.0 in magnitude, after devastating back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela’s Guaira in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August.

World.title: 21-year-old Louis Matthews charged with murder of 17-year-old Kaylon David
World.content:
21-year-old Louis Matthews charged with murder of 17-year-old Kaylon David

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have formally arrested and charged 21-year-old Louis Maxwell Matthews, a Belizean welder of Belize City, with the murder of 17-year-old Kaylon Trevor David, who was gunned down on Iguana Street Extension on Thursday evening.

According to police, David was walking along Iguana Street Extension shortly after 6:30 p.m. on October 8 when he was approached by a gunman who fired several shots in his direction. The teenager was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he later succumbed to his injuries.

During Friday’s police press briefing, Assistant Commissioner of Police Hilberto Romero confirmed that investigators had detained a suspect and were reviewing surveillance footage. Police indicated that the shooting may have stemmed from an ongoing rivalry involving threats exchanged between David and other individuals in the area.

As previously reported by BBN, investigators recovered a 9mm expended shell casing from the scene. Police also confirmed that David was not previously known to law enforcement.

Matthews was formally charged on Saturday, October 10. He is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in a court of law.

World.title: PM Briceño departs for IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok
World.content:
PM Briceño departs for IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Prime Minister John Briceño has left the country for Bangkok, Thailand.

The Office of the Prime Minister says Briceño departed on Saturday, October 10, to attend the Ancillary Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group, which run from October 12 to 18.

The Prime Minister, who also serves as Minister of Finance, is scheduled to return to Belize on Sunday, October 18.

In his absence, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Natural Resources, Petroleum and Mining Cordel Hyde will hold over as Prime Minister.

World.title: Motorcyclist injured in crash on San Martin Road
World.content:
Motorcyclist injured in crash on San Martin Road

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A man has been injured in a traffic accident on San Martin Road in Orange Walk Town.

Initial reports indicate he was riding his motorcycle when he collided with another vehicle.

Police and an ambulance are on the scene.

The extent of his injuries is not yet known.

Investigations are ongoing. BBN will update as more information becomes available.

World.title: Chon Saan opens in San Pedro today, bringing its famous Chinese cuisine to Ambergris Caye
World.content:
Chon Saan opens in San Pedro today, bringing its famous Chinese cuisine to Ambergris Caye

By Breaking Belize News Staff: One of Belize’s most recognizable restaurant brands is expanding to Ambergris Caye as Chon Saan Palace officially opens its doors in San Pedro today, Saturday, October 10, at noon.

Restaurant owner and Mesopotamia Area Representative Lee Mark Chang confirmed the opening to Breaking Belize News (BBN) this morning, sharing photos of the final preparations at the new establishment.

The restaurant, located on Middle Street in downtown San Pedro, diagonally across from Elvi’s Kitchen, occupies the ground floor of the Sun & Reef Hotel, where a casino previously operated.

Chang said the restaurant will initially accommodate approximately 48 diners, with nine tables available. However, plans are already being considered to expand operations onto the building’s second floor.

The restaurant will operate from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. and reopen from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m., with Tuesdays designated as its weekly day off.

Chang also indicated that Chon Saan remains open to recruiting talented individuals as the business expands.

The San Pedro location will feature many of the dishes that have made Chon Saan a household name in Belize, including its popular fried chicken, Chinese specialties, noodles, soups and other favourites. The restaurant will initially offer dine-in and takeout services, with delivery services planned for a later stage.

Chon Saan’s history dates back to 1974, when Chang’s parents, Armando Chang and his wife, established the original family restaurant on Douglas Jones Street in Belize City. Over the decades, the business grew into one of the country’s best-known Chinese restaurants, celebrating its 50th anniversary in 2024.

The opening marks another chapter in the restaurant’s more than five decades of operations, bringing its longstanding culinary tradition to residents and visitors of Belize’s leading tourism destination.

World.title: Chebat meets BDF top brass at Senior Officers’ Conference
World.content:
Chebat meets BDF top brass at Senior Officers’ Conference

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Newly appointed Minister of National Security Michel Chebat has met with the senior leadership of the Belize Defence Force.

The meeting took place on Friday, October 9, at the BDF’s annual Senior Officers’ Conference, held at the Biltmore Plaza Hotel in Belize City.

Chebat introduced himself to the Force’s senior officers, engaged with the leadership and shared his strategic guidance and vision for the way forward.

Also in attendance were Major (Retired) Francis Usher, Chief Executive Officer of the Ministry of National Security, BDF Commander Brigadier General Anthony Velasquez, senior BDF officers and high ranking foreign military partners.

The conference comes just days after Chebat took on the expanded National Security portfolio, which now places both the BDF and the Belize Police Department under his ministry.

World.title: BTV spots Guatemalan military boat near Sarstoon Island amid ongoing tensions
World.content:
BTV spots Guatemalan military boat near Sarstoon Island amid ongoing tensions

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize Territorial Volunteers (BTV) leader Wil Maheia is reporting another sighting of a Guatemalan Armed Forces (GAF) vessel near Sarstoon Island, as tensions continue along Belize’s southern border.

Maheia, who was travelling in the Sarstoon area early Saturday morning, shared video footage with Breaking Belize News showing the river and vessels in the distance. He reported spotting a Guatemalan military boat near Sarstoon Island, an area that has been at the centre of repeated confrontations between Belizean civilians and Guatemalan security forces.

The latest sighting comes exactly one month after a major confrontation on September 10, when the BTV was prevented from completing its traditional journey around Sarstoon Island. According to Belize’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, approximately 18 Guatemalan military and civilian vessels were deployed near the island, prompting Belizean security forces to limit the expedition to the Belize Defence Force’s Forward Operating Base.

The Government of Belize subsequently lodged a formal diplomatic protest, accusing Guatemala of violating Belize’s sovereignty and obstructing the lawful passage of unarmed Belizean nationals. Belize maintains that the international boundary follows the mid-channel of the Sarstoon River under the 1859 Boundary Treaty and that Sarstoon Island falls entirely within Belizean territory.

Tensions were further heightened on September 24 when a Guatemalan military reconnaissance aircraft entered Belizean airspace without authorization. The National Security Council subsequently directed the Government to request an investigation by the Organization of American States, citing repeated incursions by Guatemalan forces into Belize’s southern maritime territory and threats involving the Sarstoon.

Both countries remain engaged in proceedings before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which is expected to hear oral arguments in February 2027 concerning Guatemala’s longstanding territorial, insular and maritime claim against Belize.

Saturday’s reported sighting underscores the continued sensitivity of the Sarstoon area as Belize and Guatemala await a final resolution to their territorial dispute.

World.title: Tensions continue at the Sarstoon
World.content:
Tensions continue at the Sarstoon

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Sarstoon is once again in the spotlight.

On Saturday morning, Belize Territorial Volunteers leader Wil Maheia reported seeing a Guatemalan Armed Forces vessel in Belizean waters in front of Sarstoon Island during an early morning trip to the area.

The sighting comes amid rising tensions between Belize and Guatemala.

On September 10, the Guatemalan Navy made an incursion into the Sarstoon. Then, on September 24, a Guatemalan military reconnaissance aircraft entered Belizean airspace, an incursion the National Security Council confirmed this week using radar data.

In response, Government has asked the Organization of American States to investigate the airspace incident and has called on Guatemala to respect long established confidence building measures.

Government has also pointed to multiple incursions by the Guatemalan Armed Forces into Belize’s southern maritime space and threats of the use of force on the Sarstoon in recent months.

Newly appointed Minister of National Security Michel Chebat has pledged to strengthen Belize’s security cooperation and protect the country’s sovereignty.

There has been no official response yet to Saturday’s sighting.

World.title: Jarred Gongora charged with aggravated assault and firearm offenses following incident involving Kevin Trapp in Unitedville
World.content:
Jarred Gongora charged with aggravated assault and firearm offenses following incident involving Kevin Trapp in Unitedville

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have formally arrested and charged 38-year-old Jarred Denver Gongora, a Belizean laborer from the Cayo District, following an incident involving Kevin Trapp in Unitedville Village.

According to police, the incident occurred on Thursday, October 8, in the Spanishtown area of Unitedville. Gongora was arrested on Friday, October 9, and charged with aggravated assault, keeping a firearm without a gun license, and keeping ammunition without a gun license.

Trapp has previously been the target of gun violence. In November 2025, he survived an ambush near the Unitedville Community Centre when a gunman opened fire as he arrived home in his vehicle. He sustained multiple gunshot wounds and was hospitalized.

In June 2026, Trapp was also among five people jointly charged with firearm and ammunition offenses after police discovered a loaded .22-calibre pistol during a Special Patrol Unit operation at a Unitedville residence.

Police have not disclosed the full circumstances surrounding Thursday’s incident or whether anyone sustained injuries.

World.title: Seiveright questions political role in Barita card drives, $15,000 grants
World.content:
State Minister in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Delano Seiveright

Government Minister Delano Seiveright has raised concerns about political representatives from both major parties promoting Barita debit card registration drives, some advertising grants of up to $15,000.

The development comes as Barita expands its digital banking services through BPay, offering digital wallet and debit card facilities.

However, in two posts on X Saturday night, the minister of state in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce, while welcoming efforts to expand financial inclusion, called for greater transparency surrounding the incentives and consumer safeguards.

“I notice political representatives (both sides) promoting Barita card sign-ups, some advertising grants of up to $15,000,” Seiveright wrote. “Financial inclusion is welcome, but who funds the incentives and what safeguards apply?”

He also questioned what expectations constituents might have of political representatives if difficulties arise with financial products they had encouraged people to use.

His comments followed reports of large crowds attending registration drives promoted by politicians across party lines.

One promotional flyer for a September 24 registration event in western Jamaica featured a Member of Parliament and advertised a one-time debit card grant of up to $15,000.

The discussion comes amid wider national debate about consumer protection, including recent disagreements over proposed changes to penalties under Jamaica’s competition and consumer protection legislation.

Despite his concerns, Seiveright stressed the potential benefits of expanding access to affordable financial services.

“Financial inclusion and digital banking can be game changers for Jamaica,” he said, adding: “Innovation and transparency must go hand in hand.”

His posts did not allege wrongdoing by Barita or political representatives involved.

World.title: CAFFE in crisis
World.content:
Voters queue outside a polling station during the 2025 General Election. CAFFE had initially intended to recruit 1,000 volunteers on a budget of approximately $15 million for the 2025 poll, but a funding freeze forced the observer group to cut that number in half. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

AFTER almost 30 years of monitoring elections in Jamaica, the internationally acclaimed agency Citizens Action for Free and Fair Elections (CAFFE) is now cash-strapped and desperately in need of assistance from the private sector to continue observing the country’s democratic process.

CAFFE is still navigating the financial fallout from the Donald Trump Administration’s 2025 withdrawal of United States Agency for International Development (USAID) funding from non-governmental organisations globally.

Speaking at a Jamaica Observer Press Club at the agency’s New Kingston office last Thursday, CAFFE Chair Grace Baston said its financial position has deteriorated further since the September 2025 General Election.

For that poll, CAFFE had initially aimed to recruit 1,000 volunteers on a budget of approximately $15 million.

Frozen funding, however, forced the organisation to halve its target to about 500.

The shortfall has heightened concerns about its capacity to monitor future local government elections, by-elections, and the country’s next general election.

Baston warned that such a setback could erode the democratic gains the country has made.

“There is no doubting the work of the ECJ (Electoral Commission of Jamaica) and the EOJ (Electoral Office of Jamaica).

There has been remarkable progress in those electoral processes; we are the first to give credit.

That being said, we believe strongly [that a] democracy not monitored is democracy threatened.

“CAFFE’s presence has made a huge difference.

The respect people have for the CAFFE observer entering a polling station; the confidence they have in what we are going to say, or what we pronounce about the quality of the conduct of the poll — it is extremely important.

[If] you ease up on that you are inviting a return to what was before,” she insisted.

The election watchdog was established in 1997 amid lingering political strife and fears that Jamaica’s democratic process could be undermined, based on the experiences in the 1980s and early 1990s.

Although the country has moved beyond those dangers, Baston said new threats have emerged, demanding continued vigilance.

“Once, the big threat was overvoting in a polling station — [you have] 100 people on the list and 150 people voting — or the stuffing of a box.

There are other threats now, and we are working hard to make sure we can monitor those.

They are difficult.

One of the new things coming on that we have to think about is going to be precisely this AI (artificial intelligence) that you hear talked about so much,” Baston said.

“How are elections going to be free and fair if campaigning is going to involve the use of deepfake videos? How are we going to hold politicians accountable to make sure that is not happening? The public is being duped because of the power of artificial intelligence in political campaigning.

I am saying not only do we need to be there to prevent the recurrence of the old things that used to threaten our democracy, but there are new threats that we must be prepared for,” charged Baston.

CAFFE Deputy Chairman Anton Thompson also named voter apathy as a major threat to democracy, noting that the agency had established clubs in schools on a $5-million annual budget to foster political awareness and engagement among young people.

However, he told the Sunday Observer that budget cuts have since forced approximately 85 per cent of more than 40 clubs to close.

“We have about half a dozen active clubs, which is far less than we had when we launched this.

And when we launched this with some funding we were able to hire somebody to energise the schools, talk to them, arrange for them to meet.

I met with several schools online — because it was still COVID time — encouraged them, and told them what we were trying to do,” he said.

Thompson added that turnover among school and student leaders had also contributed to the closure of some clubs.

Additionally, many of CAFFE’s volunteers are sixthform students who are trained by the agency at their respective schools and receive a stipend for their civic service.

Baston added that the enthusiasm and dedication that she had seen from engaged students emphasised the need to keep the programme going.

“This is 2026.

The average young person can’t take himself or herself away from their phone for five minutes,” she said.

“When you see these young people making their way to polling locations at six o’clock in the morning because they take so seriously their duty to be there to observe the set-up of the poll.

Once you engage them; once you begin raising their awareness and their consciousness of how precious, how hard-won our democracy was, how fragile it is; once you begin engaging them, their energy and their interest levels are so impressive.

That is why the lack of the resources to have the clubs active is so painful, so difficult,” lamented Baston.

For his part, former Chairman Dr Lloyd Barnett warned that the volunteer count, having been reduced for the September 2025 General Election, could shrink further unless the organisation secures additional funding.

“We are not going to get it from the European Union or USAID anymore.

It’s clear that just like the election monitoring, it has to be Jamaicans.

And as we have said, we have been grateful to Jamaicans…

the commercial interests have been helpful [but] we need more help because of the absence of a major part of our funding from the international sources,” he explained.

“That is why we have been appealing to them.

We have a strong programme in which we are trying to convince them that it’s in their interest, and in the interest of all Jamaica, that they should participate,” added Barnett.

He maintained that the right to choose the country’s leadership is a cornerstone of democracy, and urged the private sector to help ensure that CAFFE’s election-monitoring work does not disappear.

“The electoral system is at the foundation of democracy, and democracy means the Government is of the people, by the people, for the people…

It is in everybody’s interest that democracy should be preserved, and the preservation of elections is the first step in preserving democracy.

You can’t have a democracy without free and fair elections, and that’s why we can’t afford to have CAFFE die,” charged Barnett.

World.title: ‘Effectively, it’s a drizzle’
World.content:
A drone photo of the Mona Reservoir taken on Saturday, October 10, 2026. National Water Commission data show the water level at Mona Reservoir is now 35.6 per cent.

FRIDAY, October 9, 2026, just before midday, dark clouds, pregnant with rain, hovered ominously over Kingston and St Andrew.

By early afternoon the sun had disappeared and the heavens burst open, drenching a city that had endured months of punishing drought.

“Finally, the drought done now!” one woman declared, her face lighting up as the long-awaited rain came in heavy torrents for about halfhour, flooding streets in the process.

“I hope this falling in Mona and Hermitage,” said another woman, referencing the Mona Reservoir and Hermitage Dam — the two major water storage facilities that supply the capital city.

However, Water and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda says Friday’s rain was not enough to ease the drought.

“Effectively, it’s a drizzle when you compare it to what we really need,” he told the Jamaica Observer Saturday afternoon.

“This is our rainy period where we’re supposed to have sustained rainfall from the last week in August, but six weeks later we’re celebrating an afternoon shower.

Nobody should be of the opinion that we’re out of the woods,” Samuda added.

He said while the volume of rain has improved water levels at the Mona Reservoir and Hermitage Dam, “There is no [rain] storm that has the ability, in a single day, to fill those two storage facilities.

What we have experienced is six weeks of sustained reduction in rainfall in our rainy period, on the back of our six-month reduction, so we can’t romanticise this thing.

An afternoon shower is not going to correct this problem,” Samuda told the Sunday Observer.

On Saturday, National Water Commission (NWC) data showed the water level at Hermitage dam had increased by 5.7 million gallons to now stand at 45 per cent, while Mona Reservoir saw an increase by 10 million gallons, pushing the storage to 35.6 per cent.

Against that reality, Samuda and the NWC are urging Jamaicans to continue conserving water, and the restrictions on use are still in force.

At the September 30, 2026 post-Cabinet press briefing, Samuda said the drought has impacted 106 water systems islandwide, the majority of which are in the east.

“Forty-five of our systems in Kingston and St Andrew…10 in St Catherine and Clarendon, and 42 in the north-east, are indeed experiencing the impacts of severe drought conditions,” Samuda said.

“In the western division, one is in Manchester and St Elizabeth, four in Westmoreland and Hanover, and four in St James and Trelawny,” he added.

Last week the NWC had signalled that if the drought worsens it may be forced to ration piped water on alternate days.

Asked about that on Saturday, Samuda said the inflows from Friday’s rain could result in a delay in that strategy.

“We’re evaluating and should make an announcement next week,” he said, adding that the Meteorological Service has forecast “some rainfall” for Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday this week.

“So that would ease the pressure,” Samuda said.

On Saturday the Met Service said there is a trough across Jamaica and a tropical wave across the western Caribbean.

The Met Office said that while the trough is expected to remain over the next few days, the tropical wave is forecast to continue moving westward and away from the island.

The office also forecast windy conditions across Jamaica on Sunday as “a low-level jet stream is projected to strengthen across the central Caribbean”.

It also said that Sunday and Monday will be mostly cloudy across northern parishes, with isolated showers across north-eastern parishes.

Otherwise, there will be mainly sunny mornings.

Additionally, the island will experience afternoon showers and isolated thunderstorms across sections of southern parishes and hilly areas elsewhere.

Tuesday will become cloudy in the afternoon, with showers and thunderstorms across sections of central and western parishes.

World.title: CAFFE clubs crumbling
World.content:
Voters at a polling station at Seaward Primary and Junior High School during the September 2025 General Election. According to election watchdog Citizens Action for Free and Fair Elections, the majority of its election observers are sixth-form students. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

AN initiative by election watchdog Citizens Action for Free and Fair Elections (CAFFE) to expose youngsters to the democratic process through school clubs is now struggling to sustain itself, following a severing of financial support from international donors.

Democracy clubs in schools, which began in 2021, serves as a platform for fostering discussions among high school students on various aspects of Jamaican democracy, building on the involvement of scores of students in CAFFE’s election monitoring exercises since 2011.

Launched with the assistance of the National Democratic Institute (NDI) and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), the initiative aims to encourage students who are 18 years old to enrol on the national voters’ list while also preparing those who are over 17 years old to serve as CAFFE observers.

However, while providing an update on the state of the clubs during a Jamaica Observer Press Club last Thursday at CAFFE’s New Kingston office, the watchdog’s Deputy Chairman Anton Thompson shared that the initiative has seen a significant fall-off in participants, with only six of the initial 40 schools still active.

“We launched this with some funding, so we were able to hire somebody to energise the schools, talk to them [the students], and arrange for them to meet,” said Thompson.

He explained that the initiative’s struggle is further compounded by the lack of replacement leaders.

“These activities in school require teacher leadership as well as student leadership…

Once a teacher’s leadership is absent — and they’re often absent because they go to another job or they retire — then the project will not continue until somebody else is found,” he said, adding that in those instances a central coordinator is needed to ensure that the gaps are filled.

“Not only do teachers move on from schools, but students move on, too.

And so, obviously, if the club goes dormant for two years it’s pretty much extinct until you get replacements, then you have to start again.

“But the schools that are active now tend to be very involved.

We have an event planned for next week for them — an online event because they are all over the country.

And so, essentially, we want to continue, and we are trying our best, too, if we can energise more schools to be involved,” he said.

According to CAFFE, the annual budget for the clubs’ operation is $5 million.

“The running of a club in a school is not necessarily a major financial burden for the school because you usually have provisions in your school budget for clubs, and it usually is not very expensive, depending on the type of club.

However we want to provide support to ensure that the clubs are running at a level where the students are really benefiting — particularly in support in the way of material, research ideas, and things like that — so that the students can really benefit.

That’s what we would want to do,” Thompson said.

Underscoring that the majority of the organisation’s election observers are sixthform students, past Chairman Lloyd Barnett pressed that there is an urgency to restore the operation of the democracy clubs.

“The school term start[ed] in September, and then [there were] exam preparations, and so the focus shifts; and next year we[‘ll] have a completely new set of people.

It is very difficult to keep it sustained.

You have to do all that you have done last year, the next year.

Obviously we need more help because of the absence of a major part of our funding from international sources,” he said.

Additionally, CAFFE Chair Grace Baston noted that the clubs are open to students of all grade levels, with the aim of preparing them to volunteer by the time they reach sixth form.

Despite the drop in numbers, she remains optimistic about the future of the clubs.

“It is the lack of funding that accounts for the fall-off in the number of active clubs.

It’s as clear as that..

We hope to be able to attract the funding — and we don’t envision that it will be difficult to get those clubs up and running once we have the financial support,” said Baston.

World.title: High marks for Malie Donn’s The Golden Child
World.content:
Malie Donn.

DANCEHALL artiste Malie Donn continues to make significant strides on the international music scene with his debut studio album, The Golden Child, securing multiple positions on Apple Music charts across several territories.

Released on September 4 through VP Records, the 21-track project has climbed to the #1 spot on Apple Music’s Reggae Albums chart in Bermuda, St Lucia, and the Turks and Caicos Islands.

The album has also secured the #2 position in Jamaica, Antigua and Barbuda, the Bahamas, Grenada, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Guyana, and Anguilla.

Its success extends beyond the reggae category, having peaked at #3 on the overall Apple Music Albums chart in Jamaica, St Lucia, and Antigua and Barbuda.

Internationally, The Golden Child has also made its presence felt, reaching #4 on the Apple Music Reggae Albums chart in the United Kingdom and Canada, and #5 in the United States. The project has additionally charted in France, Denmark, Singapore, and Portugal, underscoring the artiste’s growing appeal beyond traditional dancehall markets.

For Malie Donn, the album represents a defining chapter in his musical journey, reflecting both his personal experiences and artistic evolution.

“ The Golden Child represents everything that brought me to this point — the pressure, the growth, the wins, and the lessons,” Malie Donn shared in a previous interview with the Jamaica Observer. “This album gives people a chance to hear more of who I am as an artiste, where I want to take the music next, and the versatility I bring.”

The project, led by the title track Golden Child, featuring Squash, also boasts collaborations with Byron Messia, DJ Frass, Antuwang, and Javo Donn.

Adding to the momentum, the entertainer has released official music videos for two tracks from the album, Live Life and SWFT, offering fans fresh visuals to complement the project.

The album’s strong chart showing follows a successful outing in London, England, where Malie Donn delivered a sold-out headline performance at indigo at The O2 on September 5, one day after its release. His international visibility received another boost during the album’s release week when he was featured on the cover of Apple Music’s Reggae playlist.

With The Golden Child continuing to resonate with audiences across the Caribbean, North America, Europe, and other territories, Malie Donn is looking to build on the project’s success while further establishing himself as one of dancehall’s emerging international talents.

World.title: Balford Henry’s final byline
World.content:
Balford Henry, born on January 24, 1952 and died on September 14, 2026, was laid to rest on Saturday. He was 74.

WRITTEN not by the hand nor the wit of the illustrious veteran journalist Balford Henry but by the enduring ink of a remarkable legacy, his final story finds its authors in the colleagues and family whose tributes attest to the mark he left on their lives.

Gathered on Saturday at Kencot Christian Fellowship in St Andrew for the thanksgiving service for his life, mourners reflected on a career spanning more than five decades during which Henry meticulously documented Jamaica’s political, entertainment, and industrial affairs, and cemented his reputation as a respected pillar of the media fraternity.

Delivering her tribute, Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment, and Sport Olivia Grange remembered Henry as the consummate journalist — a man who was dedicated to his career, building a life around expertly sharing facts.

“Jamaica has long been regarded as a liberal democracy within which resides a diverse and active corps of journalists.

Within that corps, however, is a much smaller number of these professionals whose work has truly helped to elevate public awareness and understanding about the role and the actual workings of our Parliament, the decisions made by our elected and appointed representatives, and the electoral process itself.

“Balford Henry was such a man, a man who, through meticulous thoroughness, sheer hard work, ceaseless enquiry, and a longevity that reflected his lifelong dedication to his calling, developed into a towering figure in the field of journalism,” noted Grange.

Henry’s career took root at The Gleaner in 1971 and included work with the Jamaica Observer and the Jamaica Information Service (JIS).

He was also editor of Reggae Times in the 1990s and reporter for the Overseas Gleaner (North America Edition) in New York during the 90s.

His trailblazing work in media earned him several Press Association of Jamaica awards, including recognition for his coverage of reggae icon Bob Marley’s funeral in 1981.

In 2011 he was nationally recognised for his contribution to journalism with the Order of Distinction in the rank of Officer.

Seeking to ensure that Henry’s words would endure not only in memory but also through the body of work he produced over his many years as a journalist, Grange told the congregation that she would pursue the preservation of his writings through national cultural institutions.

“I am going to speak to the National Library [of Jamaica] and the Jamaica Music Museum about working towards collecting Balford’s writings on the entertainment industry over the years, because he did his research, and his work [is] something that is worth establishing,” she said.

Garfield Angus, a senior journalist at JIS and a colleague and friend of ‘Bally’s — as he was affectionately called — also shared anecdotes from their time together throughout the years. His tribute highlighted not only Henry’s many achievements, but also the man behind them.

“As we gather to say goodbyes and to give thanks, not only to the journalist Bally but to the human being he remained, we give thanks for his wit, for his wisdom, for his integrity, for the debates, for his laughter, for the stories, for the friendship,” he said.

“Bally, you served your profession and your country and your friends exceptionally well. You wrote your final column and the copy is clean. The story is complete, the byline remains, and the legacy endures,” said Angus.

In a tearful tribute to her ex-husband, Claudia Stockhausen-Henry told those who gathered about their love story that legally ended in 2006 but lasted until Henry’s last breath.

Emotionally recounting his last days, Stockhausen-Henry shared how she stuck by his side and cared for him.

“I heard when he took his last breath and made a rattling sound. It was a good Samaritan who offered to drive the car to KPH [Kingston Public Hospital], where he was pronounced dead. To Bally, I am always his wife. He hates to hear me say ‘ex-wife’. Here endeth our love story,” she said.

Other tributes were heard from Clarence Brodie, former president of the Press Association of Jamaica, and friend of the deceased, Ainsley Edwards. Also in attendance was Delano Seiveright, minister of state in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce.

Henry was born on January 24, 1952 and died on September 14, 2026. He was 74.

World.title: A mother’s tears, a son’s dream
World.content:
Junior Clarke, 20, and his mother Taschel Fisher pause for a photo last Sunday.

ONE young man’s dream of becoming a doctor took shape when he was just four years old. Now, at 20, after securing the academic achievements necessary to pursue a career in medicine, Junior Clarke faces another hurdle — financial hardship.

But, he’s steadfast in his pursuit of the childhood dream.

“I always wanted to not only help people but to also change how the health system works. I want to become a general surgeon,” Clarke told the Jamaica Observer in an interview last Sunday.

Born and raised in the community of Rivoli in Spanish Town, St Catherine, Clarke graduated from Jonathan Grant High School in 2024, securing 11 subjects in the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) exams. He then moved on to the sixth-form programme at St Jago High School, where he secured an additional eight units at the Caribbean Advanced Proficiency Examination (CAPE) level.

Clarke told the Jamaica Observer that his mother, Taschel Fisher, shouldered raising him alone as his father passed away when he was four months old.

“Growing up was challenging because we didn’t have the resources to make ends meet. I had to help my mother sell at the school gate where I graduated from,” he said, adding that Fisher has been a vendor at the institution for more than 30 years.

Earlier this year, Clarke applied to study medicine at The University of the West Indies (The UWI) and was offered a place in the programme, but the cost of the tuition was beyond his financial means.

“We couldn’t manage it because it’s like $4 million a year, so I decided to take a gap year and do voluntary services, especially at the hospitals, so I can get a scholarship because for a single mother, $4 million is a lot,” Clarke lamented, adding that he’s been unsuccessful in trying to secure a scholarship.

“The scholarships I applied for required me to have six or more grade ones in CAPE, but I only got one grade one. I also started an application for a scholarship but then I realised it wouldn’t be sufficient to cover the cost [of the programme],” he said.

Clarke shared that he is currently in the process of attempting, for a second time, the CAPE subjects for which he did not achieve grade ones, to put himself in a more competitive position to secure a scholarship.

“A setback doesn’t determine your future; it’s just for you to come back and try again. Even though you may face some delays, it doesn’t determine your final outcome. I am going to apply for scholarships again,” he told the Sunday Observer.

Underscoring that there are many others whose aspirations, too, are hampered by financial difficulties, Clarke said helping others will be a priority for him in the future.

“I also want to give back to my community, St Jago High and especially Jonathan Grant High. They did not only build me but they showed me that I was created for excellence. It is not where you are from, it is where you want to go. I know if I get the assistance to achieve my goal, I will later be able to assist others to reach their goals,” said Clarke.

His mother, Fisher, told the Sunday Observer that when she learned of Clarke’s acceptance to The UWI, she could not contain her emotions.

“We were coming home in a taxi, and I held down my head and I started to cry and I said, ‘God, you are in control.’ I asked

God to let him get the help that he needs because even though I am willing to go above and beyond, I know I wouldn’t be able to come up with that kind of money,” Fisher recounted.

She explained that raising Clarke by herself was no easy feat, but with “God as her guide, she was able to pull through,”

“It was very challenging to balance the bills plus attend to his daily needs. Tears after tears, I would go to bed nightly crying asking God to help me,” she said, adding that she often got help from her mother and sister.

“Junior is very driven, well-mannered and very ambitious. Even though he is from the ghetto, his mindset is different. Anyone out there who can help my son please help him,” an emotional Fisher expressed.

World.title: When letters dance
World.content:
The cover for Alex and the Dancing Letters, an educational children’s book about dyslexia.

AN educator for many years, Stephanie Campbell knows all too well what it looks like when a child is struggling to learn, growing frustrated over a word, and feeling the quiet shame of falling behind in class.

It is for this and many other reasons she decided to publish her book, Alex and the Dancing Letters, which seeks to raise awareness about dyslexia, its signs, how individuals with the condition see words, and how educators can help children who learn differently.

Dyslexia is a lifelong, brainbased learning disorder that affects a person’s ability to read, write, and spell accurately. The neurodevelopmental condition changes how the brain processes written and spoken language, often resulting in individuals reading slowly, struggling to sound out unfamiliar words, or mixing up similar letters.

A long-time advocate for children who learn differently, Campbell said her interest in the special education field began at a very young age as she watched a relative struggle with reading, even as she experienced her own challenges with learning.

“I just started having this passion for learning and teaching young children. Even growing up as a kid in Jamaica, if I didn’t know it right off the bat when it was asked, just the way that you were spoken to, it sometimes made you feel ashamed not knowing something.

It just became something in my heart, and so I wanted to just help young children,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Now living in the United States, she shared that she often sees these signs play out in the classroom, and over time, became increasingly concerned about how little understanding there is around dyslexia. While hosting webinars based in Jamaica, she said it also became evident to her that there exists a lack of information and resources on the island, and she simply wanted to help bridge the gap.

“I found that a lot of families in Jamaica were just really having a lot of difficulty even understanding what’s going on with their children. I also saw where they were having a lot of difficulty getting services, based on where they were, so I had my professors online, some therapists that I know here, and some of my colleagues just to come on and to give support to families.

I’ve done it for a while, but then I realised that I wanted to reach families in Jamaica in a bigger way,” said Campbell. “I tried to reach out to the Government to see what I could do as someone who was born in Jamaica and now educated in the United States…I have so many resources in terms of knowledge…but I’ve never really had anyone reach back out.

I think it’s a really great conversation to have around not just dyslexia, but around supporting children with disabilities, whether it’s a learning disability or cognitive,” she added.

Campbell said that through conversations with Jamaican educators, she also found that geographical and financial challenges facing many families made accessing specialised support particularly difficult.

“What I’ve heard a lot is that they see signs, but there’s no help. They will often say, ‘Where do we go?’ because they are in the rural area and they have to go all the way to Kingston, or somewhere that’s out of their way and they have to pay some money, and they don’t have it.

It felt a little frustrating for me because it felt like I was giving information, and they were still pushing back to say, ‘We don’t have the support here,’” she said, adding that even when educators spot the signs, large class sizes and limited resources make it difficult for them to provide targeted support.

It is this gap that Campbell hopes to bridge. She shared that she did not write the book simply to tell a story about a child with dyslexia; she created a tool that can be used by parents and teachers.

“It will help educators in their classroom to see that they are able to find ways of seeing signs, recognising it, and the different things that they can do to help their students, even if they don’t have a special education person, or someone who’s there to necessarily support, but just to be confident that they can.

It will help them to be patient, knowing that their children are still very smart; it’s just that they learn differently,” said Campbell.

“Children are not all on the same trajectory. They are on different timelines as it relates to their learning, so somebody may learn the letter earlier, and another person may learn later. It does not mean that they can’t learn; it’s just that they learn differently, so that’s what the book is about.

It gives some strategies in there on how teachers can use it and get other readers in their classroom as well to recognise and support their friends that they see are struggling,” she added.

She stressed that the fight to help children who learn differently has to start with awareness, listing signs such as individuals experiencing difficulty learning letters and sounds, reading words, and challenges with spelling as major indicators. “I hope that this book, Alex and the Dancing Letters, will help children to recognise that they are not alone.

For a child with dyslexia, seeing a character who faces similar challenges can build confidence, reduce their feelings of frustration, and I hope it will help them understand that learning differently does not mean they are less capable,” she told the Sunday Observer.

“For parents and for teachers, this book increases, again, awareness and it encourages also conversation about how to better support children who struggle with reading…I want readers to walk away with empathy and understanding and hope. Children with dyslexia often work incredibly hard and may feel discouraged when reading is difficult. Through this book and Alex’s story, I want children to know that they are intelligent, that they’re capable, and they’re able to succeed. I also hope that the book helps families and educators recognise the signs of dyslexia and become stronger advocates for children who learn differently,” she added.

Alex and the Dancing Letters is available for purchase on Barnes and Noble, Amazon and other book retailers.

World.title: Polish police warn of possible assassination plot against Donald Tusk
World.content:
Donald Tusk speaks to the press during a press conference in the gardens of the Prime Minister's Chancellery building in Warsaw. | Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images

“We are treating this matter very seriously,” said a government spokesperson.

Polish authorities said Sunday they were investigating a possible attempt to attack the Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

Writing on X, interior ministry spokesperson Karolina Galecka said Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński and Special Services Minister Coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak had ordered measures to be taken following a “possible assassination attempt on the Prime Minister … as well as the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense.”

Officials from the police service, the government’s protection service and the Internal Security Agency held an emergency meeting Sunday at the agency’s counterterrorism center to discuss the situation.

World.title: Deutschland reicht Irlands Vorschlag zur Kürzung des EU-Haushaltsentwurfs nicht aus
World.content:
Berlin dringt an der Spitze einer Gruppe von sechs Ländern auf einen sparsameren EU-Haushalt. Zu der Gruppe gehören Schweden, Dänemark, die Niederlande, Finnland und Österreich. Die sechs Länder tragen zusammen 40 Prozent zum EU-Haushalt bei.

Der Vorschlag der EU-Kommission für den nächsten Siebenjahreshaushalt beträgt knapp 2 Billionen Euro.

Die schwedische Europaministerin Jessica Rosencrantz bezeichnete Irlands Vorschlag als „völlig unerschwingliche Erhöhung“, da der Gesamtbetrag immer noch über dem aktuellen Haushalt liegen würde.

Die österreichische Europaministerin Claudia Bauer erklärte, der neue Haushalt sei nach wie vor „meilenweit von einem österreichischen Ja entfernt“.

Der Haushalt wird auch Thema beim Gipfeltreffen der EU-Staats- und Regierungschefs am Donnerstag und Freitag in Brüssel sein.

Die EU-Regierungen wollen bis Ende des Jahres eine Einigung erzielen – bevor die Wahlen in Frankreich, Italien und Polen im Jahr 2027 die Verhandlungen zu gefährden drohen.

Die EU ist gespalten zwischen sparsamen Ländern, die auf Kürzungen dringen, und einem rivalisierenden Lager aus süd- und osteuropäischen Staaten, die sich gegen Kürzungen bei Agrarsubventionen und der regionalen Wirtschaftsförderung aussprechen. Diese Bereiche machen fast die Hälfte des Gesamtbudgets aus.

Der Artikel ist zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO erschienen.

World.title: ‘Putin will drag you into the war,’ former Ukrainian foreign minister tells Europeans
World.content:
European officials say Moscow has upped its hybrid campaign across the continent in recent months, using cyberattacks, sabotage and disinformation to disrupt critical infrastructure and weaken support for Ukraine.

Kuleba said the failed drone attack on the Leipzig airport in Germany in August was a sign of "growing preparation" for an offensive on the continent. "They see how your intelligence operates. They see how your security forces operate. They see how you react and they draw conclusions," he added.

In the aftermath of the incident, the German government concluded that Moscow was responsible for the attack, and ordered a review of security around sensitive locations.

However, Kuleba, who stood down as Ukraine's foreign policy chief in September 2024, does not think Russia is preparing a full-scale offensive beyond Ukraine. In his view, Moscow is more likely to launch an attack on NATO countries involving drones targeting key infrastructure that would test the alliance's unity and preparedness.

"The truth is that Russia does not need 400,000 more people to wage that war. It needs five drones," he said, adding that in the event of an attack, "[Europeans] can call for NATO consultations... can call for restraint. But this will only encourage Putin to make the next step ... He will always have enough drone and missile capabilities."

Kuleba no longer believes Putin can be persuaded to end the war through negotiations. "He's not looking for a solution, for a pause, and there will be no moment when he will start looking for it," he said, concluding: "Putin is a guarantee of war: anyone after Putin is a chance for peace."

World.title: Russians face EU travel curbs to prevent hybrid attacks
World.content:
That system is a security threat to Europe at a moment of heightened concern over Moscow-sponsored acts of sabotage, arson and other forms of hybrid warfare, Sweden’s Justice Minister Gunnar Strömmer told POLITICO.

“It’s obvious I think for everyone that we have vulnerabilities in our system that can be used by our enemies,” Strömmer said in an interview.

“As far as I understand things, the Commission is preparing a proposal that, according to what I have heard, should be launched in January next year. From a Swedish point of view, we would love to see it even earlier.”

Strömmer welcomed the “progress” and “growing support” for a tougher visa regime.

Other countries are planning to push the issue during Monday’s Foreign Affairs Council meeting — and also propose more restrictions on Russian diplomats in the EU.

Estonia has proposed an outright ban on allowing ex-soldiers from Russia’s armed forces access to the EU. There are around 650,000 of these former combatants, according to Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna, which would be banned “person by person.” But a tighter EU-wide approach is vital for the bloc’s security, he told POLITICO.

World.title: Germany warns EU that €159B budget cuts are not enough
World.content:
“We are still a long way from an agreement. The amount of the new proposal is not a basis for an agreement. The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the brunt of the financing,” Merz wrote in a statement on Saturday.

Germany leads a group of six “frugal” countries — Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands, Finland and Austria — which contribute 40% of the Union’s common budget.

Most frugal countries criticized Ireland’s proposed €159 billion in cuts in current prices from the Commission’s nearly €2 trillion proposal, saying they were insufficient.

Sweden’s Europe minister Jessica Rosencrantz described the negotiating document, or negobox, on X as a “wildly unaffordable increase,” as the overall amount would still be higher than the current budget.

Austrian Europe Minister Claudia Bauer echoed that criticism, saying that the new budget remained "miles away from an Austrian yes.”

Tensions will come to a head during a summit of EU leaders next Thursday and Friday, where they will discuss the negobox.

World.title: Strikes killing 17 are Russia’s ‘thanks’ for US diesel sanctions lift, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on X.

The strikes took place just one day after U.S. President Donald Trump announced he would temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel in a bid to bring soaring prices down.

Ukrainian officials were meeting on the same day with European and U.S. officials in Miami in a fresh diplomatic push to end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.

Zelenskyy criticized the deal on Friday and accused Trump of using the peace talks as a “smokescreen” while pursuing a deal with the Kremlin.

Even though the talks were supposed to last two days, the Ukrainian team decided to return home earlier then planned “because they managed to talk everything through earlier,” a senior official familiar with the matter told POLITICO. Ukraine will continue to bomb Russian oil refineries despite US-Russia deals, the official added.

The Ukrainian armed forces said Saturday they struck a major oil facility in Russia’s Samara region overnight.

World.title: Turkey bans social media for kids under 15
World.content:
The law also includes provisions for minors over 15, stating that platforms cannot offer them services that could have "an addictive effect."

Turkey has often implemented tough restrictions on social media services, frequently banning individual accounts from media outlets or activists, and at times banning access to entire platforms. Ankara banned Instagram for a week in 2024 amid claims the Meta-owned platform censored users mourning Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh.

Last week Turkey blocked a news website and its social media accounts over what a court deemed to be "LGBT propaganda," sparking outrage from human rights and media freedom groups.

A 2025 report from the U.S.-based think tank Freedom House described Turkey's internet as "not free."

Turkey joins a growing group of states, including Australia and Indonesia, that are introducing or exploring tougher age restrictions on social media access.

In September the European Union presented a legal proposal to restrict children's access to social media and video-sharing platforms until they turn 15, following months of intense pressure from EU leaders on the issue.

Austria, Denmark, France, Greece and Spain are all pushing ahead with national laws to restrict kids' access to social media. The United Kingdom is also expected to introduce a ban next year.

Canada has also presented a bill to restrict access to social media platforms for children under 16.

World.title: EU budget slashed by €159B in new Irish proposal
World.content:
