The bloc is split between frugal countries demanding cuts of several hundred billions to the nearly €2 trillion proposal on the table and a rival camp of southern and eastern states, known as the Friends of Cohesion, opposing reductions.

In a concession to the Friends of Cohesion, Ireland shielded farmers’ subsidies and regional payouts, that account for half of the total budget and are politically sensitive, from any cuts.

Instead, the bulk of the reductions came from foreign aid which was cut by €38 billion; competitiveness which was axed by €75 billion and the EU’s administrative costs which were reduced by €10 billion.

Dublin also scrapped a rainy day fund, known as the "EU Facility cushion," that allowed the European Commission to deploy cash to tackle unforeseen emergencies throughout the seven-year budget cycle.

Ireland’s Minister of State for European Affairs Thomas Byrne, who leads the negotiations, defended the proposal as a balanced compromise between 27 countries.

“We protected … the traditional policies of the Union, which are very important for the European Union and the single market. But we also very much look to the future,” Byrne told reporters.

World.title: Hochvogel mountain at risk of major collapse as 400,000 cubic metres of rock threatens to break away
World.content:
Around 2,000 cubic metres of rock broke away from the Hochvogel mountain in the Allgäu Alps in June. Now researchers are warning that another major collapse could be imminent, potentially sending up to 400,000 cubic metres crashing down the mountainside.

 

The summit itself is at risk of breaking apart, with a fissure that has existed since the 19th century steadily widening. Records suggest the crack was once about shoulder-width, but the gap is now several metres across.

Scientists have been monitoring the hotspot for twelve years, initially on field trips and, since 2018, with permanently installed sensors and measuring equipment. A drone with a laser scanner has also been deployed to the area.

In spring, measuring instruments recorded movement rates of up to five millimetres per week. In geological terms, that is extremely fast; normally the Alps shift by an average of around 1.8 millimetres per year. Readings from the early-warning system are now prompting the researchers to raise the alarm.

Hochvogel

The Hochvogel sits on the border between Germany and the Austrian region of Tyrol. It is part of the Allgäu High Alps and stands at 2,592 metres high.

The mountain has been closed to climbers approaching from the Austrian side for some time, but the ascent from Germany remains open.

At the beginning of October, a team led by geology professor Michael Krautblattler from the Technical University of Munich (TUM) climbed the peak once again to inspect the terrain and measuring instruments.

Krautblattler specialises in debris flows and rockslides and wants to "equip areas that are dangerous with intensive early-warning systems and thus be able to read properly the warning signs the mountain gives us," as he said in an interview with the German Alpine Club (DAV) in February.

Instruments transmit data around the clock

There are now more than 30 sensors on the Hochvogel, measuring the entire summit to millimetre precision and documenting movements.

In 2024, TUM described the main fissure as up to six metres wide, around 35 metres long, and about 60 metres deep.

A new crack on the south-west ridge is now regarded as a key weak point where the highest rates of movement are recorded. The scientists refer to this hotspot as "Fissure 6."

According to Krautblatter, similar early-warning systems are currently in use at only two other locations - the Partnach Gorge and the Höllental Gorge.

"There we are learning in great detail which signals the mountain gives off and how long in advance. Often, it is just days or hours. Systems like this will be vitally important in high mountain areas, because there things are going to change dramatically, beyond anything we know from experience," Krautblatter told DAV.

The weather conditions on the Hochvogel in the Allgäu Alps are leading to changes in the rock. By Martin Kraft, CC BY-SA 3.0

The researchers receive the data from the instruments systematically, several times an hour, in their offices. Krautblatter hopes the technology will help keep the Alps accessible while allowing authorities to close off danger areas before disaster strikes.

Hochvogel rockslide could be imminent

Researchers believe the mountain could be reaching a critical point and that between 250,000 and 400,000 cubic metres of debris could break away and crash down the mountainside.

Scientists believe extreme weather could be partly behind increasing movements on the mountain.

On the Hochvogel, "we can see a clear influence from heavy precipitation events, in other words intense rainfall, thunderstorms and snowmelt," Johannes Leinauer from the TU Munich team told Deutschlandfunk.

On the summit of the Hochvogel signs warn of the danger zone: a fissure is growing ever larger. Screenshot von Google Maps Street View, 8. Oktober 2026

"And these thunderstorm events are currently becoming more frequent and more intense as a result of the climate change, and that can of course affect how quickly and how often such rockfalls occur," he added.

World.title: 'Up to our people' to pick leader, Zelenskyy responds to Trump's pledge for new elections in Ukraine
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday his country could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire, pushing back against US counterpart Donald Trump's call for Ukraine to pick a new leader.

 

"First of all, with all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader", Zelenskyy told ABC News in a televised interview, a day after Trump said Ukraine needed a new president who would agree to end the war.

Zelenskyy said he told Trump's team that if they really wanted Ukraine to hold elections, "please tell Putin to give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections".

"We want peace, we are ready for a ceasefire, we are ready to begin with any kind of steps of de-escalation", Zelenskyy told ABC in a TV interview.

"And if the Russians want us not to attack their diesel, their refineries, etc., we are asking President Trump to give them a signal not to attack the energy infrastructure of Ukraine".

'Don't kill our children, we will stop attacking your diesel'

The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data centre run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.

Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than four and a half years after Moscow’s full-scale invasion.

"It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so", Zelenskyy said on X, adding that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees.

"Don't attack us. Don't kill our children. We will stop attacking your diesel. And I think it's a fair deal", he added.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed back on Trump's comments, writing on X late Saturday that Zelenskyy was leading the country through a war for its independence. "He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well", Sybiha wrote.

Trump vows for 'new leader' in Ukraine

Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.

"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does", Trump said.

The US president, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

He has sought to blame record US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.

World.title: At least 139 migrants dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says
World.content:
At least 139 migrants died after a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti earlier this week, the UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Sunday, with 84 others still missing.

 

The vessel had been carrying 305 people from Djibouti to Yemen when it sank near Guhere, north of the town of Obock, per the IOM. The incident occurred on the night of 8 to 9 October.

The death toll climbed from 109 after 30 more bodies were recovered. Among the 109 bodies initially recovered, 52 were men, 42 were women, and 15 were children, including nine girls and six boys, the IOM said in an earlier statement, adding that more than 80 people had survived the shipwreck - all Ethiopian nationals.

"This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives,” Alexandre Coissac, the IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, said. "Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance. This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities."

Search and rescue operations are ongoing, and the IOM and local authorities are providing assistance to survivors.

According to the IOM, tens of thousands of migrants travel from the Horn of Africa through Djibouti each year as they look to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and eventually reach the Gulf countries.

"Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East," the IOM said.

In March, another shipwreck off the coast of Djibouti left nine migrants dead and 45 others missing as they attempted to make the crossing to Yemen.

"Since 10 September, more than 20,000 incoming movements to Djibouti from Ethiopia have been observed by IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix," the IOM added on Sunday.

World.title: Russian army strikes Sloviansk and Kyiv as Ukrainian drones hit third Yandex data centre
World.content:
On the morning of 11 October, the Russian army struck two blocks of flats in Sloviansk in the Donetsk region.

 

"At this point, four people are known to have been injured", said the city's mayor Vadym Liakh. "Everyone is receiving medical treatment".

There may be people trapped under the rubble, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

Warehouses are on fire outside Kyiv following an overnight Russian attack. Storage facilities at an industrial plant in the Bucha district of the Ukrainian capital caught fire, and firefighters are still working to extinguish the blaze.

A paramedic and a driver were injured when a Russian drone hit an ambulance in the Sumy region. According to the head of the regional military administration, Oleh Hryhorov, the medical workers managed to get out of the damaged vehicle on their own.

Emergency power cuts were introduced on Sunday in several regions of Ukraine because of the difficult situation in the energy sector caused by Russian shelling, the press service of the national energy company Ukrenergo said.

Previously published schedules for hourly power cuts are currently not in force. The emergency outages will be lifted once the situation in the power system stabilises.

Ukrainian drones hit Yandex, third data centre targeted

Overnight into Sunday, Ukrainian drones attacked Russian technology giant Yandex's data centre in Vladimir, east of Moscow in the third reported attack on the firm in days.

The company said the centre's infrastructure had been damaged and its operations completely halted. According to the latest information, there were no casualties in the attack.

Yandex added that it is continuing to assess the state of the infrastructure and cannot yet say how long repairs will take. This is already the company's third data centre to be attacked in October.

Yandex, often dubbed "Russia's Google", runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as food-ordering and taxi apps used by tens of millions of people.

Governor Aleksandr Avdeyev confirmed (source in Russian) the UAV attack in Vladimir and the ensuing fire. He said residential areas had escaped destruction. Residents of the houses closest to the attack site have begun to be evacuated.

In Vladimir, two substations supplying electricity to 5,000 residents were switched off. An hour later, the governor said that 80% of the power supply had been restored and heating and water supplies were back to normal.

Preliminary reports suggest that a supercomputer housed at the Vladimir data centre was damaged. An identical machine is located at the Yandex data centre in Ryazan that was also targeted.

Putin inspects a working prototype of an autonomous vehicle during a visit to the headquarters of Russia's largest search engine AP Photo

Taxi and navigation disruption

In the wake of the attack, users experienced widespread disruptions to the company's services. People were unable to order taxis in Moscow, St. Petersburg, Perm, Krasnoyarsk, Vladivostok, Ulan-Ude, Yekaterinburg and other Russian cities.

"I can't get anything to work at all", said Yevgeny, a 69-year-old sitting behind the wheel of a Yandex-branded taxi near Moscow.

"I've never seen anything like this before. It hasn't happened in the last five years. Now I don't know what to do", he said.

Similar problems were reported in Serbia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia. Drivers say they cannot log into the app or are facing navigation failures, while passengers see no available cars. There have also been reports of outages across many of the company's other services.

On 9 October, drones attacked (source in Russian) Yandex's data centre in Kaluga. On the morning of 8 October, the Ukrainian armed forces struck (source in Russian) a Yandex data centre near Ryazan. After that, malfunctions began in the internal systems of major Russian companies. Websites of major Russian media outlets also stopped loading.

Ukrainian monitoring channels reported strikes on Sunday on a movable railway bridge (source in Russian) in Rostov-on-Don, near the Black Sea. The regional authorities have not yet reported it.

In early October, Russia repeatedly carried out (source in Russian) strikes on key bridges in Kyiv. According to The Telegraph, against the backdrop of military setbacks, Putin decided to switch to attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure and the bridges in Kyiv.

The crisis centre of the Krasnodar region reported that "fragments of drones" had fallen on the grounds of Sochi airport. A fire broke out in one of the administrative buildings, with no casualties. Debris also fell in a residential area.

Russia's Defence Ministry said that overnight air defence forces had shot down 479 Ukrainian drones over 17 regions of Russia and the annexed Crimea.

World.title: Riyadh airport stays shut after deadly attack as Trump says US may join Saudi strikes on Houthis
World.content:
Riyadh’s international airport remained closed on Sunday, a day after an attack killed 12 people. US President Donald Trump said Washington might join Saudi strikes against Yemen’s Houthis.

 

Asked on Saturday whether Washington would take part, Trump told reporters, “We may. We’re going to look at it.” He did not announce a decision to join the strikes.

He later said Saudi Arabia could defend itself against the Houthis and described the airport attack as “terrible”.

The Saudi-led coalition blamed the Iran-backed Houthis for the attack on King Khalid International Airport and vowed a decisive response. Saudi aviation authorities said 309 people were injured, some critically. Four Saudis and eight foreign nationals, including an American citizen, were killed.

The Houthis renewed their warning on Sunday to airlines, airport workers and travellers against using Saudi airports, saying the facilities remained vulnerable to attack.

In a separate incident, the coalition said a projectile fell near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Saturday.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the strike a “dangerous escalation” on Sunday and expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia.

“These attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” she said, warning of the threat to international transport and energy infrastructure.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres also condemned the attack.

“Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately,” he said in a statement issued on Saturday.

Qatar condemned the strike as a violation of Saudi sovereignty and a threat to civilians and aviation safety.

UN envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg warned on Sunday that the attacks threatened regional security and further complicated efforts to secure peace in Yemen.

Airlines extend Riyadh flight cancellations

Flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said the airport’s closure had been extended until midnight local time at the start of Monday, 12 October. Saudi aviation authorities had not confirmed when flights would resume.

A senior aviation source told AFP that operators had been informed at dawn that flights would remain suspended. A second aviation source said radar and communications equipment had been damaged and the runways needed to be assessed.

Etihad Airways cancelled six flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh on Sunday and a further return service on Monday. The airport urged passengers to check with their airlines before travelling there.

Emirates also cancelled Riyadh flights on Sunday and Monday, The National reported.

Lufthansa Group had already suspended flights to Riyadh through 16 October following attacks earlier in the week.

SriLankan Airlines suspended its Riyadh flights until 18 October, citing the security incident and ongoing safety assessments.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency widened its warning on Friday to cover more Saudi airspace, citing risks to civilian aircraft from missile and drone attacks, air defence activity and falling debris.

The disruption also affected schools in the Saudi capital. An email sent to parents on Sunday, seen by AFP, said schools would switch to remote learning for the week under instructions from the education ministry.

It was the second time in less than a month that schools in Riyadh had been told to move lessons online.

World.title: Macron's popularity hits lowest level since 2017 as Bardella and Le Pen also lose ground
World.content:
Protests by secondary-school pupils, a fuel crisis and a budget debate getting off to a bad start in the National Assembly, where there is no majority, the government is facing a string of difficulties that are being reflected in opinion polls.

 

Seven months before the end of his second term, Emmanuel Macron’s popularity has fallen to its lowest level since he entered the Elysée Palace in 2017, according to a new barometer published at the weekend.

According to the Ipsos BVA-Cesi survey (source in French) for La Tribune Dimanche, only 15% of those questioned have a favourable opinion of the French President, one point down from a month earlier.

The backlash is hitting the president harder than his Prime Minister. Sébastien Lecornu’s popularity has edged up slightly, gaining two points in a month: 22% of French people now view his performance positively.

Purchasing power remains the French public’s main concern, cited by 54% of respondents, a stable figure. The future of the welfare system comes second, at 44% (+4 points), ahead of the level of public debt, which worries 33% of those surveyed (+3 points).

Three far-right figures in the top five

Among the political figures seen as possible successors to Emmanuel Macron, far-right leaders Jordan Bardella and Marine Le Pen continue to dominate the rankings, with 33% and 32% favourable opinions respectively.

Their ratings have, however, slipped compared with the previous month: Jordan Bardella is down three points and Marine Le Pen four.

This fall comes in the wake of revelations by Mediapart about antisemitic and conspiracist messages attributed to Jordan Bardella, posted from an old Facebook account. The President of the Rassemblement national has denied the accusations.

The online survey was carried out on 7 and 8 October among 1,000 adults, a few days after Mediapart published its first article on the affair, on 28 September.

Behind Bardella and Le Pen, former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe takes third place, with 20% satisfied, up one point.

Sarah Knafo, a leading figure in Reconquête, the nationalist party led by Éric Zemmour, and François Hollande, the former Socialist President, round out the top five. Both receive 18% favourable opinions. Neither has yet declared a presidential bid.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the radical left’s candidate, comes next with 17 % favourable opinions, level with centrist Gabriel Attal and the Republicans’ leader, Bruno Retailleau.

The leader of La France Insoumise party nevertheless stands out for an exceptionally high rejection rate: according to the study, 69% of French people say they would be unhappy if he were to move into the Elysée.

World.title: Denmark tests humanoid robots in supermarkets to help to ease staff workload at night
World.content:
Picking up products, placing them on shelves and repeating the same movements for hours. At a Føtex supermarket near Copenhagen, robots are learning to perform one of the most time-consuming jobs in retail.

 

Developed by Danish start-up Hive Robots and built by China's Unitree, the machines have been training since June. For now, human operators guide every movement, helping the artificial intelligence learn how to handle different products.

The ambition is to have them restocking shelves independently by early 2027, working mainly at night when the supermarket is closed.

The experiment is part of a wider trial with Salling Group, Denmark's largest retailer, which has more than 2,000 stores in six European countries.

According to Føtex, workers spend between 40 and 50 per cent of their time replenishing shelves. The retailer hopes robots will eventually take on some of this repetitive physical work, giving employees more time to assist customers.

The machines could later check expiry dates, identify empty shelves and spot misplaced goods. But they still work more slowly than people and need close supervision.

Danish law would also have to change before robots could operate autonomously among shoppers. For now, the focus remains on night-time work and tasks away from customers.

World.title: Houthi war risks dragging Israel and Turkey into Horn of Africa standoff
World.content:
The escalating clash between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia now threatens to ignite the already tense rivalry between Israel and Turkey in the Horn of Africa. This week, Turkey threw its military weight behind Saudi Arabia, while Somaliland – a self-declared state recognised only by Israel – is urgently seeking Israeli military support.

Advertising

Somaliland, a breakaway state from Somalia, is calling on Israel to provide military hardware. “We need air defence systems,” Mohamed Osman Fadal, a senior foreign affairs adviser to Somaliland’s president, said in a Middle East Eye interview this month.

Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi made a similar request last month for Israeli military support.

Last December, Israel became the first nation to recognise Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991. Because of its close ties to Israel, Somaliland now fears it could become a target for the Houthis, who operate from Yemen just across the Gulf of Aden and have previously targeted Israel.

“The Houthi threat is growing; it’s a major issue,” said Gallia Lindenstrauss of the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

“Access to the Red Sea and Somaliland’s location just across from Yemen are very important, and I think this is where Israel recognises that it’s difficult to deal with the threat only from afar, and it’s important to have allies in the Horn of Africa,” she added.

Israel, which is in the midst of an election campaign ahead of the 27 October vote, has not commented on the request. But Lindenstrauss predicts a favourable response. “Obviously, if you look at the location, there should be some military support," she said.

Turkey’s backing for Somalia

Yet Somaliland’s call for military aid is fuelled by more than just anxiety over the Houthis. Somalia’s government is still intent on reclaiming Somaliland, branding it a rogue state. At the same time, Turkey has stepped up its military support for Somalia, deploying F-16s and advanced drones in January, and running its largest overseas military base to train Somali troops.

Somaliland president makes 'historic' visit to Israel

“Turkey has strong defence cooperation with Somalia; Somaliland sees that as an issue for them. It sees them as a potential future threat down the road. And so that’s why they’re calling for Israeli security support,” explained Horn of Africa analyst Omar Mahmood of the International Crisis Group.

“I think what’s happening is both sides, Somalia and Somaliland, are drawing external actors into their local dispute,” added Mahmood. “So it’s elevating what has been an unresolved but a local dispute for quite some time into something broader, something more regional.”

Tensions between Turkey and Israel have also been mounting, fuelled by Israel’s ongoing wars in Gaza and Lebanon and Ankara’s vocal support for Hamas. Both nations now see each other as an increasing threat.

“There is a security dilemma evolving between Turkey and Israel,” warns Lindenstrauss. “What Turkey does for its security, Israel sees as threatening. What Israel does for its defences in [Syria] is seen as threatening.”

Soli Ozel, an expert on Turkey at the Institut Montaigne in France, warns that because Somalia holds such strategic value for Turkey, any Israeli military involvement in Somaliland could dangerously escalate the situation.

“They may consider the deployment of Israeli missiles in Somaliland another destabilising factor,” said Ozel. “But I don’t think that the F-16s or the drones would be used against Somaliland, honestly; at least for the moment, I wouldn’t expect that to happen.”

Lebanon becomes latest battleground in Turkish-Israeli tensions

Containment, not conflict

Ozel argues that while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan are trading increasingly bellicose rhetoric, both countries are engaged in a high-stakes battle of containment rather than conflict.

“The theatrics and the realities of Turkish-Israeli relations may not be exactly the same,” explained Ozel. “I don’t think they will fight, but they are both showing their colours, right? Israel sent missiles to Somaliland; the Turks send F-16s and drones in order to set limits to what the other party will do.”

Turkey is preparing to expand its military footprint in the region. This week, Turkey and Pakistan pledged armed support to Saudi Arabia against the Houthis under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed in August, a pact binding the three nations to mutual defence.

While the specifics remain unclear, Lindenstrauss notes that despite rising friction between Turkey and Israel, both countries may still find common cause in confronting the Houthis.

“I think the recognition that the Houthis are not something that is seen as only Israel’s problem, and it’s not just a minor proxy of Iran, but it’s a major problem that many states have to join together to deal with. I think that’s actually good news,” said Lindenstrauss.

Turkey warns it could be Israel's 'next enemy' as tensions escalate

Yet Mahmood cautions that as clashes in the Red Sea escalate, Israel’s possible deployment of military hardware to Somaliland points to a worrying new trend.

“Horn actors need to realise that while they’re inviting external actors in to support their own ambitions locally, to get one step over their political adversaries, they risk turning their theatre into a wider proxy battleground. And so certainly, I think there’s a risk that those types of tensions can spill over,” he warned.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV to undergo surgery to remove lump on lung
World.content:
The pontiff said he would be operated on "in the coming days" to remove a lung nodule, which he said was found at "a very early stage."

Pope Leo XIV said Sunday that he will undergo surgery this week to remove a lump on his lung.

"During recent medical checks, a nodule on my lung was found. It has been detected at a very early stage and is very localized," the 71-year-old said during his weekly address in St Peter's Square in the Vatican.

"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it. The operation is already planned in the coming days," he added.

What do we know about the pope's condition?

This is his first major health scare since the 71-year-old American became pope in 2025.

A lung nodule is a small, contained lesion that is smaller than 3 centimeters (1 inch) and can be benign.

According to the American Thoracic Society, fewer than 5% of lung nodules turn out to be cancerous.

The American Cancer Society says the nodules sometimes appear on CT scans of the chest or abdomen during searches for trauma or lung infections that are unrelated to cancer screenings.

Leo is younger than most popes. His predecessor, Francis, was five years older when he assumed the role, while Francis' predecessor, Benedict XVI, was 78 at the start of his tenure.

Leo is not known to have had any previous health issues, and leads a relatively active lifestyle.

World.title: A migrant boat sank off the coast of Djibouti with the UN reporting over 200 people dead or missing
World.content:
The UN migration agency has reported that at least 139 people were killed and 84 remain missing after a migrant boat sank overnight on its way to Yemen. At least 80 Ethiopians survived the incident but 15 children died.

The United Nations International Organization for Migration (IOM) on Sunday said that at least 139 people were killed when a migrant boat carrying an estimated 305 people capsized off the coast of Djibouti in northeastern Africa.

At least 84 people remained missing in what is thought to be one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.

In a statement, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac called the loss of life "devastating," adding, "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities" by trying to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and reach Gulf countries.

"Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East," according to the IOM.

IOM representatives said, "Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations as fears grow for those still missing."

Djibouti to Yemen a dangerous crossing

The IOM says it has detected more than 20,000 crossings from Djibouti to Yemen — which is currently in the middle of a raging civil war — in the past month. More than 900 migrants were killed attempting the passage in 2025.

The IOM says most of those attempting to cross are from Ethiopia and Somalia. The 80 survivors from Saturday night's capsizing were all Ethiopian nationals.

The IOM on Sunday urged "donors and partners to strengthen support for Djibouti's response, including search and rescue operations and life-saving assistance."

Of the bodies so far recovered, 52 were men, 42 were women and 15 were children.

World.title: Poland on alert amid possible attack on PM, defense minister
World.content:
Poland was holding an emergency meeting after police received information about a possible assassination plot against PM Donald Tusk. The meeting comes amid a wave of violence at Polish schools this week.

Authorities in Poland were meeting on Sunday to discuss a potential assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Defence ‌Minister ⁠Wladyslaw ⁠Kosiniak-Kamysz, Interior Ministry spokesperson Karolina Galecka said.

The emergency meeting at the Internal Security Agency's (ABW) Counter-Terrorism Center was convened after police received information about a possible attack, Galecka said in a post on X.

While the nature of the apparent threat was not immediately clear, the meeting comes as Polish authorities are on high alert after a wave of violent attacks at schools in the country this week.

Poland, which borders Ukraine, has also been facing growing security threats from hybrid attacks by Russia in recent months.

What do we know about the school attacks in Poland?

Poland is reeling from three knife attacks at schools in just four days this week, which have left at least one person dead and injured many others, including children.

The first incident was on Wednesday, when a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the central Mazovian province injured nine people when he attacked his fellow students and teachers with a sharp object.

A day later, a 15-year-old killed a school caretaker and injured two others at his former school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, also in the same province. Tusk said the suspect had worn a camera mounted to his helmet to film the attack.

On Saturday, a 21-year-old woman attacked an adult education school in Warsaw, wounding three other women.

Polish police have detained 117 people across the country for carrying knives or dangerous weapons, as well as for threatening to attack schools or students. Police checked 64,000 schools, most of them in central Mazovian province.

Police said Friday that cybercrime investigators have found no evidence that a social media challenge is fueling the wave of youth violence, or that the attacks were coordinated.

What did Tusk say about the attacks?

On Sunday morning, Donald Tusk said the attacks were "spontaneous actions" that were fueled by rising "glorification of violence" online.

"We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said during the government crisis meeting.

"In the past years and months, we have noted — globally and in Poland — a rise in the fascination with violence," Tusk continued.

The prime minister blamed "nihilistic violence" for the wave of attacks, rather than a specific political ideology. However, he did acknowledge that "some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment."

Tusk added that authorities have observed an increase in online searches for Nazi or far-right content and for "mass killers who have become idols online."

The prime minister pointed to a "civilizational phenomenon" of children becoming more exposed to violence online through video games or crime stories.

Tusk added that police checks would continue at schools across the country next week to make sure children who have been exposed to these stories of knife attacks do not "get stupid and unsafe thoughts" of perpetrating copycat attacks.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: Pakistan: President puts Khan stronghold province under emergency rule
World.content:
President Asif Ali Zardari has effectively suspended the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The northwestern state is an epicenter of support for former PM Imran Khan and run by his PTI party.

Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari on Sunday announced that the northwestern Pakistani province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been put under emergency rule, effectively removing power from former Prime Minster Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.

The imposition of emergency rule comes as thousands of Khan supporters continue to stage anti-government protests and demand the former leader be released from jail.

Current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif proposed the move, which Zardari signed into order on Sunday.

The suspension of regional government was justified under constitutional articles that allow the central government to confront security threats and give it sweeping powers in emergency situations.

Sharif's government claims regional authorities have not done enough to curb Islamist violence in the province.

Authorities have set up massive roadblocks across Pakistan to keep Khan supporters at bay Image: Abdul Majeed/AFP

Why is Pakistan's government taking control of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa?

Last Sunday, thousands of Khan's supporters began to make their way from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to the Pakistani capital, Islamabad.

Organizers had declared their intent to rally hundreds of thousands more along the way in hopes of bringing about Khan's release from prison.

Despite being jailed since 2023, Khan, a popular former cricket star, maintains great influence in Pakistan, with he and his followers convinced that his imprisonment is the result of political persecution.

Khan, who began his term as prime minister in August 2018, was ousted from office in April 2022 after losing a no-confidence vote.

Khan's supporters want him released from jail Image: Faridullah Khan/DW

He has been in prison since August 2023.

Beyond corruption and treason charges, he was also accused of inciting violence after widespread anti-government protests in May 2023. Khan rejects the charges as a politically motivated plot to keep him away from power. He remains a popular political figure in Pakistan.

Khan's supporters claim that the 2024 election that brought Shehbaz Sharif back to power was rigged — an accusation the government denies.

Pakistan has seen a resurgence of terror attacks over the past several months and the Sharif government accuses Khan's PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, which is largely thought to be behind the attacks.

The PTI rejects these accusations as a baseless smear campaign.

World.title: Yemen's Houthis warn passengers not to use Saudi airports
World.content:
The warning from the Iran-backed rebels comes a day after a missile attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and injured more than 300. The airport will remain closed until at least Sunday night.

Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday warned passengers not to use airports in Saudi Arabia, a day after a deadly missile attack on Riyadh airport.

The attack, which killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300, is the deadliest on any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.

"The Yemeni armed forces renew their warning to all aviation and navigation companies, experts, staff, workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on X.

"The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theater of operations for our forces," he said, adding that the airports of Mecca and Medina, the two holiest cities in Islam, would not be targeted.

The spokesman cautioned that the rebels' warning should be taken "seriously," and that Saudi Arabia "bore responsibility" for failing to intercept the missiles that struck the airport on Saturday.

Operations at Riyadh airport, which has no military facilities, were suspended after Saturday's attack.

Air traffic monitor Flightradar24 said the airport's closure has been extended until at least 9 p.m. Sunday.

What has Saudi Arabia said about the Riyadh airport attack?

Although the Houthis have not formally claimed responsibility, Saudi officials have blamed the Iran-backed rebel group for Saturday's attack on the airport in the Saudi capital.

The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "full-fledged war crime."

Yemeni broadcaster Al Masirah TV, which is run by the Houthis, said Saudi Arabia had struck the international airport in Sanaa on Sunday afternoon.

The Houthi missile strike on Riyadh comes amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure.

The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis.

The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies, have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago.

While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humantiarian crisis.

Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How has the international community reacted to the Riyadh strikes?

US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable."

Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels.

On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport.

The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation."

"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwaves sent through the world," von der Leyen said.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation".

"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X.

The UK's defense secretary Wes Streeting slammed the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation," while the French Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.

Russia, which is a strategic partner of Iran, also condemned the Houthis' attack and called for the hostilities to end "through political and diplomatic means."

Australia, meanwhile, has urged its citizens in the Saudi capital to "shelter in place" amid the escalating attacks.
