World.title: For the Trump Administration, Kosovo is Now Just a Bargaining Chip
World.content:
Kosovo has finally broken its political deadlock, with parliament electing a new President after 20 months of wrangling that produced two early elections and brought the country to the brink of a third.

But the political turmoil is far from over. Demonstrations have erupted over the indictment of four former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, leaders and the country remains deeply divided over its political future.

For a young country still struggling to find its political footing, one thing has been conspicuously missing: the United States. Washington once played a parental role for Kosovo, stepping in to broker deals and settle disputes, as US Ambassador Christopher Dell famously did in 2011, when he helped propose a presidential candidate after Kosovo’s political leaders could not agree on one. Today, Washington appears reluctant to play that role.

Since the end of the Kosovo war, Washington has envisioned its role as having a defined endpoint: the US would win the war, and Europe would take responsibility for maintaining the peace. Kosovo, and more broadly the Balkans, would eventually become a European responsibility.

World.title: Montenegro Detains Co-Founders of Pro-Russian Telegram Channel
World.content:
Montenegrin police on Friday arrested the two co-founders of the pro-Kremlin Telegram channel Rybar, Mikhail and Valeria Zvinchuk, along with three associates, accusing them of malicious political meddling in the Balkan state.

Founded in 2018, Rybar is a prominent Russian digital propaganda and geopolitical analysis network centred around a channel on Telegram, which is reported to have more than 1.3 million followers.

The Telegram channel administrators confirmed that the Zvinchuks had been detained along with other Russian citizens. They insisted that all of them were in Montenegro legally.

“Specifically, their plans included filming the Cetinje Monastery, for which a completely official request had previously been submitted. At present, the project team is in contact with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Russia, which is working to resolve the situation,” the channel administrators wrote on Telegram.

“Since there were no violations of local legislation, we are awaiting the release of all those detained,” they added.

Mikhail Zvinchuk is a prominent Russian military blogger who has been under EU sanctions since 2023 for allegedly spreading “disinformation and pro-Russian propaganda”.

He was a member of a working group set up by Russian President Vladimir Putin in December 2022 to coordinate Russia’s mobilisation efforts in support of the war in Ukraine.

Mikhail and Valeria Zvinchuk are officially designated on the British sanctions list.

In October 2024, the US State Department offered a $10-million reward for intelligence on Rybar over allegations that it was involved in interference in the American presidential elections intended to “sow discord, promote social division, stoke partisan and racial discord, and encourage hate and violence”.

The State Department accused Rybar of “bolstering Russia’s military capabilities and advancing pro-Russian and anti-Western narratives”. Zvinchuk was one of nine named people about whom the US was seeking information.

In June 2024, Bosnian Serb authorities announced a collaboration with Zvinchuk during his visit to Bosnia’s Serb-majority Republika Srpska entity, where he met Drazen Visnjic, director of the entity’s Agency for Information and Communication Technologies.

The Agency at the time said Zvinchuk and Visnjic had agreed to cooperate on establishing a media school, as well as other projects.

World.title: Albania Parliament Approves Municipal Reform Plan Amid Protests
World.content:
The Albanian parliament in session. Photo: Photo: Malton Dibra/LSA.



After a tense session lasting more than 12 hours, Albania’s parliament voted in the early hours of Friday morning for territorial reform legislation, as people protested against the outside the building and clashed with police.

Police said eight protesters were arrested during the clashes.

Opposition Democratic Party MPs opposed the reform. One MP, Gazment Bardhi, threw bottles of water at Prime Minister Edi Rama during the vote.

The government argues that the current map of 61 municipalities no longer reflects Albania’s demographic and economic reality.

Critics, however, say the only result will be greater centralisation and the further isolation of rural communities from public services, spurring even greater depopulation.

There was some criticism of the reform within Rama’s ruling Socialist Party, too, with MP Erion Brace expressing opposition but finally voting in favour. Asked why by journalists, he said: “I am still against the reform … I will tell you tomorrow about the motives for my vote.”

The law needed 84 votes to pass. The Socialists have 83 seats. According to media, Rama ordered Socialist MPs to “either vote in favour or leave the party”. With votes from the Social Democratic Party MPs, the law passed with 85 votes in favour.

Rama later on Friday said that the vote in parliament “gave Albania another modernising push”.

Albania’s municipalities have responsibility for waste management, drinking water, urban planning, public transport, social services, environmental protection, energy efficiency, climate adaptation, civil protection and local public procurement.

The reform comes 12 years after the last shake-up in which the number of municipalities was slashed from 400 to 61.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Reports of Trump’s Attempt to Reshape Poland’s Govt Spark Political Row
World.content:
Hungary tables wealth tax; Budapest mulls bid to host 2036 Olympics

Fulfilling a campaign promise, PM Peter Magyar announced this week his government would introduce a special wealth tax on individuals whose assets exceed 1 billion forints (2.7 million euros). The draft legislation – which is still subject to debate – uses a broad interpretation of private wealth, including real estate, assets in companies, shares, and savings held in both domestic and foreign banks. Those affected would have to pay an additional 1 per cent tax, effective from August 2027, over the 1-billion-forint threshold. For wealth exceeding 100 billion forints (272.5 million euros), the tax rate would be 1.5 per cent. The government expects the wealth tax to affect around 15,000 people in Hungary and generate an additional 800 billion forints (2.2 billion euros) in revenue over the next four years. According to Forbes magazine, the number of ultra-wealthy individuals who would come under the 1.5 per cent threshold is only around 35 or 36. As the wealth tax would be imposed on individuals, many families can breathe a sigh of relief, as their wealth would be assessed on an individual basis. Critics, however, warn that wealth taxes imposed on billionaires have not necessarily been successful internationally and could trigger an exodus of some individuals. To prevent people from circumventing the system, the Hungarian government would introduce a ten-year period during which those whose wealth was accumulated in Hungary would remain liable for the tax, regardless of their country of residence.

Hungary has expressed interested in hosting the 2036 Olympic Games, as was revealed by the International Olympic Committee this week. Under the previous government of Viktor Orban, which was keen to use international sporting events to burnish Hungary’s reputation, the country considered bidding to host the 2024 Olympics, but was forced to withdraw its application in 2017 after the newly established Momentum party collected more than 260,000 signatures in support of a referendum against the plan. Experts say that most of the sports infrastructure needed to host the Olympics has already been built over the past decade, largely due to Orban’s strong interest in sports. Budapest – and Hungary more generally – would now be well suited to hosting the Games, they say. The capital has already hosted the World Athletics Championship in 2023, while its swimming facilities are due to host the 2027 World Aquatics Championships, meaning that organising the Olympics would not require massive additional investment in sports infrastructure. A so-called Budapest Olympics Masterplan was already submitted in March by the previous government. The plan envisages a “regional Games”, with some basketball and golf events staged in Austria and Slovakia hosting equestrian events. Surfing would be held in Ericeira, Portugal. Gergely Karacsony, the mayor of Budapest, has cautiously floated the plans several times throughout the year, while PM Magyar also expressed support for hosting the Olympics in earlier interviews. “As the sports infrastructure required to host the Olympic Games has already been built in Hungary in recent years, an Olympic bid that involves no stadium construction and requires no significant investment in sports infrastructure is both feasible and realistic,” hvg.hu quoted the mayor’s office as saying. The costs are estimated at 5.5 billion euros, with 90 per cent expected to come from the private sector, while the projected economic benefits are estimated at 4.7 billion euros. According to a recent Median poll, 64 per cent of Hungarians would support hosting the Olympics. This is a considerable increase from the 50 per cent polled only two years ago. The list of countries competing with Hungary for the 2036 Games currently includes Germany, Turkey, South Africa, South Korea and Qatar.

World.title: Kosovo President’s Election Kindles Hope of Return to Stability
World.content:
Justina Shiroka Pula was inaugurated as Kosovo’s President on Wednesday after two days of unrest, three weeks of peaceful protests, and almost two years of political crisis.

The day before, Pristina woke up to the lingering smell of tear gas, which the Kosovo police had used to disperse a protest that turned violent on Monday night.

The protesters were demanding legal changes to curb the jurisdiction of the Hague-based Kosovo Specialist Chambers, after it convicted four former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, leaders of war crimes.

On Tuesday, Kosovo also braced for the announcement of a new snap parliamentary election, as October 6 was the deadline for MPs to elect a new head of state. If the deadline expired, new polls would have been obligatory under the constitution.

World.title: ‘ChatGPT Diagnosed Me’: Patients’ Faith in AI Leaves Albania’s Doctors Feeling Frustrated
World.content:
After three intensive sessions and a series of specialised tests, Albanian psychologist Sonila Jaupbashi realised that the patient sitting across from her was not suffering from obsessive-compulsive disorder, or OCD.

The young woman, a third-year medical student in Germany, insisted she had been suffering from OCD for years.

“I had spent time and three difficult sessions, using specialised tests and questionnaires that are used to establish this diagnosis, and she had spent quite a lot of money,” Jaupbashi recalled to BIRN.

“Later, she admitted that she had been diagnosed by ChatGPT.”

World.title: Will Croatian Pantheon Project be Completed Within the Deadline?
World.content:
October the 11th, 2026 – The massive and controversial Croatian Pantheon project has been a hot topic for a multitude of reasons, but will it actually be completed within the prescribed deadline?

The controversial Croatian Pantheon project is a data centre with a capacity of one gigawatt which would enable the employment of several thousand people during construction and later on. Poslovni reports that the Pantheon project is proceeding according to the planned schedule and should be completed within the set deadline, entrepreneur Jako Andabak revealed on Friday. Together with American partners, he stands behind the realisation of the Pantheon data centre in Topusko, worth a staggering 50 billion euros.

A solid and high-quality network

Andabak made the statement as part of the third edition of the Master Business Forum (MBF), a platform that brings together leaders of the business community, experts and institutional representatives from the region and beyond, which was held in Rovinj and gathered more than 80 speakers from the public, private and academic sectors. It is a data centre with a capacity of one gigawatt that would enable the employment of several thousand people during construction and later. In addition to the technological components, the construction of a 500-megawatt solar power plant is planned. With the project whose start is planned for 2027 and the start of the centre’s operation in 2029, Croatia will rank at the very top of the European and world technology industry because the latest solutions open up the possibility of development in wider application, Andabak said.

“We decided on putting it in Topusko because there we have land where it’s possible to realise a project that will not harm nature and the environment. By building a solid and high-quality network we will create the conditions for stable and safe power supply without impact on the environment, which has also been confirmed by a study,” Andabak emphasised. He added that the centre will exploit its own wells and use its own water sources and its own solution for cooling the system.

The potential of empty land

“There are solutions that I carry from childhood which say that when everyone does their part of the work, then everything is done simply,” Andabak said. He added that he has dealt with many things, and only a year ago he began to think about data centres. He also explained how the whole idea came about, and it started with livestock farming and sheep. “Back during the nineties, Croatia was home to a million sheep, and now that number is in the thousands. When you see data like that, you ask yourself how to utilise that empty land and potential,” Andabak said and added that solar first came to mind. As he stated, the area is very interesting in all segments, from cooling to energy supply.

Locals in Topusko have been vehemently against the giant Pantheon data centre, however, and concerns remain for the environment and for water usage regardless of reassurance that no harm will be done.

World.title: Why Do Croatian Motorways Cost So Much When There are Constant Disruptions?
World.content:
October the 11th, 2026 – Croatian motorways cost a lot to use, but why is this the case when there are constant road works and extensive disruptions?

Drivers in Croatia pay the full price of tolls even on motorway sections where, due to road works, traffic is slowed, doesn’t flow, is full of bottlenecks, closed traffic lanes and speed restrictions. It’s very clear that such conditions can prolong the journey, but the price of the toll remains the same. Index’s text problematised the introduction of an expensive and complex toll collection system instead of simpler vignettes, such as those used by neighbouring Slovenia. It also warned about the very high costs of using Croatian motorways, opening the question precisely opened of why drivers need to pay the full fees even when, due to works, they cannot use the motorway under normal conditions.

Vedran Salvia reports that anyone who regularly uses Croatian motorways knows very well how frequent the works are, because of which queues form that prolong the journey itself. On individual sections, these burdensome works last for many months. For example, on the A3 motorway between Nova Gradiška and Lužani, works on doing up the carriageway have been ongoing since September, with completion scheduled for mid-November. On the A1 motorway between Gornja Ploča and Sveti Rok, the rehabilitation of two bridges began at the beginning of October and is due to last until the beginning of December. In both cases traffic on part of the motorway is two-way on one carriageway. Those are only some of the works currently being carried out on Croatian motorways.

hac remains silent

According to the applicable Toll Collection Act, the possibility of granting discounts exists, but the regulations do not provide for a reduction in price due to works or difficult driving conditions. Neither do HAC’s General Terms of Use of the motorway and toll collection provide for a special refund of money in cases when, due to works, traffic takes place on a narrowed carriageway or with speed restrictions. HAC was asked for additional clarification on whether there is a legal possibility of reducing the toll during works and under what conditions such a discount could be introduced.

In addition to asking HAC for a legal clarification of that possibility, they were also asked whether they have ever considered introducing temporary discounts. We also requested data on the scope of works and the total kilometrage of motorways affected by bottlenecks and the closing of traffic lanes during 2025 and 2026. By the time the text was closed we had not received an answer.

croatia charges enormous tolls

The question of charging the full toll during works gains particular importance when the high prices of using Croatian motorways are taken into account. Drivers for non-small amounts expect corresponding quality of service, which also opens the broader question of the relationship between the price and what they receive in return. The toll Zagreb – Split for a passenger car amounts to 26.40 euros in one direction, or 52.80 euros for a return trip. Even with the ENC discount of 21.74 percent, three return trips cost around 124 euros. As a counter-argument, it could be said that the toll is paid according to the kilometres travelled, and not according to the time spent on the motorway, so road works should not affect the price. But that does not mean that it is all the same under what conditions one drives. One takes the motorway precisely in order to travel faster and with fewer delays. In Croatia, however, works and bottlenecks are very frequent, so it isn’t remotely unreasonable that drivers expect normal driving conditions when paying such sums.

slovenia smartly extends the validity of vignettes during such works

That it is perfectly possible to compensate drivers for difficult driving conditions is also shown by the example of neighbouring Slovenia. The Slovenian parliament in November last year adopted a law by which, due to numerous works and reduced motorway throughput, it extended the validity of annual electronic vignettes by four months, without additional costs. The measure applied to all annual vignettes that were valid on the 1st of December 2025, and the extension was carried out automatically. The Slovenian Ministry of Infrastructure explained that the aim of the measure was a fairer relationship towards drivers who, due to works, suffered worse travel conditions on the roads.

additional road users could be attracted by lower fees

However, does that mean that they should not pay the full price of the toll? Marko Ševrović, associate professor and vice-dean of the Faculty of Transport and Traffic Sciences in Zagreb, told Index that he understands drivers’ dissatisfaction, but warns that the problem must also be viewed from the perspective of traffic planning. “I understand that users look from their perspective and ask themselves why they pay the full price when the driving conditions are worse. But imagine that on a section we already have a jam due to reduced capacity and then we also lower the price. What will we achieve by that?

I believe that a reduction of the toll during works would be unusual, but also counterproductive. A lower price could attract additional traffic precisely to the sections on which traffic capacities are already reduced due to works. The goal in such situations should be to reduce traffic on those sections, and not to further encourage it. If there is an alternative road, it would make more sense to reduce the price of its use and thus encourage drivers to avoid the section on which works are being carried out,” our interlocutor believes.

road works go on for much too long in croatia

He emphasises that the problem is that the works last too long in Croatia, and become a constant source of irritation to all road users as a result.

“That’s partly a consequence of the situation in the construction sector. Contractors do not have enough workers, the costs of labour and materials have risen significantly, so savings are made on the number of employees and work shifts. The works could be completed significantly faster, but that is the current situation. We have a public procurement system that in practice favours the lowest price. In doing so, it is not calculated how much society loses due to long-lasting works. Because of such an approach deadlines are often exceeded and the works drag on. That is not only a problem of HAC, but also of state roads and city thoroughfares, which we also see in Zagreb,” he says.

neighbouring italy also does things differently

That it’s possible to regulate toll collection during works differently is also shown by the example of neighbouring Italy, which, similarly to Croatia, charges tolls according to the distance travelled. There drivers on the network of the largest Italian concessionaire Autostrade per l’Italia and related companies can obtain a partial or full refund of money if works significantly impede or prolong their journey. Such a system has existed for several years, and from June this year new rules are applied that have expanded drivers’ rights, as also reported by the Italian news agency ANSA.

An interesting example also comes from Spain, where courts sided with drivers over the charging of the full toll during works on a motorway in Galicia. The Supreme Court in 2025 ruled that charging the full amount during major delays was an unfair practice, thereby opening the way for a refund of money to the affected drivers.

In a separate procedure, about which the local newspaper La Voz de Galicia wrote, the court recognised a group of 21 plaintiffs, mostly craftsmen and local carriers, the right to a refund of half of the paid toll amount due to significantly worse driving conditions. The same question that was raised was also opened back in 2023 in the French Senate, where it was problematised why drivers pay the full toll when works prolong the journey and reduce the quality of service. The French Government replied that the prices are determined by concession contracts and that their reduction would require legislative changes or changes to the contracts, with possible financial compensation to the concessionaires. It also warned that such costs could be compensated by a later increase in tolls.

World.title: Croatian Geophysicist Explains What Sort of Winter Awaits Croatia as El Niño Bites
World.content:
October the 11th, 2026 – A Croatian geophysicist has explained what sort of winter awaits Croatia this year as what is perhaps the strongest El Niño takes hold.

The well known climate phenomenon El Niño is rapidly strengthening and could become the strongest since measurements began. Index reports that according to the latest forecast by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the peak is expected to arrive in December, and it’s almost certain that El Niño will last until February next year. Croatia could, as a direct result, expect an above-average warm and rainy winter.

Academician Mirko Orlić from the Department of Geophysics of the Faculty of Science in Zagreb explained for Dnevnik Nova TV what the strengthening of this phenomenon could mean for Croatia and warned about the combination of an extremely warm Adriatic and atmospheric disturbances.

croatia can expect an above-average warm winter

“We have two sources of information. One is what happened during previous similar El Niños – and three such have been recorded since the middle of the last century – and each time it was above-average warm. Second, the models that provide seasonal forecasts show the same: it will be above-average warm. Therefore, that is realistic to expect,” Orlić said. El Niño occurs when the surface layer of the sea in the central and eastern part of the equatorial Pacific warms above usual values. This changes atmospheric circulation and weather patterns around the planet and in certain regions increases the risk of droughts, floods and extreme temperatures.

According to the WMO, the average deviation of the sea surface temperature in the key Pacific area during the period from October to December could reach 3.7 degrees above normal, which would surpass the previous record.

a warmer adriatic could increase precipitation

Orlić warned that the winter in Croatia could also be above-average when it comes to rainfall. A considerably warmer Adriatic Sea plays an important role in this.

“Both sources of information, previous cases and forecast models, say that it will be above-average wet, with above-average amounts of precipitation this winter. But there is also another reason – the exceptionally warm sea. This summer on the open Adriatic we recorded temperatures of 28 and 29 degrees, that is, significantly higher than the usual 27 degrees back in August,” he said. He explained that the sea has accumulated a large amount of heat, which can contribute to strong atmospheric instabilities when colder and moist air arrives over the area. “If moist and cold air arrives over such a surface, that is a real recipe for great instability and heavy precipitation,” Orlić warned.

Weather conditions in Croatia will not be influenced only by El Niño. Orlić also warned about processes in the Arctic, where warming is more pronounced than in the rest of the world. Due to the reduction of the temperature difference between the Arctic and the equator, patterns of atmospheric circulation can change, including the position and waviness of the jet stream, which plays an important role in shaping the weather over Europe. “Figuratively speaking, this winter above our heads we’ll have a battle – El Niño on one side and Arctic processes unfolding on the other. If El Niño prevails, the changes will probably be milder and will alternate more quickly. If the Arctic processes prevail, the disturbances will be greater and will pass more slowly,” he explained.

potential food production disruption

A strong El Niño could also have consequences for world agriculture because it changes the distribution of precipitation and increases the risk of droughts in certain production regions. Orlić recalled the previous El Niño from 2023 and 2024, when a weaker cocoa harvest contributed to a large rise in chocolate prices.

“Since this El Niño is significantly stronger, it’s only logical to expect disruptions,” he concluded. Nevertheless, seasonal forecasts do not mean that every part of Croatia will have an equally warm and rainy winter, nor do they enable reliable prediction of individual storms or floods several months in advance. They indicate an increased probability of certain weather patterns, and their development will also depend on other atmospheric factors.

World.title: Croatian Geothermal Wells Explored in Four Areas
World.content:
October the 11th, 2026 – Croatian geothermal energy potential is enormous, with wells currently being explored in four different areas.

Velika Gorica, Osijek, Vinkovci and Zaprešić could be heated with geothermal energy by as early as 2030, it was announced at the signing of the Grant Agreement “Investment in the Development of Geothermal Energy”, worth 35 million euros. Ana Blaskovic reports for Poslovni that geothermal energy should serve for heating households, schools, kindergartens and other public buildings, and a total of 86 million euros will be invested in the project in two phases.

Geothermal deposits have so far been confirmed by research in the mentioned four cities. The contract that represents the basis for the construction of additional wells was signed by Minister of Economy Ante Šušnjar, Director of the Central Agency for Financing and Contracting Dragan Jelić and President of the Management Board of the Croatian Hydrocarbon Agency Marijan Krpan.

Above-average potential

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković pointed out that Croatia has a significantly greater geothermal potential than is commonly thought. Geothermal energy, he said, will be very useful for heating, and the state is approaching it strategically in order to improve the conditions for the use of this energy source in the long term. “This is domestic, renewable and low-carbon energy,” Plenković emphasised, stressing that, unlike energy that depends on the sun or wind, it is available regardless of weather conditions and that geothermal equipment does not take up much space. In the first phase geothermal deposits have been confirmed, while in the second technical preconditions for their sustainable use will be created. For the construction of additional geothermal wells 30 million euros of non-repayable funds from the European Regional Development Fund have been secured. The total value of that project amounts to 35 million euros, while more than 50 million euros have already been secured through the NRRP for the exploration of geothermal potential.

Pannonian Basin

“Croatian geothermal potential is not the future; it’s a reality that the country still needs and must fully utilise. In the Croatian part of the Pannonian Basin the geothermal gradient is as much as 60 percent higher than the European average,” said Minister of Economy Ante Šušnjar. The geothermal gradient denotes the increase in temperature in the Earth’s interior with increasing depth and is a key indicator for assessing the potential for exploiting geothermal energy.

In Zaprešić, geothermal energy should enable the heating of sports halls, schools, kindergartens, swimming pools, the municipal company and a new business zone. Vinkovci are planning a central heating system that would meet the needs of 1,700 households as well as the heating needs of schools and other public institutions. In Velika Gorica geothermal energy should cover more than 60 percent of the population, while Osijek has assessed the project as strategic for the city’s economy, agriculture and energy independence. According to Marijan Krpan, if everything goes according to plan, works should begin in 2028 and the project be operational in 2030.

World.title: Hajduk Beats Dinamo 2-1 in Poljud Derby
World.content:
Hajduk beat Dinamo 2-1 in the first derby of the season at a rain-soaked Poljud on Saturday, with a spectacular Bamba strike settling a match that ran 14 minutes into stoppage time and saw Dinamo hit the post at the death.

Hajduk and Dinamo met at Poljud on Saturday in the ninth round of the SuperSport HNL. It was also a meeting of the league’s top two, with both sides coming into the match on 16 points, the same tally as third-placed Osijek.

Igor Pajač of Sveti Ivan Zelina refereed the derby, with Ivan Bebek of Rijeka on VAR duty. Pajač was assisted by Bojan Zobenica of Velika Gorica and Ivan Starčević of Bjelovar, with Dario Bel of Osijek as fourth official. Goran Pataki of Đakovo was the assistant VAR.

Poljud was nearly a sellout, even though heavy rain was forecast, which luckily didn’t start until about the 30th minute. And it was relentless until the end.



Lineups

Hajduk: Silić – Acapandie, Raci, Marešić, Hrgović – Del Moral, Fayad – Bamba, Dalisson, Šotiček – Šego

Dinamo: Kotarski – Tabinas, Dominguez, McKenna, Vinlof – Zajc, Kravcov, Kačavenda – Lisica, Beljo, Ivanušec

Match report

Dinamo were the first to threaten in the highly anticipated ‘Eternal Derby’. In the 4th minute they worked the ball down the left, Ivanušec played in Zajc, and his cross found Lisica, whose shot caused little danger.

Hajduk’s reply two minutes later was a far better chance. Bamba burst past Vinlof on the wing and crossed into the middle, where Šego met the ball in an excellent position but sent his shot over the bar.

Dinamo went close from a corner in the 11th minute. Ivanušec delivered, McKenna headed the ball across to the far post, and Kačavenda could not get the touch needed to turn it in. Three minutes later Beljo was booked after a duel with Del Moral.

Beljo made his mark in the 21st minute. Vinlof sent in a superb cross and the striker, left alone in the penalty area, simply guided his header into the net to give Dinamo a 1-0 lead at Poljud.

But Hajduk hit back almost immediately. In the 24th minute, Hrgović whipped in an excellent set-piece delivery, and McKenna clumsily turned the ball into his own net to make it 1-1.

There was controversy in the 31st minute. Dalisson found Šego with a ball over the top, and he looked for Šotiček in the middle, but Kotarski gathered. As the Dinamo goalkeeper went to kick the ball clear, Šotiček crept up behind him and took it off him, only for referee Pajač to stop play, to the fury of the home crowd.

Hajduk had taken over possession and control by the 38th minute. In the 43rd minute Beljo was left alone again, this time from a Zajc cross, but he failed to connect cleanly. A minute later Silić’s poor clearance went straight to Vinlof, who set up Ivanušec, and the Hajduk goalkeeper made amends by saving the shot.

Two minutes of stoppage time were added as a torrential downpour swept over Poljud, and the sides went in level at 1-1.

Dinamo started the second half on the front foot. In the 48th minute, an attack down the right began with a Lisica cross, which Beljo knocked down, but Kravcov could not make clean contact with the ball.

Hajduk broke forward in the 55th minute, with Bamba racing towards the Dinamo goal and only McKenna ahead of him. Teammates were arriving in support, but he chose to shoot, and his effort was blocked.

Four minutes later he made no mistake. In the 59th minute, Bamba latched onto a loose ball after a cross had been cleared and thundered a shot towards goal, leaving Kotarski helpless and putting Hajduk 2-1 up with a spectacular strike!

Raci was booked in the 62nd minute for a hard foul on Kačavenda.

Dinamo responded with a triple substitution in the same minute, as Galešić, Stojković and Almena came on for Tabinas, Lisica and Kačavenda, with Almena jeered by the home crowd as he entered. Play was briefly halted in the 66th minute because of flares.

Stojković nearly made an immediate impact in the 70th minute. Given far too much room on the edge of the penalty area, he sent his shot just wide. Kovačević then went all out in attack, bringing on Dani Rodríguez for Zajc.

Hajduk should have settled it a minute later. Bamba broke down the right once more and picked out Šotiček, alone at the far post. It looked like match point for Hajduk, but Šotiček slipped and never got his shot away.

Dinamo made their final change in the 73rd minute, with Valinčić replacing Domínguez. Two minutes later, the ball was worked through the middle to Stojković, who moved it on to Rodríguez on the right, and Silić dealt with his shot.

Hajduk made their first substitution in the 76th minute, as goalscorer Bamba came off for Šutalo.

The match was stopped again in the same minute. After the earlier flares from the Bad Blue Boys, this time it was Torcida’s pyrotechnics that brought play to a halt. The interruption dragged on, with García heading to the dressing room in the 78th minute, and play did not resume until the 82nd.

Šutalo tested Kotarski in the 87th minute with a fierce shot towards the near corner, which the Dinamo goalkeeper saved. Hajduk then made a triple substitution in the 89th minute, with Dendoncker, Hadžikadunić and Melnjak coming on, and Fayad and Raci among those making way.

Twelve minutes of stoppage time were signaled at the end of the 90, and by then the rain had turned the match into something closer to water polo. Conditions were almost unplayable, with the ball barely moving across the sodden pitch. In the fourth minute of added time, referee Pajač called both coaches over for a conversation, and play was briefly suspended before resuming in the 97th minute.

Dinamo threw everything forward in the closing minutes, pumping crosses and long throw-ins into the box in search of an equalizer as the drama stretched deep into stoppage time.

Hajduk made one more change in the 14th minute of stoppage time, with Martin replacing Dalisson, and the real drama followed straight after. Beljo struck the post, and Dinamo wasted another good chance as the attack continued. The score did not change, and Hajduk held on for a 2-1 win.

The win takes Hajduk to 19 points, three clear of Dinamo.

Hajduk coach Gonzalo Garcia spoke after the match.

“This means so much to me. This is what football is all about. This team has heart, and the lack of heart and passion makes us lose games. Tonight, we had it all.”

World.title: The Empty Croatian Hotel That Has Been Waiting for its First Guests for 18 Years
World.content:
October the 10th, 2026 – There’s an empty Croatian hotel that has been waiting for its very first guests for 18 long years. It boasts 36 rooms that nobody has ever stayed in.

The somewhat eerie Hotel Velebitska kraljica by the A1 was constructed 18 years ago and has never received a single guest. After six tenders and two failed contracts, it is still waiting for an investor. Putni kofer writes that most of those who have driven from the interior to the coastline have noticed a large red-and-white complex that stands right next to the A1. It appears just after you exit the Sveti Rok tunnel on the way to the sea.

the velebitska kraljica hotel has stood empty for almost two decades

Only recently, when I again passed the Maruni rest area where Hotel Velebitska kraljica stands, did I realise what was strange about it. No matter how many times I had driven past there over all these years, I had never noticed a larger number of people or parked cars; the space was always somehow eerily empty. I only discovered the explanation for that a few days ago. Although it looks like a hotel that is just about to open its doors, that “just about” has already lasted for eighteen years. Hotel Velebitska kraljica was built back in 2008, has three floors and 36 rooms, and the accommodation section has never received a single guest. The restaurant and shop operated for a while, but the hotel part remained unfinished. And this is where the story becomes interesting. Because it is not a ruin hidden far from view, but a large hotel right next to one of the busiest roads in Croatia.

IT ALL STARTED WITH THE so-called “KING OF PROSCIUTTO”

The story begins in 2006. The company Mataš-M.N., behind which stood the Posedarje entrepreneur Mladen Nekić, then concluded a contract with Croatian Motorways on the use of land at Maruni, according to Tportal. Nekić was known as a successful producer of prosciutto, so the media nicknamed him the “king of prosciutto”. The idea was clear: to create a year-round catering and accommodation complex where rivers of cars pass towards the sea during the season. The construction of Velebitska kraljica was financed by a loan from the Croatian Postal Bank of 22.4 million kuna, or around three million euros, and in 2009 HAC assessed the value of the complex at around 27.84 million kuna. Everything then looked like a project that had both location and logic.

THE HOTEL REMAINED, but THE BUSINESS DISAPPEARED

The financial crisis arrived before the hotel welcomed its first guests. Mataš-M.N. ended up in bankruptcy in 2010, and the assets and obligations were taken over by another of Nekić’s companies, Jasen. It too later ended up in bankruptcy. From that moment Hotel Velebitska kraljica became the subject of a long-standing dispute. The building stands, looks finished and is located on a site that many caterers would desire, but for years it could not be normally disposed of. In June 2023, the Municipal Court in Zadar ruled that Nekić must hand the facility over to the Republic of Croatia. The County Court in Split confirmed the decision on 15 May 2024, and in November of the same year the complex was handed over to the state through enforcement proceedings, and then to Croatian Motorways.

AS MANY AS SIX TENDERS HAVE BEEN HELD

The first three tenders ended without a single bid. In the fourth HAC lowered the price and adapted the concept. Additional accommodation capacities were abandoned, and TRCZ and Pag Spa Hotel, behind which stand Chinese investors, appeared. Both bids fell through because the bidders did not prove the required capability. The fifth procedure, announced in 2025, brought an interesting turn. Among those interested was again Mladen Nekić, the man who originally built the hotel. The job was nevertheless awarded to Flota Energy from Sesvete.

THE STATE DEMANDS ONE THING, but all INVESTORS want ANOTHER

The contract was signed, but the company did not provide the required guarantee and withdrew. The sixth tender attracted only one bidder, the company Degusto from Grebaštica. HAC declared its bid the most favourable in February this year, and the contract was signed at the end of the same month. The plan was first to arrange the facility and open the catering section, and to prepare the hotel for the next season. HAC, however, demanded a bank guarantee of 300,000 euros. Degusto warned that this amount would slow down the renovation and proposed a smaller one. The condition remained the same, the guarantee was not delivered on time and the contract was already automatically terminated in March.

the hotel awaits successful investors… still

According to the latest available information from August 2026, Velebitska kraljica still has no investor. The state has twice found an interested party, twice a contract has been signed and both attempts have failed before the start of renovation, both times over the guarantee. Perhaps that is precisely the most reliable lesson of this story. The building is not the problem: it stands, it is visible and it is located on a road that millions of travellers pass every year. The problem is in the gap between what the state demands and what investors can or want to offer. Until then drivers will continue to slow down before the Sveti Rok tunnel, stare at the red-and-white floors and wonder what purpose is served by a hotel that has never opened its doors to anyone. The queen on Velebit is still waiting; we can only hope that one day she will finally welcome her first guests.

World.title: Croatian Tourist Results for 2026 Satisfying at Over 20 Million Arrivals
World.content:
October the 10th, 2026 – Croatian tourist results for 2026 are more than satisfactory with over 20 million arrivals and around 150 million overnight stays recorded.

Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina said that Croatia is recording good tourist results this year and that more than 20 million arrivals and around 105 million overnight stays have been achieved so far. Index reports that according to data from the eVisitor system, from the beginning of the year to the end of September 20.1 million arrivals and 104.9 million overnight stays were recorded. That is two percent more arrivals and one percent more overnight stays than in the same period last year. In September alone 2.6 million arrivals and 14.3 million overnight stays were achieved, which is growth of three percent in both cases. “With the physical tourist results and financial indicators we can certainly be both happy and satisfied,” Glavina said after today’s Government session.

revenue increases from foreign visitors

Glavina also singled out the financial results of tourism. According to data from the Croatian National Bank, revenues from foreign tourists in the first six months of this year amounted to 4.587 billion euros, which is almost five percent more than in the same period last year. In the second quarter 3.642 billion euros in revenues were achieved. Domestic tourism is also recording growth. In the first six months domestic guests achieved 1.5 million arrivals and 4.2 million overnight stays, or seven percent more arrivals and six percent more overnight stays than last year. Glavina expects that the good results will continue until the end of the year, especially through the post-season and Advent events. The Days of Croatian Tourism will be held on 19 and 20 November in Poreč, when the line will traditionally be drawn under the tourist year and annual awards presented.

a major investment in split’s sport infrastructure

Glavina also commented on today’s Government decision on a major investment cycle in Split’s sports infrastructure. The Croatian Government gave consent for the co-financing of the renovation and modernisation of the Gripe Sports Centre, Spaladium Arena and the Park mladeži Sports Centre. The total value of these investments is estimated at 72.7 million euros, of which the state through the Ministry of Tourism and Sport will provide 54.5 million euros. At Gripe, a comprehensive reconstruction and energy renovation is planned, at Spaladium Arena construction rehabilitation and the renovation of technical and safety systems, and at Park mladeži the reconstruction of the football and athletics stadium.

“This is a major impetus for the development of sports infrastructure, because these buildings are in a rather poor condition due to the passage of time, and they are capital and important for holding sports events, preparation and the creation of athletes,” Glavina said. The investments are also linked to Split’s preparations for the European University Games 2028, but the Ministry states that the goal is to long-term renovate facilities that will remain available to athletes and citizens even after the competition.

Glavina also said that his Ministry will achieve around 22 million euros in savings through the budget revision. He claims that this will not mean abandoning the announced projects, but that some of them will be implemented with a different dynamic. “Everything we promised and planned we will also realise, just with a slightly different time dynamic,” he concluded.

World.title: Committee: Croatian Prisons are Too Overcrowded
World.content:
October the 10th, 2026 – The Croatian Helsinki Committee for Human Rights has warned that Croatian prisons are too overcrowded.

Index reports that the aforementioned committee has said that Croatian prisons and penitentiaries and called for greater use of alternative sanctions, conditional release and other measures that would reduce the number of people behind bars. The HHO states that it is increasingly receiving complaints from prisoners about lack of personal space, hygiene, healthcare, the conduct of individual officials and an ineffective complaints system. “The central problem, overcrowding, turns into a chain of other violations: lack of personal space, impaired hygiene and privacy, more difficult healthcare, a higher risk of violence, limited opportunities for work and education,” the HHO said.

some croatian prisons have an occupancy exceeding 200%

The problem of overcrowding in Croatian prisons is also confirmed by official data. According to the latest report of the Ombudsperson, at the end of 2025 the Croatian prison system was 126 percent full, meaning that there were 1,033 more people in prisons and penitentiaries than the existing accommodation capacity. The situation is even worse in closed conditions, where occupancy reached 142 percent. The prison in Osijek was at 205 percent of capacity, Karlovac at 195 percent, Varaždin at 191, Zadar at 188, Dubrovnik at 184, Zagreb at 180, Rijeka at 159, and Split at 151 percent. The Council of Europe, according to data for the beginning of 2025, ranked Croatia among European countries with serious prison overcrowding, with 123 prisoners for every 100 available places.

The Ombudsperson particularly warns that frequent ordering of investigative detention contributes to overcrowding. At the end of last year, investigative detainees accounted for as much as 41 percent of all persons in Croatian prisons and penitentiaries. During the whole of 2025, 16,797 people passed through the prison system. The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture, after its visit to Croatia in 2022, concluded that overcrowding is a serious problem, especially in investigative detention and closed departments, and recommended wider application of alternative sanctions, electronic monitoring and probation.

issues with mould and healthcare

The HHO states that prisoners report unhygienic sanitary facilities, showers without partitions, damp, mould, poor ventilation, pests, lack of hygiene supplies and high temperatures. A particular problem, the HHO claims, is healthcare. Complaints relate to long waits for doctors, dentists and specialist examinations, as well as a shortage of doctors, nurses and psychiatrists. The HHO also reports complaints about insults and belittling of prisoners, routine use of restraints during transport, and responses to their complaints that they describe as delayed and formulaic. These are claims from the complaints received by the HHO, and it does not follow from the statement itself that every individual allegation has been independently verified.

the european courts are concerned

The HHO also recalls the judgement of the European Court of Human Rights in the case of Muršić v. Croatia. The Grand Chamber of that court found that in multi-occupancy cells less than three square metres of personal space per prisoner creates a strong presumption of a violation of the prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment. In the specific case the Court found a violation of the European Convention during 27 consecutive days in which the prisoner in Bjelovar prison had less than three square metres of space.

The HHO therefore calls on courts, when circumstances and risk assessment allow, to more frequently use alternatives to prison. It particularly proposes that persons punished for misdemeanours and those with sentences of up to one year should not be sent to prison if the prescribed conditions are not ensured for them. For persons serving sentences of up to two years, the HHO demands that after serving at least half of the sentence it be individually checked without delay whether they meet the conditions for conditional release or a milder form of serving the sanction. “Imprisonment must be a measure of last resort, and not an automatic response to lighter criminal offences, misdemeanours or circumstances in which the purpose of sanctioning can be achieved without placement in an overcrowded prison system,” the HHO said.

The HHO also claims that the National Preventive Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture “does not function in practice” and calls for greater and more transparent involvement of human rights associations. The National Preventive Mechanism operates under the Ombudsperson and during the year visits prisons and other places where persons deprived of liberty are held. It is precisely through this mechanism that the Ombudsperson, in the latest report as well, established that overcrowding remains one of the greatest problems of the system. The HHO concludes that a lack of space, staff or money cannot be a justification for conditions that may cross the boundary of permissible punishment and become degrading or inhuman.

World.title: Estonian foreign ministry strongly advises against travel to Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Due to increasingly frequent attacks by Houthi rebels, Estonia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs strongly advises against travel to Saudi Arabia and the surrounding region.

Estonia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it strongly advises against travel to Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region due to the rapidly changing and unpredictable security situation in the Middle East. New attacks could occur with little warning, while further escalation could cause major disruptions to air traffic and even the temporary closure of national borders.

The ministry urged Estonian citizens currently in the region to exercise extreme caution, avoid large gatherings and other high-risk locations and follow instructions issued by local authorities.

Estonian citizens should also register their stay abroad through the ministry's Reisi Targalt travel advisory portal so that they can be contacted quickly if necessary.

Yemen's Houthi rebels have significantly intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent days, targeting both civilians and civilian infrastructure.

On Sunday night, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was targeted in the deadliest terrorist attack in the past decade. According to preliminary reports, 12 people were killed and more than 300 injured.

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that killing civilians and attacking civilian infrastructure constitute flagrant violations of international law, adding that Estonia unequivocally condemns the Houthi terrorist attacks.

World.title: Estonia experiencing a garmoshka boom
World.content:
Estonia is experiencing a boom in the popularity of the garmoshka, the simplest type of accordion. On Saturday, 70 garmoshka players from across Estonia gathered at the Oisu community center to make music together.

Toomas Valk, a man from Setomaa, has been playing the garmon, garmoshka or, in Estonian, karmoška for more than 25 years and has been named the best instrumentalist in the Seto Kingdom. Two years ago, he was awarded the title of National Folk Musician. Valk said the garmoshka, which originated in Russia, has spread throughout Estonia via the Seto people.

"Accordions in general are very popular instruments that pushed out other folk instruments in their day. And the charm of the garmoshka is that it's easy to carry around. It's a small instrument, but it makes a lot of noise and is easy to play," said Valk, who admits he cannot read music.

Many people have learned to play the garmoshka on their own or taken lessons from an experienced player. Vaike Pärn, from Oisu, joked that she has become an in-demand musician in just five years.

"For example, we went to Tallinn to play in the courtyard of the chancellor of justice's office. We get invited to all sorts of places and we're quite famous," she said.

Playing the garmoshka has become a predominantly female pursuit in Estonia. Rasmus Mattias Hanga, a 17-year-old from Harju County, is something of an exception.

"I was visiting relatives in the countryside. My relatives were playing it and I thought I'd actually like to learn how to do that too," Hanga said.

The Oisu Karmoška Day was organized by two virtuosos of the instrument, Piret Aus and Ruti Enn. Workshops were also led by Toomas Valk, Siim Sarv, Kadri Lepasson and Rasmus Kadaja. Ülo Saaremõts demonstrated what goes on inside a garmoshka. The gathering's longer-term goal is to put on a strong performance at the 2028 Folk Music Festival.

"We're working hard and learning so that when the repertoire is released in the spring, garmoshka players can start practicing the pieces for the festival," Aus said.

Aus estimates that there may be around 1,000 garmoshka players in Estonia.

World.title: Eerik-Niiles Kross: The true impact of Trump and Putin's diesel deal
World.content:
The agreement's economic impact will likely be minimal, while its moral and political consequences could be far more lasting and extremely damaging to the U.S. in the long run, writes Eerik-Niiles Kross.

Under an alleged diesel deal reached by phone between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin, Russia is expected to supply the global market with an initial 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel, followed by another 500,000 metric tons in November, then 1 million metric tons and, later, another 3 million metric tons "if possible." A total of 4.8 million metric tons of diesel has been promised.

At first glance, this seems like a large quantity. However, the actual impact depends on how quickly the fuel can be delivered and how much of it represents genuinely additional supply to the global market.

The U.S. consumes approximately 16 million metric tons of diesel per month, most of it domestically produced. The first promised shipment of 300,000 metric tons therefore represents less than 2 percent of one month's U.S. consumption. The 500,000 metric tons promised for November amounts to about 3 percent.

The entire promised 4.8 million metric tons would equal roughly 30 percent of one month's U.S. consumption, but no deadline has been set for its delivery and much of it may never reach the U.S. at all. If those 4.8 million metric tons were indeed delivered to the U.S. over the course of a year, for example, that would amount to 400,000 metric tons per month or 2.5 percent of U.S. consumption. It is ridiculous to assume that this could actually affect fuel prices in the U.S.

Still less is this a quantity that could fundamentally reshape the global fuel market over the longer term.

Another important consideration is that the diesel promised by Russia may not be — and most likely is not — newly produced fuel. At least some of it has already been produced and is sitting in storage facilities or export pipelines. Bringing this fuel to market could temporarily increase supply. However, if Russia simply sells fuel originally intended for existing customers to new buyers instead, total global supply will not increase at all.

Meanwhile, Trump's main objective in reaching the agreement, at least according to his own statements, is to lower fuel prices. The conclusion must be that Trump either hopes releasing Russian diesel onto the market will have a psychological effect and influence markets, intends to further ease sanctions on Russian oil exports or has simply allowed the Russians to pull the wool over his eyes. All three possibilities are rather depressing.

Agreement far more significant for Putin

Russia produced approximately 85 million metric tons of diesel in 2025, of which around 61 million metric tons was summer-grade diesel. Successful Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have significantly reduced production in 2026. At the same time, the Russians are facing a familiar seasonal problem: Winter always catches Russia by surprise. In winter, northern regions need cold-resistant diesel, but refineries that have been damaged and require repairs are unable to switch production quickly enough, if at all.

As a result, Russia may simultaneously face a surplus of summer-grade diesel and a shortage of winter-grade diesel. The summer-grade fuel must either be exported or stored. Once storage tanks are full, refineries have to cut production, further worsening Russia's fuel supply situation.

Putin therefore stands to gain considerably more from this deal than the relatively insignificant increase in export volumes might suggest. The temporary easing of U.S. sanctions allows Russia to sell fuel that would otherwise occupy storage capacity, leaving nowhere to put newly produced fuel. Refineries can now continue operating, generating additional export revenue.

Whether the Russians can actually deliver the promised quantities is another matter. According to various estimates, Russia exported approximately 27 million to 40 million metric tons of diesel in 2025. In the third quarter of 2026, seaborne exports had fallen to around 190,000 barrels (this may be an optimistic estimate from our perspective and does not appear to be based on complete statistics, but no better figures are currently available) or 26,000 metric tons, per day. That represents an 80 percent decline from the beginning of the year.

Thus, delivering the first 300,000 metric tons should not pose an insurmountable problem, provided sufficient stocks are available. The 500,000 metric tons promised for November is also feasible in principle.

However, exporting the entire promised 4.8 million metric tons at the current rate would take approximately six months. Even that assumes Russia diverts all its existing export volumes to the U.S. to fulfill the agreement. If Russia wanted to deliver those quantities in two months, for example, exports would have to roughly triple from their current level. That should be impossible, at least without restoring refinery capacity, particularly assuming Ukrainian attacks continue.

Trump can, of course, announce that he has brought millions of metric tons of additional fuel onto the global market and taken steps to lower prices. As we saw, his post to that effect on Friday drove oil prices down by more than 4 percent.

An actual, sustained decline in prices, however, requires that the promised fuel actually reach the market and that the shipments represent additional global supply rather than simply a redirection of existing exports — for example, diesel going to the U.S. instead of Brazil. A one-off shipment could affect prices for days, perhaps weeks, but it certainly would not resolve a longer-term shortage. Ultimately, I do not see the price decline Trump is hoping for materializing either in the U.S. or on the global market.

The most important effect of the agreement is political and psychological

The biggest weakness of the diesel deal is its striking asymmetry. As usual, the Russians have already gotten what they wanted, while the U.S. has received promises that are unlikely to be fulfilled. So far, Russia has had to do essentially nothing that was not already in its own interests. On the contrary, Russia has effectively received U.S. approval to continue destroying Ukraine's infrastructure.

The U.S. Treasury Department has already issued a sanctions exemption allowing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel until April 7, 2027. The exemption is not conditional on the promised deliveries actually taking place and contains no quantitative limit. This means Russia is already benefiting from sanctions relief, regardless of whether Putin can or even intends to deliver the 4.8 million metric tons of diesel promised to Trump.

Russia's contribution to the deal consists of a promise to sell its diesel fuel. Not to give it away, not to provide it as humanitarian aid, but to sell fuel on the global market that Russia itself has a vital interest in exporting. Putin has gained an opportunity to earn additional revenue and mitigate the impact of Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil industry.

Russia has made no known reciprocal commitment to stop attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, scale back military operations or make concessions in peace negotiations. Instead, Trump has pressured, if not outright threatened, Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure.

The moral problem with the agreement is colossal. For years, Western countries have sought to restrict Russia's energy revenues in order to reduce its ability to wage its war of aggression against Ukraine — yes, sometimes hypocritically, but they have made the effort nonetheless.

Europe and the U.S. have largely been united on this issue. Now the U.S. president is opening up a new opportunity for the Russians to sell fuel and presenting it as a step that serves the interests of the global economy and American consumers. At the same time, he has previously threatened third countries that buy Russian petroleum products with sanctions — India, for example, as recently as a short while ago — and Congress has just passed the so-called Lindsey Graham bill, which would make it possible to impose effective sanctions on Russia.

Trump's deal stands in stark contradiction to all of this. The Russians are being rewarded for destroying Ukraine's infrastructure with an opportunity to earn additional revenue and portray themselves as the saviors of the global energy market.

For Putin, this is an important political and psychological victory in any case. He can demonstrate both to his domestic audience and internationally that the policy of isolating Russia is unsustainable and that even the U.S. needs Russia's help. What is more, Russia has achieved this outcome without making a single concession in Ukraine. I would call that a 4-0 victory for Putin...

For Ukraine, the message is particularly damaging. Ukraine has taken enormous risks to damage Russia's refining industry and thereby weaken the aggressor's economic and military capabilities. It is depressing to recall the damage Ukraine itself suffers every day in this context. And now our principal ally is helping to alleviate, at least in part, the economic consequences of precisely those attacks that have so far been one of Ukraine's main tools for putting pressure on the Russians. Meanwhile, the Russians continue attacking Ukraine's power plants, heating systems and energy infrastructure and murdering civilians.

You can bet that Russia will use the promised diesel deliveries as a tool of political pressure. If Trump starts linking lower American fuel prices to the operational capacity of Russian refineries, Putin will say Ukraine is to blame and that Trump should make the Ukrainians stop attacking them. Trump already seems to be following this logic — or, more accurately, this absurdity. The result is a situation in which the aggressor continues destroying Ukraine's energy infrastructure while Ukraine is pressured to abandon attacks on the aggressor's energy infrastructure.

The agreement also creates problems for relations between Europe and the U.S. The European Union has sought to reduce its dependence on Russian energy and restrict the revenues flowing into Russia's war economy. The U.S., and Trump in particular, has spent years lecturing Europe for continuing to buy Russian petroleum products. Now he is blatantly disregarding all of that.

The U.S. sanctions exemption does not, of course, invalidate European sanctions, but it makes maintaining a common sanctions policy more difficult. Operating Russia's shadow fleet will become cheaper, insurance companies may begin insuring tankers carrying Russian cargo again and so on. All of this has implications extending well beyond diesel.

European companies must continue complying with EU restrictions while the Americans allow the Russians back into the market. It is reasonable to expect European oil companies to start pressuring their governments to make similar concessions.

U.S. credibility has taken a serious blow in both Europe and Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has already criticized the deal, understandably and as the only possible response. The only people in Europe who might be celebrating are Putinist right-wing forces such as the AfD.

Against this backdrop, the economic benefits of the agreement for the U.S. are uncertain, to put it mildly. Its impact on U.S. gasoline prices is even more indirect than its impact on diesel prices and is likely nonexistent. Russia, meanwhile, gains an opportunity to expand its customer base, reduce the discounts it offers, earn export revenue and ease storage problems at its refineries. Fortunately, this deal will not resolve Russia's own shortage of winter-grade diesel or restore production capacity damaged by Ukrainian attacks.

So there we have it. Trump gets to promise cheaper fuel, which will not actually help him, while Putin has already secured tangible sanctions relief.

There is probably a longer backstory to all of this. According to an October 10 report in the Financial Times, U.S. representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner warned Ukrainian negotiators in Miami that Washington could restrict intelligence sharing if Ukraine did not stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure. The Ukrainian delegation cut its visit short. In other words, the U.S. is threatening to end the last significant form of assistance it still provides Ukraine while simultaneously providing direct assistance to the aggressor.

The agreement's economic impact will be modest at best and probably minimal. Its moral and political consequences could be far more lasting and extremely damaging to the U.S. in the long run. It undermines the credibility of sanctions, puts Ukraine under pressure and deepens divisions between Europe and the U.S.

Ultimately, this is another Sputnik-style spin operation. During the coronavirus pandemic, Putin marketed a vaccine around the world that did not work and that Russia was unable to produce in sufficient quantities, creating the impression that Russia was coming to the rescue of those in need. Now, in a single stroke, he has eased his export difficulties, demonstrated that Western sanctions do not hold up and dealt a blow to America's reputation.

World.title: Foreign online studies not enough to meet Estonia's compulsory education requirement
World.content:
Children under 18 living in Estonia must attend an Estonian school to fulfill compulsory education requirements, even if they are enrolled in a foreign online school, the Ministry of Education has said.

At an information seminar for local governments and schools, the Ministry of Education announced that all children under the age of 18 who have moved to Estonia, with certain exceptions, must fulfill their compulsory education requirement at an Estonian school. Attending online classes at a foreign school does not exempt them from this obligation.

The Tartu city government's education department asked the ministry which legal provision the requirement was based on as the Education Act does not explicitly establish such a rule.

Marika Peekmann, a senior expert at the Ministry of Education, said the requirement stems from the combined provisions of the Education Act and the Basic Schools and Upper Secondary Schools Act.

"The law does not provide for the possibility of considering the compulsory education requirement fulfilled for a person residing in Estonia solely on the basis of enrollment in a foreign educational institution. This is also supported by the objectives of the compulsory education reform, the obligation of local governments to monitor compliance with compulsory education requirements under the law and so on," Peekmann said.

She added that accepting enrollment in a foreign school as fulfilling the compulsory education requirement for children living in Estonia would raise the question of why the law links compulsory education to residence in Estonia in the first place.

"The central idea of the compulsory education reform is that local governments monitor and ensure the education of young people living in Estonia. If enrollment in a foreign school or participation in an online school were sufficient, local governments would have no real way of verifying whether a student is actually studying, how much they are studying, whether the instruction meets the required educational standards or whether their studies are continuing without interruption," the senior expert said.

According to Peekmann, this would create a gray area in which compulsory education requirements would formally be met, but the state would have no real overview of a young person's educational progress.

"The Estonian state cannot automatically assess the legal status of a foreign school, the standard of its curriculum, how instruction is actually organized or whether learning outcomes are being achieved," she explained.

Peekmann said the problem is particularly acute in the case of foreign online or alternative educational institutions, as the state would have no clear basis for determining which forms of foreign education meet the objectives of compulsory education and which do not.

The ministry's senior expert said the aim of the compulsory education reform was not merely to ensure that young people receive some form of education, but also to reduce school dropout rates and the number of young people who are neither studying nor working.

"Achieving this objective requires students to be monitored within the Estonian education system, their educational progress to be recorded in the Estonian Education Information System (EHIS) and support measures to be made available when necessary. In most cases, this is not possible with foreign educational institutions," Peekmann noted.

Starting this academic year, the Ministry of Education extended compulsory education to the age of 18, meaning that students who complete basic school must continue their education at an upper secondary school, vocational school or in preparatory studies. The compulsory education requirement does not apply to the children of foreign diplomats.
