World.title: President Alar Karis: Difficult to convey others' messages when you're sidelined
World.content:
Reflecting on his five years in office, President Alar Karis defends his decisions to veto legislation and his approach to foreign policy, arguing that the president should have a greater role in shaping Estonia's foreign policy.

Which decision do you consider the most important and influential for Estonian society during your presidency?

I believe that if you make decisions, they should all be important. A president doesn't deal with minor decisions, although some decisions may seem small and insignificant.

But the decisions that invariably cause controversy are those involving vetoes of legislation. Those are important decisions, sending a law back for reconsideration.

Looking back today, is there any decision or action where you feel you could have acted differently as president?

There may be several, but again, time comes into play here. Right now, it's difficult to say what I should have done differently. I've always believed that what you should regret isn't what you could have done differently, but what you've left undone. Those are the things that weigh more heavily on your conscience. If you ask me what those things are, I can't say.

What do you consider the greatest achievement of your presidency?

Again, we come back to the same point. We need a little time. We can see from previous presidents that it's only now that people are beginning to assess Lennart Meri's presidency more or less objectively.

And I expect that time will come for me as well. I believe in history and the value of history. I hope there will be journalists and historians capable of critically evaluating sources who won't judge a president solely on the headlines of the day, but will also be able to delve into the substance of the work.

I'd now like to explore some of the more significant issues or those that have attracted the most attention. To begin with, you've said yourself that you've declined to promulgate more laws than your predecessors. How do you assess your record in this area? Does that mean you've been particularly vocal in defending the Constitution?

I think all presidents defend the Constitution. The question is always what kinds of laws come before them. Laws differ from one period to another and ultimately it all comes down to the Constitution or, in fact, to the Riigikogu and the quality of its work.

Sometimes laws are drafted in great haste and certain things are simply overlooked. Sometimes the political desire to achieve something is so strong that the Constitution is forgotten. And that's what has led to all the decisions I've had to make.

But I don't consider it something to boast about, saying, look how many laws I've rejected. Rather, it's a cause for concern. And I've always emphasized that parliament, the Riigikogu, could do its job better and examine things more thoroughly. When a law is returned to the Riigikogu, it shouldn't look only at the specific provision I've drawn attention to as president, but at the law as a whole, to see whether it's really the best it can be. It's a second opportunity to review the legislation.

But very often that hasn't happened. The mistake is corrected and the law still turns out to be less than ideal. Because a president cannot reject a law simply because he doesn't like it or because it's very poorly drafted. There are limits and those limits are set by the Constitution.

With that in mind, let's look at the motor vehicle tax. How do you assess it in hindsight? You sent the law back, emphasizing its impact on a particularly vulnerable group in society. Ultimately, the law was adopted anyway. How do you view it today? Is it now a complete and satisfactory law or were the interests of some groups in society ultimately left unrepresented?

It's exactly as you say. People don't like laws that impose financial or other restrictions on them. But it's necessary to explain why a law is needed and that explanation probably wasn't as good as it could have been. Although the finance minister at the time even said to me, "Let the president come to me and I'll explain it to him."

But I convey what the people are saying and if people don't understand something, I say so. What was particularly interesting about this law was that I ultimately signed it, but it later emerged that the implementing regulations were unconstitutional, so the chancellor of justice had to draw attention to that.

So there are two aspects here: the law itself and how it's implemented. Both need to be thought through.

Another issue is the Churches and Congregations Act. You repeatedly declined to promulgate it and it eventually reached the Supreme Court. Was this the most fundamental confrontation with the Riigikogu during your presidency?

With very complicated laws like these, which stir up strong emotions, it's extremely difficult for a president to make a decision. The easy thing would be to let the law through and think politically, well, what are they up to here? But we already have laws today that allow us to arrest criminal elements and expel them from the country, as has been done. In principle, I wasn't opposed to preventing these people from operating here. Quite the opposite: they must not be allowed to operate here.

And the second element, which people probably don't fully understand, is that the legal and secular world is one thing, but the canonical world is another. Churches don't have borders in that world. Whether we're talking about Orthodox, Lutheran or Catholic churches, the ecclesiastical world operates in a different sphere. We can amend the law on churches and change their statutes, but those ties will remain. That has to be taken into account. They won't disappear.

That's why I repeatedly asked for the law to be reconsidered. And as you saw, when it reached the Supreme Court, quite a few judges there also expressed dissenting opinions. Now we've reached the European Court of Human Rights, which is actually something I warned about from the outset. I said, think through what the next steps will be and how this law is going to be implemented. I don't know how long the proceedings at the European Court of Human Rights will take, but they'll probably take quite some time.

So these are the things I've constantly tried to emphasize: think a couple of steps ahead. Don't rush to adopt legislation based on emotion!

Turning to your foreign policy during the final year of your presidency, it seems to me that this is perhaps the area that has attracted the most criticism. Looking back, how do you assess the claims that some of your messages were unclear to both the government and ordinary citizens? Would you do anything differently today?

I don't think so. Perhaps I should actually have spoken out a little more on the subject. I recently read that President Karis wasn't interested in foreign policy, which is an outright lie. I've visited more than 100 countries. Foreign policy can be conducted in very different ways and today, in a sense, if I can use that expression, people are barking up the wrong tree.

That's because the main responsibility, particularly in the context of the war in Ukraine, lies with the prime minister and the foreign minister. They're the ones who carry that responsibility because they attend NATO meetings and European Council meetings. The president only attends the UN and that's once a year. That's where he delivers his national address and gives interviews. I've also given interviews that have gone completely unnoticed in Estonia. One year, I gave six interviews, including to CNN and the BBC, and none of them received any coverage here.

To understand what the president does in foreign policy, it would be worthwhile for politicians and journalists alike to accompany him on visits. Very few have done so. As I said, I've made more than 100 visits. You could count on the fingers of one hand the occasions when a journalist or a member of the Riigikogu has accompanied me. Those who have done so understand that foreign policy can be conducted in very different ways.

And then there's soft diplomacy, which I've considered very important. It doesn't generate headlines, but its impact lasts considerably longer.

Or take the so-called Kazakhstan incident. When I ask what actually happened there, I don't get an answer because nothing happened. Quite the opposite. I went there with a specific objective: to help curb sanctions circumvention by securing a cooperation agreement for our Tax and Customs Board. They thanked me for that, as they did several other companies.

The fact that the president chooses where to say one thing or another is the president's choice. And there have been many instances where I've decided for myself what to say, whom to speak to and for how long. But the foreign policy framework has remained the same.

If some people have problems with reading comprehension or literacy, I can't help them. I can only recommend that they educate themselves a little and I hope they do. Even starting with something as simple as understanding that a sentence continues after a comma. That makes it easier to understand the meaning.

In light of that, have you developed any proposals or ideas about how this area should be changed or what should be done differently to prevent similar misunderstandings in the future?

Yes, certainly, and we've tried to address this and talk about it. Estonia's president doesn't participate in shaping foreign policy. To put it rather bluntly, the president is given instructions and told to carry them out! That's unlike other countries in our region where presidents participate in the process. And as a former scientist, I find it very difficult to convey other people's messages when I haven't been involved in the process myself or don't believe in what I'm saying.

The simplest example is Rail Baltica. Everywhere I go, I'm told that I have to say it will be completed by 2030. I said I couldn't say that because I know it won't be completed by 2030! And today we're in a situation where it won't be completed. But there's this pressure to demonstrate internationally how important it is! Why do we have to lie? Or convince ourselves that things are working?!

That's a simple example people might understand. Perhaps there's no point going into the finer nuances of foreign policy.

The other issue is that the president doesn't participate in NATO summits or European Council meetings. He could attend one of them and perhaps NATO would be the right choice. That would also create an opportunity for discussion. If the president attended NATO meetings, it would be possible to communicate better with the government and pass on the information he receives there. That's how it works in Finland, Latvia, Lithuania and elsewhere.

That's why it's very difficult to compare the Estonian president with other presidents, because their functions are completely different.

If we were to compare the Estonian president with someone, it could be German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier. He's served as foreign minister twice, but he doesn't exactly stand out in foreign policy today. You can't say he doesn't understand foreign policy, because his role is different. Germany has a chancellor.

Or take Italy. I doubt anyone on the street here even knows who the Italian president is. But he's a very important and well-loved president in Italy. It's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni who handles these matters there.

So people need to learn what the roles of the president, prime minister and foreign minister are in Estonia. And once that's clear, I think perceptions will change considerably.

But it's certainly worth discussing whether attending NATO summits could be one of the president's responsibilities. Then it would also make sense to give the National Defense Council a more substantial role, so there would be something to discuss and talk about.

Because at the moment, we exchange information and often it's information we both already know. We simply get together to issue a press release saying that discussions were held. Well, of course I'm exaggerating, that's understandable.

Finally, I heard an interesting statistic: over these five years, you've spent a month on airplanes...

...and another month in airports.

Is there anything else from your time in office that stands out in your memory, perhaps something enjoyable or another statistic you'd like to highlight from this period that's now coming to an end?

Well, I only heard that statistic myself yesterday. I'm not familiar enough with the data to pick out any other statistics. But just the fact that I've spent two months of my life on airplanes and in airports...

I've never been particularly good at using those moments to get work done. I need longer stretches of time and an environment where I can concentrate. I don't want to say those two months were wasted, but they certainly weren't used as effectively as they could have been.

But I'm sure there are more statistics to be found if someone wants to look for them.

What I tend to remember most, though, are the happy moments. The occasions when I've presented state decorations have always been moving, seeing the emotions people experience. It's so wonderful to watch, all that surprise. It's genuine.

I received my first state decoration in 2007, I think. And that was a very special occasion, knowing that your work had been recognized.

And I think every president would like to award even more decorations. At one point, one president awarded nearly a thousand. But we don't want to devalue the decorations either, so it's better to keep the number limited.

Then again, every president decides how many to award. Those are the kinds of positive moments I remember. And you can find statistics there too, on how many decorations have been awarded.

World.title: Prime minister slams US-Russia diesel pact: Deals with dictators 'road to hell'
World.content:
Prime Minister Kristen Michal has sharply criticized the US decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying agreements with dictators lead to hell.

Trump said Friday that Russia had agreed to bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the world market immediately, with more to follow, under a temporary US licence.

Ahead of next month's midterm elections, US President Donald Trump has struck a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply millions of tonnes of diesel to the world market, a move Trump said was essential to bring down fuel prices.

The US issued a temporary license for Russian diesel supplies to the world market, valid until April 7 next year.

"This is a major miscalculation, because deals with dictators are the road to hell. Innocent people are being killed for gas and fuel money. And what is very likely is that the hoped-for fuel will not come," the prime minister noted on social media.

"Such an agreement runs counter to the Western world's long-standing efforts to limit the flow of money from energy carriers to [Vladimir] Putin. The US has until now persuaded its allies to abandon Russian fuel — we have too," Michal said.

According to him, the long-term line of cutting Russia off from money is correct and must continue.

"It is worth discussing in Estonia and at the European Council next week whether we can quickly contribute more to Ukraine so they can blast Russia's oil refineries to smithereens," Michal added.

Reform MP: Trump is thinking about the midterms

MP Marko Mihkelson (Reform), chair of the Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee, earlier said he believes the upcoming midterm elections prompted Trump's diesel agreement with Russia, but at the same time, Russia will draw encouragement from the deal to continue its war in Ukraine.

Marko Mihkelson. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

"The Trump administration is on its back domestically over its moves and is trying to do everything to avoid a major Republican defeat in the midterm elections less than a month away," Mihkelson wrote on his social media account.

He said the hope of reducing diesel prices at US pumps with Russia's help is short-sighted and carries a much higher strategic cost for the United States.

"At the same time as the Graham sanctions bill approved in Congress would give the president the opportunity to increase economic pressure on Russia, the White House is instead lowering pressure on Russia and demanding that Ukraine stop attacking refineries," the MP went on.

"If it is true that this was accompanied by a Washington threat to Kyiv to stop sharing intelligence if the attacks continue, then this gives Moscow only one unambiguous signal — kill and destroy Ukraine, the US will not stand in the way," he added.

Mihkelson said Trump's efforts to end the war through negotiations have produced not the slightest result.

"The fighting is bloodier than at any previous moment in the entire full-scale invasion," he said. "If you give an aggressor oxygen, the war will not stop."

He stressed that Europe's allies have only one path — to ensure Russia's strategic attack goals fail and the Kremlin's imperial wars end in defeat.

"This clear strategic goal should also be in the US interest, because Russia's long-standing desire, together with China and Iran, to weaken the United States' leadership role is reaching a decisive phase," Mihkelson continued.

Ahead of next month's midterm elections, U.S. President Donald Trump has struck a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply millions of tonnes of diesel to the world market, reversing years of Western pressure on the Kremlin. Trump said the move was essential to bring down fuel prices, which have soared since Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and warned of a diesel export ban on any EU states that do not release reserves to counter the spike. The G7 agreed earlier this week to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from reserves.

MEP: The important thing is to keep that fuel from reaching Europe

Member of the European Parliament Riho Terras (Isamaa) said Trump's deal with Russia looks like a betrayal, sending a negative message to both Ukraine and Europe.

"I would hope this will lead European allies to realize even more clearly the need to support Ukraine and try to close the loopholes in their own sanctions, so that even if this fuel reaches America, it won't find its way into Europe through the back door. I think this could mobilize Europeans to provide even more support for Ukraine because that's the only option," he said.

Terras added that Trump's actions are unpredictable and may not benefit him.

"The deal struck with Putin is a win-win for Putin. He came out ahead both economically and politically. He demonstrated to the world that Putin is needed to save the global economy. That's actually absurd," Terras said.

Kallas: US-Russia diesel agreement helping to fund Kremlin's war of aggression

An agreement between the United States and Russia to lift sanctions on Russian diesel fuel provides Moscow with "more revenue to wage the war," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Saturday. Kallas added that Russian attacks have caused the death of more than 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days and that Moscow has "intensified its hybrid attacks against Europe, both against EU member states and NATO allies."

Russian strikes killed over 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days. Moreover, it has stepped up its hybrid attacks against Europe, both EU Member States and NATO Allies. Suspending sanctions on Russian diesel provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war. This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't. On Monday, EU Foreign Ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia's war machine since the start of the war. — Kaja Kallas (@kajakallas) October 10, 2026

"Suspending sanctions on Russian diesel provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war. This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't. ," she wrote.

World.title: Estonian Artists' Association's charity auction brings in record-breaking €2.3 million
World.content:
The Estonian Artists' Association (EKL) charity auction concluded with total sales of €2.3 million, the highest amount ever recorded for a single art auction in Estonia.

A total of 159 works were sold, representing 98 percent of the 162 works put up for auction.

Thanks to the auction, the association will be able to repay the losses incurred through a fraud scheme ahead of schedule, while all remaining proceeds will go toward supporting Estonian artists and the country's art scene, EKL said.

According to EKL President Maarin Ektermann, the auction's results exceeded all expectations.

"When planning the auction, we didn't dare hope it would cover the entire €700,000 loss, as art auctions are unpredictable. That's why we cut the association's expenses and looked for other ways to free ourselves from the debt burden. But thanks to the people who decided to purchase treasures from the art collection and donated works, showing such strong support for the artists and the association, we can now repay our obligations ahead of schedule and develop plans for how best to support our members and Estonia's art scene," Ektermann said.

The partial sale of the art collection was an exceptional step that could only be taken once in this form.

"We knew from the outset that this was a one-time decision. That's why it was important to us to organize a public auction where everyone would have an opportunity to acquire works from the collection, with starting prices as low as €100," Ektermann said. "Together with experts, we selected the works very carefully to preserve the integrity of the collection. Far fewer works went to auction than we had originally planned, which made the result all the more surprising."

Jaanus Samma, who coordinated the artists' donations, said the artists who donated their works to the auction deserve special thanks.

"Not all the works could even be included in the auction and those remaining will be offered for sale at a separate exhibition in EKL's galleries at the end of the year," Samma said.

Historic records

The auction raised €23,500 on the first day and €786,400 on the second, while 80 works from the third day's selection of paintings, sculptures and applied art sold for a total of €1.5 million.

On Saturday, Tiit Pääsuke's "Lapi kakk" fetched the highest price of the day at €185,000.

The highest hammer price of the entire auction went to Jaan Elken's painting "Juhikabiin," which sold for €205,000. This is the highest price ever paid at auction for a work by a living Estonian artist.

Ludmilla Siim's "Rõdu" set a new auction record for a work by an Estonian female artist, selling for €150,000. Olev Subbi's "Keskpäev" sold for the same amount, setting a new auction record for the artist.

Art market expert Tiina Määrmann said she was particularly pleased that the works' art historical significance was positively correlated with their market value.

Where will the proceeds go?

The auction proceeds will primarily go toward covering losses incurred as a result of the fraud scheme in the spring, including repaying a loan. A portion of the proceeds will also be paid to artists: the creators of works sold from the association's art collection or their heirs will receive 5 percent of the hammer price, while artists who recently donated works will receive 15 percent.

"Although the resale royalty rate under the Copyright Act drops to 3 percent for more expensive works, we will pay the creators of works sold from our art collection 5 percent regardless of the hammer price," Ektermann said.

The association will use the remaining proceeds in accordance with its statutes, which stipulate that EKL's mission is to support Estonian artists and the country's art scene. The management board will submit proposals on how to use the funds to the association's council and some of the money will be allocated to developing the art collection and making it more accessible to the public.

"We want decisions to be made openly and together with our members. We hope to present more detailed plans at the extraordinary general assembly on November 16," Ektermann said.

The Estonian Artists' Association, in cooperation with Eesti Kunstioksjonid OÜ, held an extraordinary art auction from October 8 to 10, offering 162 works from the association's collection and recent donations by artists. The selection ranged from paintings and graphic art to photographs, sculptural objects and textile art. The association selected the works together with an expert committee comprising art historians, critics and art market specialists.

The association organized the auction to cover losses caused by financial fraud. On May 15, 2026, the association discovered that nearly €700,000 had been transferred out of its bank accounts as part of a criminal scheme.

World.title: Vegan powerlifter says diet change solved his health problems
World.content:
Koovit, who grew up with six brothers and a sister, all fed on good countryside fare, said his wife suggested make the change. He now eats 180–240 grams of protein a day, but plant-derived, something which is viable nowadays without getting boared.

"There were six boys and one girl of us. We usually went through eight liters of milk a day, and everything else that goes with it," he said.

"I'm fully vegan, but that doesn't mean I only eat onions and potatoes. AS I'm a powerlifter, I need to be heavy. There's a very wide choice of vegan food. My daily protein intake is between 180 and 240 grams. On top of that comes about three times as much in carbohydrates — oatmeal, rice, potato and the rest. For me it's very important to get a lot of energy from food and for my weight number to be high," Koovit said.

His wife had been vegan for longer. "I reached a point in my sport where my joints started hurting and I felt I'd taken my body so far that if I pushed a little more, health problems would start. That was nine years ago. My wife then very cleverly suggested I try vegan products. When I get stuck with something, my dear wife comes up with a solution — without her I probably wouldn't be here," Koovit explained.

Pretty much every foodstuff has a vegan alternative, he noted. "In my case, it was that after four days of eating vegan food, I realized there was no way back, as I felt so good. For an athlete, the best thing is that the recovery becomes faster."

Koovit recalled that at the time he was living in London, and in the club where he trained he was one of the smallest men. "I was a little squirt there. As things started going so well for me, and I started setting Estonian records and winning medals, burly men who I'd been afraid even to talk to at first started asking me what I was doing to do so well. One after another they started trying vegan food too."

Meat dishes tend to be highly acidic and can cause inflammation in the body, he says. "When heavy training is added to that, more and more inflammation builds up in the body. Eventually the body can't cope with it anymore — that's why more and more athletes in the sports world have been finding vegan food," went on.

"Eating vegan food is very contagious, because you feel good and get the feeling that you'd like to try more. After eating, you don't get a heavy feeling. In sporting terms, that's the charm of it — since I can eat more often, I feed my muscles and cells more often. There are more nutrients, and through that recovery is faster too," Koovit said. "Protein can be obtained from vegan food in concentrated form."

The annual Veganmess food festival takes place in Tallinn this weekend.

World.title: Iraq’s oil exports to South Korea hit 38.3 million barrels in eight months
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – South Korea’s state-owned Korea National Oil Corporation (KNOC) announced that it imported 38.34 million barrels of crude oil from Iraq during the first eight months of 2026.

The volume represents a decrease of 45.6 percent compared to the same period in 2025.

Saudi Arabia was the largest oil supplier to South Korea, with 196.21 million barrels between January and August 2026, a 15.65 percent decline compared to the same period in 2025.

The United States was the second-largest oil supplier to South Korea, with 131.09 million barrels, and the UAE followed with 101.55 million barrels.

Iraq’s oil exports to South Korea fell from 70.55 million barrels during the first eight months in 2025 to 38.34 million barrels in the same period in 2026.

Iraq was the fourth largest crude oil supplier to South Korea in the first half of 2026, accounting for 7.4 percent of the country’s total oil imports.

Iraq’s average oil shipments to South Korea totaled 113.7 million barrels in 2025, which is an average of 311,500 barrels per day. This represents a 12 percent increase compared to 2024.

World.title: Iraq, Turkey discuss oil-for-financing deal to fund Development Road project
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is discussing an oil-for-financing agreement with Turkey to establish a fund for the Development Road project, where Turkish companies will execute construction in exchange for crude oil, while the project’s first phase will be backed by a World Bank loan.

Director of Projects at the General Company for Iraqi Railways, Fadel Abbas, confirmed that a joint financial framework is being shaped to let Turkish firms carry out infrastructure works paid for through oil exports.

The initiative aims to upgrade Iraq’s railway network, connect several provinces, and provide passenger and freight transport services, according to Abbas.

The Development Road’s primary objective is to transport goods from al-Faw Grans Port to Turkey—and onward to Europe—and vice versa.

Work is currently underway to finalize an agreement with Turkey to establish a fund that would finance the project’s implementation by Turkish companies through an oil-for-financing arrangement, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The $17 billion project, which will connect the al-Faw Grand Port in southern Iraq to the Turkish border by constructing a railway and road network, is anticipated to transform Iraq into a transit center by cutting the time it takes to travel from Asia to Europe.

In addition to pipelines for energy transportation, the project’s railway will significantly assist in the transportation of commodities, with a first-phase capacity of 3.5 million tons and a second-phase capacity of 7.5 million tons.

By connecting the port city of Basra to Turkey via an overland route, the logistics project will compete with Egypt’s Suez Canal and establish Basra as a gateway to Europe.

World.title: Iraq and Libya foil 1.2M Captagon pill smuggling operation
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – A joint intelligence-driven operation conducted between Iraqi and Libyan security authorities thwarted the smuggling of 1.2 million Captagon pills on Libyan soil, Iraq’s Ministry of Interior announced on Sunday, October 11, 2026.

The cross-border interdiction, executed in close operational coordination with the Libyan National Anti-Narcotics Apparatus, also culminated in the apprehension of a Libyan national identified as a key operative within the illicit transit ring.

According to a ministerial statement received by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), specialized task forces from Iraq’s General Directorate for Narcotics and Psychotropic Substances Affairs initiated the operation based on high-level intelligence gathered by its International Coordination and Cooperation Department.

Iraqi intelligence operatives compiled and relayed actionable tracking data concerning the transnational syndicate to Libyan security counterparts, facilitating the formulation of a synchronized tactical plan that successfully neutralized the shipment before distribution.

The Ministry of Interior emphasized that the tactical success illustrates the growing efficacy of regional intelligence-sharing networks in combating transnational organized crime. Security officials noted that transforming real-time intelligence into proactive multilateral interventions remains critical to severing international trafficking routes and dismantling supply lines employed by regional cartels.

The ministry reaffirmed that curbing the proliferation of synthetic narcotics requires durable security partnerships extending well beyond national borders.

Coordinated operations between sovereign enforcement agencies represent an essential cornerstone in identifying cross-border syndicates, disrupting trafficking itineraries, and drying up financial channels underpinning illicit drug economies in the Middle East and North Africa.

World.title: Iraq’s 2027 budget faces 50 trillion dinar deficit amid ballooning payroll
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s sovereign finances face severe structural strain as parliamentary estimates project a deficit approaching 50 trillion Iraqi dinars within the draft 2027 federal budget.

The widening fiscal gap highlights the federal government’s deep vulnerability to volatile crude oil markets and bloated operational entitlements, raising concerns regarding the treasury’s ability to cover civil service payrolls, contain public borrowing, and sustain capital investment projects amid ongoing regional security volatility.

The overall expenditure ceiling of the draft budget stands at approximately 217 trillion dinars, according to Abbas Ahyal, a member of the Parliamentary Finance Committee.

The draft framework benchmarks crude export revenues at an assumed baseline of $58 per barrel, an export capacity of four million barrels per day, and the newly established official exchange rate of 1,500 dinars per U.S. dollar, formally anchored following Cabinet Resolution No. 544.

Official budget execution metrics published by the Ministry of Finance for the first seven months of 2026 reveal the acute scale of the funding squeeze. Through the end of July, aggregate state revenues reached only 39.096 trillion dinars against realized public spending of 65.424 trillion dinars, generating an actual seven-month fiscal deficit of 26.329 trillion dinars.

Hydrocarbon receipts accounted for 30.356 trillion dinars, representing approximately 78 percent of total inflows, while non-oil revenues collected from customs, border ports, and domestic taxation generated a modest 8.740 trillion dinars.

The expanding deficit mirrors an unprecedented expansion in the sovereign payroll, with roughly 15.05 million Iraqi citizens drawing direct, recurring income from the public treasury. This demographic burden encompasses 4.55 million civil servants, nearly 2.9 million retirees, and 7.6 million recipients enrolled in social safety net programs.

During the initial seven months of 2026, employee compensation and public sector salaries consumed 35.875 trillion dinars, while social protection allocations reached 15.989 trillion dinars, driving total mandatory social transfers above 51.8 trillion dinars alongside 6.239 trillion dinars dedicated to sovereign debt servicing.

Economic analyst Ziad Al-Hashemi cautioned that a planned deficit ranging between 43 and 50 trillion dinars presents an unsustainable drag on the macroeconomy. Al-Hashemi argued that the cabinet should have enacted strict austerity discipline, curtailed redundant administrative outlays, and addressed state payroll bloat and corruption rather than inflating sovereign spending toward 217 trillion dinars.

He noted that relying on exchange rate devaluations yields only temporary accounting relief for the state treasury while directly taxing the public through imported inflation and reduced household purchasing power.

Conversely, Rabie Al-Mousawi, a member of the Parliamentary Oil and Gas Committee, contended that elevated crude export volumes could partially cushion the deficit if ongoing regional security tensions maintain global energy prices at higher premiums. However, historical volatility illustrates the limits of this reliance.

During the height of disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, Iraq’s crude exports dropped by nearly 75 percent, causing monthly hydrocarbon revenues to plunge from approximately $6.8 billion in February to around $2.3 billion across May and June, demonstrating that price gains cannot offset severe maritime export bottlenecks.

The monetary landscape remains intricately tied to the deficit dilemma following the Central Bank of Iraq’s decision on October 7 to reset its pricing structure to 1,500 dinars per dollar for purchases from the finance ministry, 1,510 dinars for bank transfers, and 1,520 dinars for retail cash sales.

Parliamentary sources confirmed that Central Bank Governor Ali Al-Allaq informed the Finance Committee that the 1,500 rate serves as the foundational metric for the national budget, warning that any legislative reversal would necessitate recalculating the entire fiscal framework.

Financial researcher Ahmed Eid observed that while devaluing the local currency increases the dinar value of dollar-denominated crude proceeds, it fails to solve underlying structural imbalances.

Eid warned that persistent budgetary pressures could force the state to accelerate domestic borrowing from state lenders, postpone commercial contractor dues, or slash capital expenditures, thereby shifting fiscal strain onto the private sector and dampening economic growth.

The public wage bill continues an uninterrupted multi-year upward trajectory, expanding from 57.6 trillion dinars in 2022 to 68.2 trillion in 2023, 78.7 trillion in 2024, and projected between 83 and 86 trillion dinars across 2025 and 2026.

With International Monetary Fund projections indicating that petroleum sales will continue to supply over 90 percent of state revenue through 2030 and public compensation could devour 54 percent of all state spending, the federal government faces an urgent balancing act between guaranteeing essential public payrolls and securing capital investments required for long-term economic diversification.

World.title: Power, water, jobs: Google on India data centre concerns
World.content:
Bengaluru – Construction of a massive Google data centre in the Indian city of Visakhapatnam has been met with resistance from residents who fear the impact on the environment and their lives.

But the tech giant says its “gigawatt-scale” AI facility in southern Andhra Pradesh state — part of a $15 billion investment — will use air cooling systems, and not water from an area already facing shortages.

Alexander Smith, Google’s head of infrastructure and energy for the Asia-Pacific region, answered AFP’s questions about the project:

– How do you view the concerns? –

Smith said Google takes questions raised by the public seriously.

“Independent environmental assessments — covering grid stability, power supply, water risk, ecology, acoustics and more — are conducted 12 to 24 months before a project begins,” he said.

“If there is insufficient power in a location, or if operating a data centre would mean taking power away from a community, Google will either find ways to develop more power, or it will not build there.”

The data centre — Google’s biggest “AI hub” outside the United States — is set to become operational in 2028.

It is one of several huge new tech sites planned in Visakhapatnam, but activists are demanding a moratorium on new data centres across Andhra Pradesh until there is more evidence of their impact on the environment and local community.

Smith called the project “a multi-decade commitment” that carries “an obligation to be a good neighbour”.

“That means the watershed, the grid and the communities around our facilities must be better off for our being here.”

– What are its water and power needs? –

As AI use accelerates, construction of power-hungry data centres is booming worldwide, especially in Asia.

Critics say they will add demand to electricity grids still heavily reliant on planet-warming fossil fuels, and place new pressure on often-stretched local water supplies to cool down hot servers.

Google’s water assessment for Visakhapatnam “pointed to pressure on the local watershed”, Smith said.

“That finding shaped our choice of cooling configuration from the outset,” with “advanced air cooling” chosen instead of water cooling.

“For the freshwater consumed by non-cooling facility needs, Google is committed to replenishing 120 percent of the volume we consume across our operations by 2030,” he added.

Google does not disclose site-level capacity figures for power.

But the US giant “fully funds the cost of required power infrastructure upgrades”.

“We are planning to invest in new clean energy projects — built above and beyond what regulations require — in Visakhapatnam,” Smith said.

– Why did Google choose Visakhapatnam? –

A Finnish authority recently ordered work to halt on two Google data centre sites pending mandatory environmental assessments, and worried residents have also mounted protests in Visakhapatnam.

To select global sites, Google looks for “proximity to customers and users, access to talent, potential for new clean energy and opportunities to establish mutually beneficial partnerships with local communities”, Smith said.

“Visakhapatnam is one of the few places where all of these come together.”

The city’s coastline also allows undersea cables to link Visakhapatnam to South Africa and Australia, “positioning Andhra Pradesh as India’s third major subsea hub”, Smith said.

– Will promised jobs benefit people? –

Data centre opponents say the benefits of the vast warehouse-like sites rarely trickle down to local residents.

Smith said that “a development of this kind is projected to generate approximately $688 million in local economic activity every year”.

“For every job inside a Google data centre we support nine additional jobs in the surrounding community,” he added.

“Over a typical three-to-five-year construction period, an average Google data centre development employs about 4,200 construction workers annually.”

“Each facility is designed to operate for at least 20 years, and once live it sustains hundreds of specialist on-site roles,” he added.

World.title: Google faces backlash against India data centre
World.content:
Visakhapatnam – Handcuffs encircle Google’s logo on one campaign poster, while another warns that people “cannot drink data”, as opposition mounts to the tech giant’s planned AI mega-facility in India.

Excavators have swung into action, clearing forest and farmland on the southeast coast for the $15 billion construction of Google’s largest data centre outside the United States.

The project at Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh state, a port often called Vizag, is championed by India as a cornerstone of its technological ambitions.

But many residents fear the data centre — one of several huge new tech sites in Vizag — will strain water and power resources, damage the environment and bring too few jobs in return.

Farmer Chandala Sadamma told AFP that when she sees the red-earth scars where her plot of mango and cashew trees once stood, “I feel like crying”.

She was paid more than $82,000 for the two-acre (0.8-hectare) stretch of land, but the transaction left a bitter taste.

“Some company came and, without showing any respect, they took the land and we accepted it,” the 50-year-old said.

Vizag is a landing point for submarine internet cables linking the country to Singapore, so for India, the location of the 600-acre site — more than 340 football pitches — is ideal.

The “AI Hub investment is a multi-decade commitment” carrying “an obligation to be a good neighbour”, said Alexander Smith, Google’s head of infrastructure and energy for Asia-Pacific.

“The watershed, the grid and the communities around our facilities must be better off for our being here.”

The Andhra Pradesh government told AFP that in addition to financial compensation, new housing is being built and handed over to people who had lived on the site.

– ‘Why here?’ –

Governments and tech firms worldwide are spending trillions of dollars on data centres — boxy buildings stuffed with racks of computer servers that power apps and AI tools.

But the developments have sparked backlash in many countries, with a Finnish authority recently ordering work to halt on two Google data centre sites pending mandatory environmental assessments.

Activists in Andhra Pradesh are also demanding a moratorium on new data centres across the state until independent environmental and social impact evaluations are published.

“The United States has a huge coast… They can simply set it up there,” Gutta Rohith of the local campaign group Human Rights Forum told AFP at a meeting of around 150 people.

“Why are they coming here?”

Opposition to data centres, including in the United States, often takes aim at the use of local water resources to cool hot servers down.

Google said it will use “advanced” air cooling technology instead at the India hub, while the state plans six 1.2-gigawatt nuclear power plants as energy demand soars.

Still, water use worries residents, especially given plans for Vizag to become a tech megahub.

“They are saying that Google is being established for the education and employment opportunities of our children,” said shopkeeper Gubbala Ramanamma.

But “we are already struggling with water scarcity”, the 57-year-old said, standing beside a dry well.

– Land prices –

Google said its data centre will generate $688 million in local economic activity each year and support about 4,200 jobs during construction, with hundreds of specialist jobs once operational in 2028.

Andhra Pradesh’s government also said it expects “188,000 direct and indirect jobs to be generated”.

But Rohith said the economic benefits would not necessarily trickle down from the warehouse-like facilities.

“We need mass employment and labour-intensive industries, not high-capital industries.”

Google is not alone — a joint venture between Reliance Industries, Brookfield and Digital Realty is investing $11 billion in another AI data centre in Vizag.

Land prices have risen by an average of “more than 45 percent” since the city unveiled its development plans, said E. Ashok Kumar, Visakhapatnam head of the Confederation of Real Estate Developers’ Associations of India.

Meanwhile, as AI use accelerates, the world’s most populous nation has rolled out incentives to attract big tech companies, including tax cuts.

Despite its widespread internet and app use generating nearly a fifth of the world’s digital data, India has only about three percent of global data-centre capacity, government figures show.

Andhra Pradesh Technology Minister Nara Lokesh, in an interview with AFP in February, spoke of investment agreements worth $175 billion involving 760 projects — and vowed to “execute these projects at a pace that the country has never seen”.

Lokesh has also insisted that “residential requirements will always be prioritised over data centres”, according to a statement.

“The water needs of our people will always come first.”

Visakhapatnam environmental campaigner E.A.S. Sarma, a former senior government official who worked in the power and finance ministries, has called for a water audit by an independent agency.

“Civilisations have vanished because of water shortages,” he warned.

World.title: 'Cops wanted to torment my parents at 3.30 am': Dipke's rebuttal to Delhi Police's clip

NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke shot back at the

after they released a video claiming that while under detention, he was offered to speak to his family after his grandmother's demise.

Dipke disputed the force's claim that he had declined assistance to contact his relatives and travel home for her last rites, saying he wasn't given his phone to access contacts.

In a statement reacting to the police's account, Dipke said he had repeatedly requested access to his phone to retrieve his cousin's number and speak to a lawyer, but was denied both requests. He also questioned why officers asked him to call his father at 3.30 am and tell him that he could be sent to jail for a long time.

"I had requested to let me speak to my cousin who lives with my grandmother. Asked for my phone just for a couple of minutes so I could at least take out the number of my cousin."

"Why Delhi Police didnât let me use my phone? I had also asked for a call with lawyer which was again denied."

Dipke said the call to his father was particularly distressing because his family had just lost his grandmother.

"At 3.30 in the morning, Delhi Police asks me to call my father and inform him that tomorrow Iâll be going in jail for a long time. The same father who has just lost his mother. How much more trauma did you want to put my family through after we already lost my grandmother?"

Questioning the timing and purpose of the call, he added, "What was the purpose of trying to call my parents at f-ing 3:30 in the morning? You wanted to torment them?"

Police say Dipke declined assistance

Dipke's allegations came after Delhi Police released a video showing officers informing him of his grandmother's death while he was in detention in the national capital.





Deputy Commissioner of Police Neha Yadav said officers approached the CJP founder after learning about the death and offered to help him contact his family, arrange flights and travel to his hometown for the funeral. According to the police, he declined the assistance.

âAs soon as the Delhi Police received information about the passing away of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke's grandmother, officers approached him to convey this sad news and offered all possible assistance.

They sensitively asked if he needed help with flights, phone calls, or anything else. They repeatedly asked if he wished to speak to his parents, but he declined,â DCP Yadav said.

The police released the video after Dipke's mother, Anita Dipke, accused the force of lying about informing her son of the death. She had said the family was unable to contact him and had postponed the last rites until he could return home.

World.title: 'Your confidence is most vital': Supreme Court to Kapil Sibal after his 'no faith' remark
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Sunday said its purpose was to instill faith of the people in the system and addressed

's "no faith" remark, saying his "confidence is most vital" for the top court's "fight against injustice".

âOur purpose is to instill faith of the people in the system and in that process your (Sibalâs) confidence is most vital for our fight against injustice,â the bench said.

The Supreme Court on Sunday directed authorities to prevent illegal detention of people participating in peaceful gatherings amid the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests in Delhi. It also asked the Centre to ensure that metro services operate normally and internet access remains uninterrupted, subject to law and order requirements.

Sibal welcomed the court's order in connection with the restrictions imposed in Delhi amid protests, saying it restores faith in the country's justice system.

âWe are deeply grateful to the Supreme Court for having passed an order that restores faith among professionals in the system of justice in this country,â Sibal said.

A bench comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued notice to the Centre while hearing a petition seeking contempt proceedings over alleged violations of the court's earlier order against a "complete prohibition" on metro and train services in the national capital during the protests.





The CJP and several student organisations had called for demonstrations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the functioning of the Election Commission.

The authorities prevented a planned mass mobilisation at Jantar Mantar on Saturday following a major security clampdown. More than 7,000 protesters were detained, including CJP leader Abhijit Dipke, several opposition leaders and YouTuber Dhruv Rathee.

During the special hearing, the bench asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to ensure that Delhi Metro operates according to its regular schedule and that internet services are not disrupted, subject to law and order requirements.

The court also directed authorities to ensure that lawyers, journalists and others are not prevented from carrying out their professional duties.

"Internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, as per law....When

we are saying internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, we are not taking away the powers under the Information Technology Act.

"There shall not be illegal detention, save and except by procedure established by law, particularly with regard to assemblage of people beyond the area within which it's imposed," the bench said.

The Supreme Court also directed authorities to remove a notice board outside its premises announcing the imposition of Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which empowers authorities to restrict assemblies in certain circumstances.

"We have been informed that a notice board stating imposition of Section 163 BNSS in and around the vicinity of the Supreme Court has been put up.

"We direct the authority concerned to take down this board, if not already done, so that citizens as well as lawyers can have access to justice," the bench ordered.

World.title: 'Security agencies face challenge from Starlink:' Nishikant Dubey
World.content:
Saurabh Sinha/TNN

NEW DELHI:

âs diatribe over Starlinkâs entry into India has now become a full blown political battle. On Sunday, chairman of the standing committee on communications and IT Nishikant Dubey said this panel has âunderstood the challenges facing the countryâs security agencies through Elon Muskâs Starlink.

The defence and home ministries, and our investigation agencies are being affected by the dangerous games of these threats.â

Last week, govt has pointed out that all the three satellite communication (satcom) service licence holders â Sunil Bharti Mittal-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, Mukesh Ambaniâs Reliance Jio and Starlink â are at the same stage and will need to individually get security clearances and meet other regulatory requirements.

âIn 2013-14, the government of Manmohan Singh ji had informed TRAI about these threats. First, provide connections to the poor in your own country, America, at affordable rates, and then level accusations. India is a healthy democratic, sovereign nation. It does not change its security policy under pressure or social media. If our policy were driven by money, we would have rolled out the red carpet welcome for you despite opposition from the security agencies.





â

The senior BJP leaderâs said on X in response to a X post by Musk that said: âThe ridiculous arguments by Ambaniâs army of Internet shills make no sense. On the one hand, they say Starlink couldnât possibly compete with the amazing low prices offered by Ambaniâs de facto monopoly in India and then, in the same breath, they essentially claim that Starlink would be too strong of a competitor! This is absurd hypocrisy and hyperbole.

â

âThe reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambaniâs profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business. And, obviously, if Starlink is too expensive in India, no one will buy it, so SpaceX will need to make pricing affordable,â Muskâs post had said.

Mittal-backed Eutelsat OneWeb manages a fleet of more than 630 low-earth orbit (LEO) satellites.

Jio is working on a proposed constellation of around 1,600 LEO satellites and plans to establish 23 ground stations across India. Starlink has about 11,100 LEO satellites in orbit.

LEO satellite internet operates between 300 and 2,000 km above earth. Starlink has them at about 550 km; Eutelsat OneWeb at about 1,200 km and Jim plans them at about 650 km. Amazon Kuiper, which also plans to get a satcom licence in India, has satellites at about 630 km.

Given strained India-US ties over multiple issues like the stuck trade deal, threat of tariffs over buying Russian oil and most importantly security concerns over Starlink, people in the know say Mittal-backed Eutelsat OneWeb and Mukesh Ambaniâs Reliance Jio are likely to get the nod before Musk, whose wait could be much longer.

World.title: Dasara festivities commence at all major temples across Nandyal district
World.content:
The Dasara Navaratri festivities began on a grand note across all the major temples in Nandyal district on Sunday.

As part of the celebrations at the renowned pilgrimage site of Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy temple in Ahobilam, the ‘Thirumanjana Seva’ (celestial bath ritual) was performed with great devotion on Sunday. The Thirumanjana Seva was conducted for Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy using sacred waters amid the chanting of Vedic mantras.

The darshan of the Lord and the special rituals evoked a sense of devotion among the devotees at Ahobilam. Devotees prayed for longevity, health, prosperity, and happiness for all, seeking the blessings of Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Swamy.

Meanwhile, at Sri Bhramaramba Mallikarjuna Swamy temple in Srisailam, the ‘Sri Devi Sarannavaratri Mahotsavams’ commenced in accordance with the tradition and scriptural injunctions. As part of the festival proceedings, the temple board of trustees chairman Pothugunta Ramesh Naidu, executive officer M. Srinivasa Rao accompanied by his spouse, along with the presiding priests, Sthanacharyas, temple priests, Vedic scholars, and officials, entered the temple in a traditional manner, carrying turmeric, vermilion, fruits, and flowers.

To mark the commencement of the festivities, rituals such as ‘Yagashala Pravesham’ (entry into the ritual pavilion), ‘Ganapathi Puja’, ‘Deeksha Sankalpam’ (vow of observance), ‘Kankana Puja’ and ‘Kankana Dharana’ (consecration and tying of the sacred wristband), and ‘Ritvigvaranam’ (selection of officiating priests) were conducted in the Goddess’s temple pavilion.

For the welfare of the world, a ‘Sahasra Chandi Parayana-sahita Shata Chandi Maha Rudra Yagam’ was conducted for the first time this year during the Sri Devi Sarannavaratri festival.

‘Kumari Puja’, a ritual in which a young girl aged between two and ten years is worshipped with offerings of flowers, fruits, and new clothes, will also be performed daily as part of the Dasara festival, the officials said.

As part of ‘Navadurga Alankaram’ (adornment in the nine forms of Durga) during the Navaratri celebrations, the presiding deity was adorned as Goddess Shailaputri in the evening. The ‘Bhringi Vahana Seva’ was also performed in the night as part of the ‘Vahana Seva’ (divine vehicle procession) rituals conducted for the Lord and Goddess during the festivities.

World.title: Karnataka Chief Minister, Congress legislators to join Delhi protest against SIR on October 12
World.content:
Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar and ruling Congress legislators from Karnataka will be in New Delhi on Monday (October 12) to participate in the All India Congress Committee’s protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls and the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.

Speaking to reporters in Bengaluru on Sunday (October 11), Mr. Shivakumar said the Congress would hold its own protest against the SIR exercise and demand the Chief Election Commissioner’s resignation.

Anti-CEC protest LIVE updates

When asked whether the Congress was supporting the protest by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), he said the party was taking its own course of action, while some INDIA bloc allies had participated in the other protest.

“We are holding our protest tomorrow. I had said that we did not want to go to Delhi in large numbers, but our legislators will be there. I am also going to Delhi to protect every voter,” he said.

“You cannot delete voters from electoral rolls. How can you delete the names of voters in Karnataka? This is not democracy. We have to protect the right to vote of Dalits, minorities and backward-class people,” he said.

Mr. Shivakumar has frequently participated in protests organised by the Congress in Delhi under the leadership of Congress leader Rahul Gandhi against the NDA government and the Chief Election Commissioner.

On October 1, the Chief Minister and his Cabinet colleagues staged a dharna on the premises of the Chief Electoral Officer’s office in Bengaluru, demanding the registration of a criminal case and an investigation into an alleged conspiracy to delete eligible voters’ names using Form 7 applications.

Criticising the Centre for shutting down the internet in Delhi during the protest on Saturday, October 10, Mr. Shivakumar said the Prime Minister should explain whether the country was witnessing democracy or ‘Emergency’.

“Everyone has the right to protest. Detaining people on flights and elected representatives is an insult to the nation and to democracy,” he said.

India was known across the world for its democratic traditions, he said, adding that such incidents would damage the country’s reputation. The Centre should allow protesters to meet the Chief Election Commissioner, he said, stressing that criticism was part of public life.

When asked about an open letter by 124 former IAS, IFS and other civil service officers defending the Election Commission and the SIR exercise and arguing that allegations of vote-rigging should be backed by credible evidence, Mr. Shivakumar said, “The officers have done their duty. Congratulations to them. But our protest represents the voice of the country, not the voice of any political party.”

World.title: Anti-CEC protest LIVE: Delhi Police detain women protesters after 6 p.m.
World.content:
Top Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders on Sunday (October 11, 2026) vowed to expand their protests nationwide on the SIR issue after they were released from preventive custody though 100 more people were detained as police maintained the security chokehold on the national capital.

Also read | Restores people’s faith in justice system: Sibal after SC’s directions to government on protests

In a special sitting, the Supreme Court directed that people gathering peacefully should not be illegally detained and asked authorities to ensure that Delhi Metro functions normally, and that there is no disruption to internet services, subject to law and order conditions.

CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, who were set free on a condition that they would not “breach peace” for a year, claimed that their detention was illegal and their protest would continue till Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar resigns.

Also read: Four Hindu Raksha Dal members arrested after video shows man, woman assaulted during Delhi protest

The CJP and the Opposition parties alleged that the detentions were illegal, while Delhi Police asserted that the “preventive arrests” were done following “all due legal procedures”. Members of several student organisations, including the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), All India Students’ Association (AISA) and Krantikari Yuva Sangathan (KYS), along with CJP supporters, were detained while trying to march to Jantar Mantar from different parts of the capital.

Also Read | Keralam Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas allegedly assaulted by CRPF personnel; SFI activists suffer injuries

Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge said he and the Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi have sought a meeting with the Chief Justice of India between 4 p.m. and 5 p.m. on Monday (October 12, 2026) to seek his intervention on the issue of “vote chori”.

World.title: Probe agencies, courts should no longer drag their feet in cases against Jagan, says Excise Minister Kollu Ravindra
World.content:
Minister for Excise and Mines & Geology Kollu Ravindra has said that it has been characteristic of YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) president Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy to distort facts related to his alleged involvement in major economic offences being investigated for the past 15 years.

Mr. Ravindra has expressed the hope that the Telangana High Court will, at least now, bring the cases to a conclusion following a fresh appeal by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) to speed up the proceedings.

Addressing the media at the TDP central office, near Mangalagiri, on Sunday, Mr. Ravindra said that Mr. Jagan Mohan Reddy had been trying to deflect attention from his own cases. Amassing of wealth amounting to nearly ₹48,000 crore was no small crime to be taken lightly, the Minister said, and pointed out that his misdeeds landed even his father and former Chief Minister Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy in trouble.

“Rajasekhara Reddy is among the accused in some of the cases of money laundering, inflating the value of company shares and creation of shell companies,” the Minister said.

Mr. Ravindra alleged that Mr. Jagan Mohan Reddy had managed to delay the court hearings by filing more than 4,000 discharge petitions. The Supreme Court had observed that economic offences were like cancer to society and the country’s economy, he said, insisting that the investigating agencies and courts could no longer drag their feet on these high-profile cases.

‘Cases gathering dust’

Meanwhile, in a video message to the media, Sarvepalli MLA Somireddy Chandramohan Reddy said that “unfortunately the case files are gathering dust for a decade and a half.”

He noted that it had taken only two years for the courts to pronounce their judgment in the cases registered by the CBI against former Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao in the Jharkhand Mukti Morcha MPs’ bribing scandal.

Similarly, no sooner than a case was booked against him, senior BJP leader L.K. Advani stepped down as a Member of Parliament, and returned to the Lok Sabha after being acquitted in two years.

In contrast, Mr. Jagan Mohan Reddy had successfully escaped from the clutches of law by using all the resources at his disposal, Mr. Chandramohan Reddy alleged.

​Now that the ED made a forceful plea to the Telangana High Court to speed up the proceedings, it should brook no delay to show to the world that nobody was above law.

World.title: Yaduveer ascends golden throne as royal Navaratri begins
World.content:
The erstwhile Mysuru royal family’s private Navaratri celebrations began on a ceremonial note on Sunday, with the titular head of the royal family, Yaduveer Krishnadatta Chamaraja Wadiyar, ascending the iconic golden throne at the Durbar Hall of Mysuru Palace for the Khas Durbar (private durbar).

The rituals evoked the grandeur of a bygone era as the Wadiyars continued the traditional Navaratri ceremonies that have been observed by the royal family for centuries. The symbolic durbar is now held only during Dasara, with only a select audience permitted to witness the proceedings.

The rituals began in the morning with ‘Kankana Dharana’, the tying of sacred threads around the wrists of Yaduveer and his wife, Trishikha Kumari Wadiyar. Yaduveer later offered prayers as part of the rituals inside the palace.

The Pattada Ane (royal elephant), Pattada Kudure (royal horse) and Pattada Hasu (royal cow) were also part of the rituals, upholding the traditions of the erstwhile Mysuru kingdom.

Following the rituals, Yaduveer, who is also the Mysuru-Kodagu MP, proceeded to the Durbar Hall amid the chanting of ‘Bahu Parak’ by the courtiers. He performed puja to the golden throne before ascending it, formally marking the commencement of the ‘Khas Durbar’.

Priests from various temples offered teertha prasada to Yaduveer, while the Police Band played ‘Kayo Sri Gowri’, the anthem of the erstwhile Mysuru kingdom.

Royal family members, including Pramoda Devi Wadiyar, Trishikha Kumari Wadiyar and their sons, Aadyaveer Wadiyar and Yugadhyaksh Wadiyar, along with a select group of invitees, witnessed the proceedings on the opening day.

The ‘Khas Durbar’ will be held in the evening on the remaining days of the private Dasara celebrations. The Navaratri rituals of the royal family will culminate at the Palace on October 21 (Vijayadashami).

World.title: Woman, paramour wanted in 2022 murder case arrested from Andaman
World.content:
A woman accused of murdering her husband with the help of her paramour in 2022 was arrested by the Bheemunipatnam police in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands on October 9, 2026. A special team from the Visakhapatnam City police travelled to the remote Swaraj Dweep to track down and apprehend the absconding duo, who had allegedly assumed false identities to evade the law.

The arrested were identified as V. Nookaraju, a resident of Vasuvanipalem, and V. Jyothi (26), a resident of Bheemunipatnam mandal. The duo had reportedly fled after non-bailable warrants (NBWs) were issued against them for repeatedly failing to appear before the court.

Addressing a press conference at the Police Conference Hall in the city on Sunday (October 11), Deputy Commissioner of Police Ch. Manikanta Chandolu said that on December 22, 2022, Jyothi, with the support of her alleged paramour V. Nookaraju, murdered her husband Paidiraju by mixing sedative tablets into his food. Nookaraju and another accused, K. Bholoka, subsequently arrived at Jyothi’s house and allegedly strangulated her husband, resulting in his death. Nookaraju and Bhooloka allegedly transported the body to Nookaraju’s room at Visalakshi Nagar. The next day, the duo shifted the body in a private ambulance to a cremation ground at Pedawaltair and cremated the body.

On December 30, Jyothi lodged a complaint with the Bheemunipatnam police stating that her husband was missing. During the investigation, Paidiraju’s family expressed suspicion about Jyothi’s behaviour. On January 12, 2023, police took Nookaraju and Jyothi into custody, and the third accused, Bhooloka, was also subsequently arrested.

Based on the findings, the case was altered to murder, and all three accused were produced before the court. However, Nookaraju and Jyothi allegedly stopped appearing before the court, fearing that they could be sentenced to life imprisonment. This led the court to issue non-bailable warrants against them.

The two accused switched off their mobile phones and left their residences to evade arrest. They reportedly travelled to Chennai and later reached the Andaman and Nicobar Islands by boat. From there, they allegedly travelled by boat to Swaraj Dweep, where they had been living under different identities using forged Aadhaar cards.

Following directions from Commissioner of Police Shanka Brata Bagchi, Bheemunipatnam Police Station Inspector G. Diwakar Yadav led a team to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and arrested the accused on October 9.

The police also found that Jyothi had two children. After their arrest, the accused were produced before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court in Port Blair, where the police obtained a transit warrant to bring them to Visakhapatnam.

In a humanitarian measure, Mr. Shanka Brata Bagchi facilitated the return of Jyothi’s two children along with the accused by air to Visakhapatnam. The children were handed over safely to their relatives. The arrested accused are yet to be produced before the court in Visakhapatnam, the police said.

World.title: Police seize 1,410 kg of dry ginger, 20 kg of cardamom
World.content:
Ramanathapuram police have seized 1,410 kg of dry ginger and 20 kg of cardamom that were to be allegedly smuggled to Sri Lanka near Marakayar Pattinam beach close to Mandapam in Ramanathapuram district.

The Q Branch police received a tip-off that contraband goods were to be transported from Marakayar Pattinam beach to Sri Lanka. Promptly, a team led by Q Branch Inspector Jeevamani rushed to the spot early Sunday morning.

Upon spotting the Q Branch police, the smugglers abandoned 47 sacks right on the beach and fled. The sacks contained 1,410 kg of dry ginger and 20 kg of cardamom. Subsequently, the seized dry ginger, cardamom, and the country boat used for smuggling were handed over to the Customs Department.

Preliminary investigations by the Q Branch police revealed that the dry ginger and cardamom were kept to be smuggled to Sri Lanka by boat. Further, the Q Branch police and the Customs Department are trying to trace the smugglers who escaped.

World.title: Emergency, governor's rule imposed in KP as president approves cabinet decision
World.content:
Key developments:

Emergency imposed under Article 232, governor’s rule under Article 234

Cabinet recommended move due to KP govt’s ‘deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism’

Dr Muhammad Fakhr Alam appointed as KP chief secretary

PTI’s Gohar condemns decision as undemocratic, says peace cannot be established by weakening provincial autonomy

Governor Kundi calls for unity for ‘new chapter’ in KP’s development

ISLAMABAD: The federal government on Sunday imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa following the president’s approval of the recommendations by the federal cabinet.

The measures have been approved under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, the President House said in a statement. The two provisions pertain to the proclamation of emergency and governor’s rule.

Following the imposition, internet disruptions were being reported from parts of Peshawar, with Dawn unable to contact its correspondents there. Earlier in the day, massive police deployment and increased barriers on certain routes using containers were witnessed in the city.

According to sources in the telecom sector, mobile network and data services have been slowed or shut down in selected areas of some cities. However, there is no province-wide shutdown of mobile data or internet.

The decision to impose the provisions came during an emergency meeting of the federal cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, where he was briefed on the security situation in KP.

A statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said cabinet members reviewed the situation and took note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”.

The members proposed, given the “gravity” of the situation, that the PM advise the president to exercise “his constitutional authority and impose an emergency in the province under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution”.

A couple of hours after the decision was announced, KP Information Minister Shafi Jan, who had been accompanying Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on the PTI’s long march, claimed that the KP CM had been taken into custody.

Dawn has reached out to police for a comment.

The emergency imposition comes a day after PM Shehbaz met President Zardari and discussed the country’s overall security situation.

That meeting came amid heightened tensions between the PML-N-led federal government and the KP government led by the PTI — which is in opposition in the Centre. They have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks .

The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations.

On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban.

It may be recalled that in July 2024, when Afridi’s predecessor Ali Amin Gandapur was the chief minister, the KP Assembly passed a resolution urging the federal government to consult with it and the provincial government before launching a new military operation.

The resolution, passed by a majority vote, cautioned that proceeding without provincial consent could hinder the offensive’s success and result in adverse consequences, for which the federal government would be responsible.

In December that year, the assembly voted unanimously against a potential military operation in parts of Khyber and Bannu districts.

About a year later, after Afridi became the KP CM, the provincial assembly convened a grand jirga with Governor Faisal Karim Kundi and other parties in attendance. The moot unanimously demanded that the Centre prioritise negotiations with Afghanistan and consult the KP government over Afghan policy.

Constitutional provisions

Emergency

Article 232 of the Constitution provides for the proclamation of emergency in a province.

It says, “If the president is satisfied that a grave emergency exists in which the security of Pakistan, or any part thereof, is threatened by war or external aggression, or by internal disturbance beyond the power of a provincial government to control, he may issue a Proclamation of Emergency.”

However, invoking this article “due to internal disturbances beyond the powers of a provincial government to control” requires a resolution from the provincial assembly of that province.

In case the president “acts on his own” — which is not currently the case — the Proclamation of Emergency is to be placed before both houses of Parliament for approval by each house within 10 days.

According to this provision, parliament “shall have power to make laws for a province, or any part thereof, with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Federal Legislative List” during the time of the proclamation of an emergency.

Nothing in this Article shall restrict the power of a provincial assembly to make any law which the Constitution empowers it to make, but if any provision of a provincial law is repugnant to any provision of an Act by Parliament, the latter would prevail and the provincial law would be void as long as the parliamentary Act is in effect.

Governor’s rule

On the other hand, Article 234 deals with the imposition of the governor’s rule “in case of failure of constitutional machinery in a province”. For imposition of the governor’s rule, the president simply requires a request from the provincial governor, it says.

“A proclamation issued under this Article shall be laid before a joint sitting and shall cease to be in force at the expiration of two months, unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolution of the joint sitting and may by like resolution be extended for a further period not exceeding two months at a time,” the Constitution reads.

However, it adds that no such proclamation shall in any case remain in force for more than six months.

Article 233, which provides powers to the president to suspend certain fundamental rights during the emergency period, was not mentioned in the summary signed by President Zardari.

Chief secretary appointed

Following the approval, the federal government appointed Dr Muhammad Fakhr Alam Irfan as the chief secretary of KP, according to an official notification, a copy of which is available with Dawn.

The appointment will take effect immediately and remain in place until further orders, it said.

Dr Irfan, a Grade 22 officer of the Pakistan Administrative Service (PAS), was previously serving as secretary of the Power Division in the federal Ministry of Energy. He hails from Mardan.

In a separate notification, the federal government also placed Muhammad Yahya Akhunzada at the disposal of the KP government with “immediate effect and until further orders”.
