World.title: 'Shovel money upwards, starve everyone else' - ACT under fire over proposed disability benefits cuts
World.content:
ACT is facing criticism from across the aisle over health and disability cuts in its fiscal plan, and copping friendly fire after criticising National's Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis.

Defending her record, Willis says she has delivered a significant fiscal repair job despite global headwinds - as well as ACT policies like the Regulation Ministry, charter schools and housing funding for councils.

ACT released its fiscal plan on Sunday at a photography studio on Auckland's Karangahape Road, promising to lift the retirement age and bring the books back in order faster.

In his speech and media standup, leader David Seymour repeatedly criticised the government's government's economic handling over the past three years, saying the "fiscal blowout during Covid ... has not been repaired" and warning that spending remains closer to the height of Covid spending than to the pre-Covid finances he wants to get back to.

"What is needed is political leadership on the big cost drivers."

Unlike previous ACT fiscal plans, it opts for "small and strategic" cuts to taxes rather than broader-based income tax cuts, with Seymour saying it was "irresponsible to cut taxes when you're borrowing money against your children's taxes".

That's the same argument put forward by Willis about why this is not the time for further income tax cuts. While he did not name her, the government this term continued borrowing while also delivering the tax cuts Willis had promised at the last election.

He said the Pre-election economic and fiscal update (Prefu) set out a surplus in two years time - but so had the Prefu from 2023.

"If we don't start doing something different with some courage and some leadership, Prefu 2029 will also say the government's going to be in surplus two years later.

"John Key and Bill English are looking better and better, and Helen Clark and Michael Cullen look better still," he said. "This country has drifted so far to the left, the ACT Party is left a little bit like England in May 1940 as the only ones holding the line for sanity."

But Willis pushed back.

"We agree with the need to focus on careful spending and debt reduction. However, our approach will prioritise more funding to ensure frontline public services are resourced to respond effectively to an ageing and growing population," she said.

"The Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update showed a credible path to balanced books and debt reduction proving we have delivered significant fiscal repair despite global headwinds. This reflects National's efforts to reprioritise wasteful spending, with savings averaging about $12 billion a year.

"This repair job has been accomplished even while accommodating the significant spending needed to support ACT's policies including a Ministry for Regulation, a charter schools' agency and housing funding for local councils."

The party's plan would also cut disability benefits by $653 million dollars over four years.

Semour said ACT would require independent medical certification against clear criteria for health and disability benefits.

"People who are genuinely disabled and don't have a chance to get to work, they should be looked after well - I've always believed that," he said.

"But you can't tell me that we've had a massive blowout in mental health problems and sickness over the last six that explains the increase in people who supposedly can't work.

"Now, there's one of two failings: either New Zealand has become a much sicker place in the last seven years, or we have got a lot worse at managing and helping people who could be working. And I suspect it's the latter," he said.

He said he was not worried about pushback from disability communities in response because "people who are genuinely disabled are tired of having to go and prove that they're disabled every year".

Independent disability advocate Jane Carrigan said it would be a "vicious blow" to people who relied on those benefits.

"I've always found ACT to be quite helpful in supporting people with disabilities who have problems, so I'm particularly disappointed that such a proposal is coming from them, and the social welfare sector has been beaten around the head by its current minister ... frankly, looks like a race to the bottom."

"What will that money go towards? What, new roads filling in a few potholes? It's just, yeah, it's my personal view is it's obscene."

The Green Party accused ACT of cutting support for disabled people to hand more money to the super-rich.

"This plan continues to shovel money upwards, starving everyone else," Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406628567112

"The cutting of KiwiSaver Government contributions and removal of tax on gains will most benefit the richest, and they know it.

"At the same time, ACT is saying the quiet part out loud, budgeting cuts worth hundreds of millions of dollars to support for disabled people. These New Zealanders are often on the lowest incomes and have already had support cut by this callous Government."

Labour's finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said ACT was "punching down" with its fiscal plan.

"ACT is proposing nearly $10 billion in cuts, including scrapping some ministries and reducing funding for foreign aid and environmental programmes.

"He also wants to end annual Government KiwiSaver contributions for eligible workers, raise the superannuation age to 67 and cut disability entitlements.

"New Zealanders deserve to know exactly who will be affected and what support they'll lose.

"Overall, its just cut, cut, cut," Edmonds told RNZ.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said ACT must explain how they intended to deliver a $100-a-household carbon tax refund when the government's carbon auctions had not generated any revenue since 2024.

"ACT has budgeted $200 million for its carbon tax refund in 2027/28, but the most recent ETS auction attracted no bids at all. You can't refund money you haven't collected," she said.

"ACT needs to explain what assumptions underpin its $200 million forecast, and whether households will receive anything if carbon auctions continue to fail."

An ACT spokesperson said the reason auctions are not clearing is because the Government currently refuses to sell carbon units below $75, while they currently sell on the secondary market for around $51.

World.title: ACT promises to cut foreign aid by $1.1 billion over four years, Pacific and Ukraine protected
World.content:
The ACT Party wants to cut more than $1.1 billion in foreign aid over four years from 2028 onwards.

The proposal was announced on Saturday by list candidate Paul Henry, who said it would mean a "reality check" for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) on behalf of taxpayers.

"New Zealand has good reason to spend overseas - a stable, prosperous Pacific, strong trade ties and the ability to help when disaster strikes. But foreign aid is taxpayers' money and should face the same scrutiny as spending here at home," Henry said.

The fiscal plan unveiled by leader David Seymour on Sunday stated that "overseas spending must be weighed against domestic priorities" and that a foreign aid cut would lessen the government's need to borrow.

"ACT will reduce foreign aid to 2017 levels, excluding support for Ukraine... this will save around $283 million a year," the proposal said.

Based on the current 2024/25 to 2026/27 triennium aid budget of $3.06 billion, reducing foreign aid by $283 million per year would amount to a 28 percent cut.

It comes off the back of a National Party promise to reduce aid by $431 million last week, as a means of funding a commitment for new medicines and a lower bowel screening age.

Like National, Seymour said there would be no aid cuts to the Pacific.

"We believe that we should be looking after our friends in the Pacific, that's critical to New Zealand," Seymour told reporters on Sunday.

It would also protect spending to support Ukraine, which so far has totalled around $152 million since the war began.

He called the rest of the budget "a blowout".

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406628567112

"When I see $15 million for transgender passionfruit, that's not the sort of expenditure people thought they were getting.

"I think some of these boondoggles make people laugh at us."

The aid item in question was the "Vietnam Climate-Smart Fruit Value Chain," on which around $4.5 million has so far been spent. None of the information provided about the project on MFAT's DevData website makes reference to gender-diverse people.

Aid expert Terence Wood told RNZ Pacific that ACT's proposal would wreak havoc on New Zealand's aid programme and its workers.

"It would be incredibly disruptive to the aid work that New Zealand does," he said.

"If you're got to implement a massive cut over a short period of time, you're gonna cut things here, there and everywhere - there's not going to be much scope for carefully selecting the projects that go.

He said a carve-out for Pacific aid suggests that cuts to the rest of the world - for example South East Asia - would be massive.

"If a politician cites a silly sounding project to justify aid cuts, they're almost certainly trying to hoodwink you."

Labour's leader Chris Hipkins said cuts to foreign aid would mean New Zealand's role as a good global citizen could take a hit.

"Our foreign aid is a small but important contribution we make as a good global citizen. Our trading relationships across the world depend on our good reputation as a good global citizen, and that's going to be undermined if you have a National, ACT, New Zealand First government still in office after the election."

He said a lot of New Zealand businesses were involved in delivering foreign aid, and it was on ACT to explain that their business could be cut.

Both National and ACT's policies were a waste of time, he said.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters - who has been the foreign minister this term - also criticised the policy, calling it "mindless".

He said it was "training wheel stuff" and would leave New Zealand with no influence on the world stage.

"It's high time that they left it to the adults in the room on this matter. This is extraordinary," he told RNZ.

World.title: Marine biologist fears effects of increasing carbon dioxide levels on sealife
World.content:
Marine biologists say aquatic life is facing growing challenges as the ocean absorbs more carbon dioxide.

Victoria University marine biologist Dr Christopher Cornwall said carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels was absorbed by the ocean, changing the chemistry of seawater and making it more acidic.

The process, known as ocean acidification, affects organisms such as calcareous seaweeds and abalone, which rely on calcium carbonate to form and maintain their protective structures.

Increasing carbon dioxide levels could also fuel the growth of some opportunistic species, while marine heatwaves and coastal darkening were creating further pressures on ocean ecosystems, Dr Cornwall said.

"So what's happening is our oceans are becoming warmer as the world is becoming warmer," he said.

Coastal darkening occurs when sediment washed into the sea reduces the amount of light reaching underwater environments. It can affect photosynthesis in marine plants and algae.

Reducing greenhouse gas emissions was the solution, Dr Cornwall said.

"If we can do that, it's going to be the biggest thing we can do to stop the effects of climate change manifesting even more intensely."

Protecting and restoring marine ecosystems was another important measure, he said.

"So restoring these systems for the future with climate change resistant organisms, being able to more better manage these marine ecosystems and sustainably harvest from them."

World.title: Loosening of US peptide standards worries NZ expert
World.content:
Reports the Trump administration plans to allow some compounding pharmacies to dispense peptides that have not been fully tested for safety have a University of Auckland professor worried.

The Washington Post reports its sources as saying there are plans to allow the sale of some previously restricted peptides while health officials devise new regulations for the controversial products.

However, Food and Drug Administration scientists have raised alarms about the move because the products' claims have not been through FDA-approved clinical trials to assess safety and efficacy, the Washington Post reported on Friday.

A compounding pharmacy prepares custom medications for prescriptions that cannot be filled with mass-produced formulations.

Professor of cellular signalling Peter Shepherd said it was worrying for the whole world when politicians were making decisions about access to unproven medicines "and overruling the safety procedures that have been built up over the last 50 or 60 years".

"The fact that it's gaining some sort of validation and approval in America will justify to many New Zealanders that these are somehow safe when they're really not.

"They haven't been proven. There's very little data on many of these peptides that we're talking about and really could lead to people getting into some serious harm."

Peptides were a whole range of drugs targeting different things and it was not known what some new ones did or how they worked, Shepherd said.

He was also concerned that many people were using peptides for cosmetic rather than true medical purposes.

"When you start using quite dangerous products for cosmetic reasons, that to me is also very worrying."

The companies developing the drugs would be taken out of the loop and the work they had been doing to validate the safe use of the drugs "could be totally undone by a few terrible incidents", Shepherd said.

In the long term that could mean they get banned, and "drugs that could have been really potentially useful may never see the light of day".

World.title: Election 2026 as it happened 11 Oct: Greens label ACT fiscal plan 'welfare for the wealthiest', Opportunity seeks answers over 'assumptions'
World.content:
ACT unveiled its fiscal plan, Dame Jacinda Ardern returned, and the two major parties unveiled their own fresh policies during another busy Sunday on the campaign trail.

ACT promises to cut debt and spending, raise retirement age

ACT revealed its fiscal plan on Sunday afternoon, promising to cut debt and spending, raise the superannuation age by three months every year, and cut disability benefits by $653 million.

This would be achieved partly by abolishing "demographic" ministries, bringing disability benefits "under control", cutting foreign aid and back-office spending, and preventing migrants claiming benefits for five years after entering the country.

Two policies in the plan remain mysterious: one costing $100 million a year, and the other being some kind of tax relief costing $264m in its first year, rising to $303m in 2031.

Multiple parties promptly spoke out against the plan. The Greens labelled it "welfare for the wealthiest", while Labour accused ACT of "punching down".

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong then found herself at odds with ACT after questioning how it would deliver a $100 household carbon tax refund when there were no bids in the most recent ETS auction. An ACT spokesperson quickly responded, saying the party would remove the price floor on carbon units to ensure they sell.

The Greens announce the youth jobs policy on Sunday. Calvin Samuel/RNZ

Greens announce youth jobs policy

Earlier in the day, the Green Party announced it would guarantee jobs for every young New Zealander aged 16 to 24 who has been out of work for six months or more.

The party said, if elected, it would establish a pilot programme called Jobs for Young People, which would provide jobs through iwi, business, the public sector and non-profits.

The party would also scale up the Mayors' Taskforce - an initiative between local and central government to get young people into work - to get 32,000 young people into work.

National leader Christopher Luxon at the Smales Farm walkabout Calvin Samuel/RNZ

National to require students to complete Year 11

As the day progressed, the major parties turned their attention to schooling, with National vowing to make completing year 11 mandatory.

Education spokesperson Erica Stanford said students can currently leave school when they turn 16, but many reach that birthday during year 11, allowing them to leave before completing the year.

"Students should complete at least a full Year 11 of compulsory science, English and maths, and have the opportunity to gain the new Foundational Award in literacy and numeracy."

Students would still be able to apply for a leaving exemption if they have a job or are moving into other training, she said.

Labour's announcement came as leader Chris Hipkins toured an independent grocer in Takanini. Giles Dexter/RNZ

Lunchtime for Labour

Next it was Labour's turn for a school-related announcement, with the party confirming more details of its plan to reinstate the former school lunch programme from the start of 2028.

The party's cost of living action plan said the lunches would continue to cover 244,400 students in the 1014 schools already included. Lunches would be $5 a meal, and $6.50 for students in years 9 to 13.

The lunches would be made in school kitchens, by iwi and hapū partners or by local caterers.

The cost of living policy plan also included a commitment to restore rural school bus routes.

Winston Peters on the campaign trail earlier this week. RNZ / Nick Monro

NZ First promises visa changes

New Zealand First is promising to scrap the Accredited Working Visa and replace it with a "shortage-led" Skilled Work Visa if re-elected.

Entry into New Zealand under the scheme would be tied to an occupation, region and "demonstrated need", not an employer getting accreditation.

In a statement, the party said skilled migrants were needed where New Zealanders could not "reasonably fill" a job and the current system had become a "general recruitment channel" for jobs with little connection to a genuine skills shortage.

"The policy will put New Zealand workers first, lift confidence in the immigration system, protect migrant workers from exploitation, and preserve a clear route for employers who genuinely cannot find critical skills here."

Former PM Dame Jacinda Ardern re-entered the arena of New Zealand politics on Sunday - somewhat - in a drive for more Labour donations. SUPPLIED

Ardern: Hello from the other side (of the Tasman)

Former PM Dame Jacinda Ardern has re-entered the arena of New Zealand politics - somewhat - in a drive for more Labour donations.

Ardern, who has stayed quiet on New Zealand politics since leaving Parliament in 2023, sent has sent an email to Labour supporters encouraging them to donate to the campaign.

The email - with the subject line of 'Hello!' - was sent with a short two-minute video of Ardern

"It has been such a long time since I have popped into your inbox, but I couldn't think of a better time to jump on and just say quick hello, and also share two very quick messages."

The first of those, which Ardern acknowledged was "completely obvious," was urging support for Labour and "old colleague and friend" Chris Hipkins.

The second message was to share her memories of her time as Labour leader during a campaign, and what it meant when someone volunteered, door-knocked, or gave financial support.

"In 2017, I still remember when the general secretary told me not just the amount we were able to raise online, but when he told me how many people had given."

World.title: Calls for better Dunedin dermatology services after 'debilitating' rare cancer went undiagnosed
World.content:
A Dunedin cancer patient is calling for better access to public dermatology services after his rare blood cancer went undiagnosed for years.

Mark Baxter has launched a petition calling for permanent, in-person public dermatology services in Dunedin and the wider Southern region.

His symptoms began about three years ago, initially resembling a fungal infection affecting his toenail. He later developed a rash, blisters that would not heal, and unusual rashes elsewhere on his body.

His GP carried out tests over several years but was unable to establish what was causing the symptoms.

With no public dermatology service in Dunedin to refer him to, his GP sought advice through a medical network.

Supplied / Mark Baxter

"My GP sent some photos and descriptions to some kind of network that his practice is involved with," Baxter said.

A dermatologist reviewed the images and recommended further biopsies and tests, which eventually revealed T-cell lymphoma, a rare blood cancer.

Baxter said the diagnosis came down to chance.

"It was just down to luck that this particular dermatologist happened to notice the pictures and take an interest in the case."

He described the impact of his illness as "pretty debilitating".

"Since about May I've been only sort of able to lie on the sofa 90 percent of the time and the last couple of months I'm now effectively bedridden," he said.

Baxter wants to ensure other patients do not face the same difficulties trying to access specialist care.

He welcomes plans to restore dermatology clinics in Dunedin through a regional service based in Christchurch, expected to reopen in late November.

However, he would prefer a dermatologist based in Dunedin and said the service needs adequate funding to ensure patients can access timely care.

He said the world-wide shortage of dermatologists means the Government needs to pay specialists appropriately if it wants to provide an adequate service.

The petition says the lack of locally accessible public dermatology places an unacceptable burden on patients, families, GPs and other hospital services.

It notes that severe skin conditions can cause chronic pain, infection, disability and death, and that delayed diagnosis can affect outcomes.

World.title: NZ First promises to implement 'shortage-led' skilled work visas
World.content:
New Zealand First are promising to scrap the Accredited Working Visa and replace it with a "shortage-led" Skilled Work Visa if re-elected.

Entry into New Zealand under the scheme would be tied to an occupation, region and "demonstrated need", not an employer getting accreditation.

In a statement, the party said skilled migrants were needed where New Zealanders could not "reasonably fill" a job. The current system had become a "general recruitment channel" for jobs with little connection to a genuine skills shortage.

"The policy will put New Zealand workers first, lift confidence in the immigration system, protect migrant workers from exploitation, and preserve a clear route for employers who genuinely cannot find critical skills here," the party said.

"Immigration must serve New Zealand's economic interests, fill identifiable shortages, and complement our workforce, not become a general source of labour for ordinary jobs. Nor be used as a back door to bring in friends and family or exploit the system."

If re-elected, New Zealand First will:

Scrap and replace the Accredited Employer Working Visa

Limit access to genuine shortages

End routine retail access

Apply a New Zealand worker safeguard

Restore a proper wage floor

Require real domestic recruitment

Strengthen employer accreditation

Target enforcement where risk is highest

Publish meaningful transparency data

Protect workers without rewarding bad sponsors

The party said New Zealand had around 171,000 unemployed people and an underutilisation rate of 13.8 percent.

"There will still be genuine shortages, in particular occupations and regions, but employers seeking migrant workers for routine roles should have to prove that they have made a serious effort to employ or train New Zealanders.

"We are a country with an immigration system, not an international labour-hire agency with a flag."

The party said if New Zealanders could be trained to do a job, they should be.

"If the shortage is real, prove it. If the skill is critical, New Zealand will welcome it.

"But if the job is routine, the evidence is fiction, and the so-called shortage can be solved by offering a proper wage, the answer will be no," the party said.

World.title: ACT sets out plan to raise retirement age, cut debt, spending and disability benefits
World.content:
The ACT Party's fiscal plan promises to cut debt and spending, raise the superannuation age by three months every year, and cut disability benefits by $653 million.

The superannuation changes would also put contributions to the NZ Super Fund on hold, and would include "compassionate access" for those who had spent "a substantial portion of their career in physically demanding jobs".

Similar to the plan unveiled at the last election, the document sets out a goal of returning to 2017 per-capita spending, adjusted for inflation and population growth.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406628567112

This would be achieved partly by abolishing "demographic" ministries, bringing disability benefits "under control", cutting foreign aid and back-office spending, and preventing migrants claiming benefits for five years after entering the country.

Operating allowances - spending - would be reduced by $400m a year, while non-welfare spending would be reduced over three years to 2017 levels - adjusted for inflation and wage growth, with increases in health, education, defence, police and children's services remaining untouched.

Two policies in the plan remained mysterious: one costing $100 million a year, and the other being some kind of tax relief costing $264m in its first year rising to $303m in 2031.

Leader David Seymour announced the plan at The Ever Room photography studio on Auckland's Karangahape Road, saying it was fully costed and showed ACT was "taking the hard road of truth-telling this election".

"Taxpayers know the Government has too much debt. When you're paying over a million dollars an hour in interest on government debt, it's not time to make a virtue of saving money slowly," he said.

New spending in the plan includes the party's proposed $2b cancer centre. The idea for the centre was put forward by candidate Paul Henry. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"Labour and their allies seem to believe greater spending is needed ... ACT rejects that thinking for two reasons. The New Zealand Government already spends as much as, or more than, most of our Pacific Rim neighbours and competitors. More fundamentally, nobody who has seen how government works would think it can make better decisions than families and businesses."

The promise to scrap KiwiSaver tax is tempered by scrapping the scheme's subsidies, and revenue from the Emissions Trading Scheme would be paid out rather than reinvested in cutting emissions.

The document laid out the plans to curb disability benefits by $12m in the first year, rising to $124m, $231m and $286m in subsequent years.

The party would achieve this by requiring "independent medical certification against clear criteria" to access them, with "phased reassessment of existing recipients".

"People with genuine, enduring conditions will retain appropriate long-term support. Consistent assessment helps distinguish those unable to work from those who can work with support, protecting the safety net and reducing avoidable dependency.

"Our costing is based on bringing the number of mental health claimants back to its pre-pandemic level, relative to the working-age population, over four years."

New spending in the plan includes the party's already-announced policies like electronic money management for beneficiaries, a $2b cancer centre, an overstayers investigation unit, $2m for cameras to detect "anti-social noise", $150m capital contingency for a new secondary school in Epsom, and $500 investment funds for Year 11 students.

World.title: Roos get past Dockers as Blues and Hawks taste victory
World.content:
Ash Riddell and Jasmine Garner have delivered a devastating one-two punch as North Melbourne recovered from an early scare to post a 28-point win over Fremantle at Arden Street.

In this afternoon's other AFLW matches, Nell Morris-Dalton kicked a career-high four goals to lift Carlton to a 27-point win over Sydney, while Hawthorn defeated Brisbane by 25 points.

Against the Kangaroos, the Dockers looked set to cause an almighty upset after kicking three straight goals to take a one-point lead during the second quarter.

But with Riddell and Garner in top form, the Kangaroos turned on the afterburners to kick six goals to one, sealing a 9.4 (58) to 4.6 (30) win.

Riddell finished with 38 disposals, four clearances and a goal.

Suns continue to shine in AFLW Gold Coast Suns continue their run as the surprise packets of the AFLW season, consolidating their top-four spot with a victory over Melbourne.

Garner was also destructive with 33 disposals, four clearances and a goal.

Kiara Bowers battled hard for Fremantle on the way to 31 disposals and eight clearances, with Aisling McCarthy (26 disposals) providing support.

The result ensures the Kangaroos finish the round on top of the ladder, while Fremantle slipped out of the top eight.

Fifth-placed Carlton is just 1.7 per cent adrift of fourth-placed Gold Coast after defeating Sydney 8.11 (59) to 4.8 (32) at Henson Park.

Morris-Dalton was the star of the show with 4.1, while Darcy Vescio kicked two goals.

The Blues will sweat on the availability of skipper Abbie McKay, who limped off with an ankle injury in the second half.

Brisbane's Jade Ellenger (left) attempts to get a disposal away while being tackled by Mackenzie Eardley. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

In Melbourne, out-of-form Brisbane threatened to pull off an upset against Hawthorn after taking a two-goal lead into quarter-time.

But the Hawks turned the match with a five-goals-to-nil second term to set up the 9.11 (65) to 6.4 (40) win.

Aine McDonagh kicked three goals from 20 disposals for Hawthorn in a powerful display.

Former Lion Kaitlyn Ashmore celebrated her 100th AFLW match with a stunning set-shot from the boundary-line pocket in the second quarter.

The victory moved Hawthorn into eighth spot, while the Lions are out of the finals equation.

AAP

World.title: Gravel cycling championship brings global audience to tiny town
World.content:
A tiny town in southern Western Australia has become the first location outside Europe to hold an elite gravel cycling world championship.

Nannup, about 268 kilometres south of Perth, hosted thousands of cyclists and spectators this weekend for the 2026 UCI Gravel World Championships.

It was a major coup for the historic timber town, which is building its reputation as a mountain biking destination.

Crowds line the streets of Nannup for the Gravel World Championships. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

With the event expected to draw a global audience of up to 130 million people, Shire of Nannup Deputy President Vicki Hansen said securing it had taken years of work.

"Not many people even knew how to pronounce Nannup," she said.

"Now, Nannup, Western Australia is across the world."

Vicki Hansen says it took years of work to secure the event. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

The hills and forests surrounding the town have proven the ideal terrain for mountain biking, with Ms Hansen hopeful the event would showcase the local trails.

The event attracted almost 1,000 competitors from all over the world. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

"We want all these international riders, who didn't qualify, but have seen the event, to come on over," Ms Hansen said.

Competitors raced over two days, traversing courses of up to 144km through the Blackwood Valley.

Close to 1,000 cyclists are racing through the Blackwood Valley. (Supplied: SWPix)

"Nannup itself is only 70 metres above sea level but within a kilometre or less than that it suddenly increases to 300 metres above sea level," Shire President Tony Dean said.

"In that elevation … we've got the gravel itself."

Dutch cyclist Marianne Vos is the first person to win the gravel world championships twice. (Supplied: SWPix)

Dutch cyclist Marianne Vos took out the elite women's title in 4 hours and 30 minutes, followed by Germany's Rose Kloser and the Netherlands' Larisa Hartog.

It was the second championship victory for the two-time Olympic gold medallist.

The men's elite championship was taken out by Denmark's Magnus Bak Klaris, in 4 hours and 9 minutes, in an upset win over 2025 champion Florian Vermeersch.

Journey to Nannup

This year will be the fifth UCI Gravel World Championships event held, with previous events taking place in Italy and Belgium.

Wendy Oosterwoud, who travelled almost 30 hours from the Netherlands to compete in Nannup, said it was her first time outside of Europe.

"I think the flight was 21 hours, the drive to Amsterdam was almost two hours, [and] from Perth to Nannup was almost three," she said.

"I'm really happy to see this part of the world."

Wendy Oosterwoud says travelling to the Nannup gravel races was her first time outside Europe. (Supplied: Wendy Oosterwoud)

The Dutch cyclist has claimed seven podium titles, including winning the women's elite at a gravel world series in Poland this year.

She said the Nannup course was broader than those overseas.

"Here in Nannup, it's wide gravel roads," she said.

"But in the Netherlands … you have, I think, 200 corners, left right, left right."

Nils Lageman says the race is the most significant of its kind in the world. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

German cyclist Nils Lageman made the journey from his home near Cologne to compete in the 35-39 age group.

"The world championships were calling, and I just had to respond, wherever it is," he said.

"It looks great because of the nature."

US cyclists Tim Borsetti, Mark Litrell and John Steward had never heard of Nannup until the the event (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

Many international cyclists said they had never heard of Nannup, until the event, including US cyclist Tim Borsetti.

"I targeted this because I knew it would be an awesome event, because you guys have big wide roads like we do in the States," he said.

'Spreading the love'

With a regular population of about 1,000 people, accommodation in Nannup has been fully booked for the event.

Mr Dean said a tent city, and visitors staying in other nearby towns, had helped share the load.

Nannup welcomed the visiting cyclists and spectators with open arms. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

"We're spreading the love between Nannup and the rest of the South West," he said.

"With that many visitors, they're going to have to commute, unfortunately."

It has proven a win for some local businesses, with cafe owner Hayley Rubery registering one of the busiest days she could remember.

Tents and accommodation in surrounding communities helped Nannup handle the bumper crowds. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

"We had a 700 per cent increase in revenue to a normal Friday. It's insane," she said.

"We sold five days' worth of milk in one day, and we've never made more toasties in our entire lives."

Hayley Rubery says the event brought a 700 per cent jump in business. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

With the town's previous events leaning towards smaller-scale arts and culture festivals, Ms Rubery said they had been unsure what to expect.

"We prepped anyway and thank God we did."

World.title: Running legend Kipchoge sets race record at Melbourne Marathon
World.content:
Eliud Kipchoge has lived up to his star billing at the Melbourne Marathon with a race-record performance.

Kenya's two-time Olympic champion and former world record holder has delighted several thousand fans at the MCG on Sunday morning with a dominating run.

Kipchoge broke away inside the last 10 kilometres of the 42.2km race and won in 2 hours 9 minutes 10 seconds — 2 seconds inside the previous race best.

He would have finished a few seconds quicker, but was waving to the crowd on the half-lap inside the MCG to the finish.

Thomas Do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35 while fellow Australian Reece Edwards came third in 2:15:57.

In the women's race, New Zealand's Camille French was first to the tape in 2:28:25. Australia's Sinead Diver was 23 seconds back in second place, with Irish runner Nichola Sheridan a further 24 seconds back in third.

The 42km journey took participants down St Kilda Road, past Flinders Street Station, around Albert Park Lake, before a finish inside the MCG.

Kipchoge, 41, last won a marathon in 2023. He looked at the finish like it had been an easy training run, spending several minutes with fans alongside the MCG boundary line.

Kipchoge said it was a great feeling to finish at the famous stadium that also hosted the start and finish of the marathon at the 1956 Olympics — 70 years ago.

"So I come here to celebrate the 70 years and tell the people of Melbourne, 'Let us run together here at the MCG' so it was a beautiful time for me, happy to enter this stadium," Kipchoge said after the race.

This is only his second visit to Australia and his Melbourne Marathon debut.

It is part of Kipchoge's world tour, featuring a marathon on all seven continents, including Antarctica.

AAP/ABC

World.title: 'Knew we were cooked': Last-lap drama as Bathurst leader runs out of fuel
World.content:
A shattered Anton De Pasquale has said he knew his hopes of winning the Bathurst 1000 "were cooked", moments before his car ran out of fuel while leading on the final lap.

Brodie Kostecki and Todd Hazelwood took full advantage of De Pasquale's misfortune, securing a victory for Dick Johnson Racing that they appeared to have blown earlier in the race.

The number 18 car, by Team 18, appeared to have played a blinder late in the race when De Pasquale held a big lead in the final laps.

But his team urged him to "maximum fuel save" as the chequered flag neared.

A late safety car with five laps to go, the only one of the race, appeared to have potentially saved Team 18 and secured De Pasquale and co-driver Lee Holdsworth a famous win.

But the number 18 ran out of fuel on the 161st and final lap, allowing Kostecki to breeze by in the number 17 car and claim the most dramatic of victories.

"Once I knew how much fuel short we were, I knew we were cooked," De Pasquale said in the aftermath of his dramatic final lap.

"Very disappointed. We had a really good day, and the chequered flag was 6km away.

"The car was amazing at the back end of the race, where we wanted it; everything went our way, until it didn't."

De Pasquale and Holdsworth had driven a wonderful race on Sunday, and were in a fight with the number 10 Matt Stone Racing entry of Zach Bates and Aaron Seton for the race lead late.

Anton De Pasquale was less than one lap away from winning the Bathurst 1000. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Team 18 had saved fuel well at Mount Panorama and took the lead of the race after the final pit stop, with Matt Stone Racing having the fuel pump in their number 10 car for 15 more seconds than their rivals.

But Team 18 got their sums wrong and were pleading with De Pasquale to save fuel with less than 10 laps remaining.

"I can't believe it. I didn't know we were so close on fuel, or what happened," Holdsworth said after watching from the garage as his teammate was left helpless in a spluttering car.

"Massive disappointment. I've got no words."

Kostecki and Hazelwood were in control of the Bathurst 1000 for much of Sunday, but their second-to-last pit stop was slow and dropped them from the lead to fifth.

Kostecki roared in the final laps, and then was gifted the chance to win when the late safety car was deployed.

"We executed so well up until that second-last pit stop with the brake change," Kostecki said.

"But, like I've always said, the mountain chooses the winner.

"We definitely had the fastest car today — so super proud of everyone … this Ford Mustang was on rails."

Dick Johnson was holding back tears in the DJR garage, while those from Team 18 were left devastated.

"That's amazing," an emotional Johnson said after the race.

"I tell you what, I want a couple more before I fall off the perch."

Will Brown and Scott Pye were second for the Triple Eight team, while Matt Stone Racing's pole sitters Zach Bates and Aaron Seton were third.

Bates and Seton were able to snag a tremendous third place, but will leave Mount Panorama with the knowledge they would have won the race had the safety car never come out.

On the third-last lap, Bates was pushed wide by Kostecki into the final corner for second, and Will Brown was able to take advantage to relegate Bates to fourth, before Team 18's fuel drama.

World.title: Suns stamp AFLW top-four credentials as Crows rebound
World.content:
Gold Coast have rubber-stamped their AFLW top-four credentials with a historic 22-point victory over Melbourne.

The Suns posted their sixth straight win on Saturday night, faring better in sweltering heat at Mackay's Great Barrier Reef Arena to down the Demons 9.7 (61) to 5.9 (39).

Gold Coast had not beaten Melbourne in their four previous clashes since the Suns entered the women's competition in 2020.

"It's been a long few years for us and we've been slowly building every year," Suns co-captain Lucy Single told Fox Footy after the landmark triumph.

"So to kind of get that win under our belt has been so awesome and I think that's really boosted our confidence."

The Suns find themselves sitting pretty with three rounds left before finals, drawing level with Melbourne at 7-2.

Melbourne took a three-point lead into quarter-time, but Gold Coast kicked away in the second term and did not look back.

Midfielder Charlie Rowbottom had a game-high 33 possessions and six clearances as Ava Usher, Mikayla Nurse and Havana Harris (two goals apiece) all fired up forward.

Despite the mercury hovering in the mid-20s, Usher said the Suns were not fazed by the conditions.

"We knew it was going to be a really tough arm-wrestle and in the end we just got over the line in really hot conditions," the first-year Sun said.

"We're pretty used to it."

Adelaide had too much firepower for Richmond in the earlier game, winning 9.8 (62) to 4.6 (30) at Melbourne's Princes Park.

The 32-point victory put the Crows back in the finals hunt at 4-5, although they remain just outside the eight with three games of round nine to play.

Prolific ball-winner Ebony Marinoff collected 40 disposals, 13 tackles and a goal.

St Kilda send Dal Santo out a winner It's been an AFLW season to forget for St Kilda, but Saturday's win over Collingwood has given departing Saints coach Nick Dal Santo a perfect send-off.

The 40-possession game was one shy of her career-best mark.

The Crows captain said it had been a tough week following a 14-point Showdown loss to Port Adelaide.

"I'd be lying [to say] we didn't know what was on the line tonight," Marinoff said.

"But really proud of the girls' efforts just to really start well … because we hadn't over the last fortnight."

Earlier in the day, Geelong took top spot — at least for now — with a 63-point win over GWS at Kardinia Park, with Jacqueline Parry and Aishling Moloney each kicking four goals.

The Cats will fall back to second, however, if North Melbourne beats Fremantle on Sunday.

The other early game saw St Kilda win their first game for the season, with a two-point win over Collingwood at Moorabbin.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Matt Renshaw's 190 turns Durban Test, providing Aussie batting blueprint
World.content:
Like many great plans, it was deceptively simple. Stillness. Balance. Patience. Concentration. No frills, no fast moves and no undue risks, just decisive action when needed.

Not for the first time at Test level, a burly Queenslander, a three-pound cleft of willow and a healthy dose of self-confidence was the difference between Australian success and failure.

That Matt Renshaw resurrected an Australian first innings which teetered near oblivion at 6-124 was the first point of order.

Of consequences further-reaching, the left-hander resurrected his entire Test career overnight in Durban, sweeping, clipping and crashing his way to 190 from 397 deliveries across 465 minutes of life-affirming Test batting.

Numerous records fell or threatened to. Renshaw's epic was the highest score by an Australian in Durban, the fourth highest overall by an Aussie against South Africa, and the best by a number-five of any nation at Kingsmead.

It was also a new Test personal best for Renshaw, usurping the 184 he made nine years ago as a boyish tyro against Pakistan in Sydney, back when the world was at his feet.

Renshaw is 30 now — a husband, a father of two children and an entirely different cricketer. He knows his own mind and understands his place in the scheme of things.

For a nation which has been crying out for big, important runs by someone not named Smith or Head, his Daddy hundred here was one for the ages.

Practically speaking, Renshaw helped Australia to a first-innings total of 390, which was at least 150 more than had seemed optimistic when he first took guard.

On a deeper level, it restored belief in the value of grinding out an innings of depth and character. It was the real deal — the proper Test match batting the Australian cricketing public has been craving.

No mistake should be made about the high degree of difficulty, either. When Renshaw began shepherding the tail a day earlier, Australia was at the mercy of a vigorous and versatile South African pace attack jagging the ball all over the place.

Waiting in the wings were the Proteas' twin spin options of Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer, with 1700+ first-class wickets between them.

Australia has struggled against left-arm spin in recent times. Last time they played a Test in Durban, Maharaj took nine wickets. And Australia's selection for this match — four left handers in the top six — was said to favour right-arm off-spinner Harmer even more.

Matt Renshaw blunted South Africa's spin attack with judicious use of the sweep and reverse sweep in Durban. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

So much for that, in the end. Renshaw swept, reverse-swept and paddled Maharaj into irrelevance and by the time Harmer finally removed the top-scorer for spin's first wicket of the game, the horse had well and truly bolted.

As it turned out, the sterner challenge was curbing the influence of the quicks, who'd posed constant difficulties for the rest of Australia's batters.

A microcosm came when Renshaw was on 130, yet still not able to relax. He was struck a scary blow to the grille of his helmet from an absolute snorter by Anrich Nortje, who bowled with genuine pace and accuracy in short, sharp spells.

Handling the wily and indefatigable Wiaan Mulder was no cinch either. Early on day two, the all-rounder scythed through Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc and threatened to blow the game open.

Wiaan Mulder (centre) took two wickets on day two and proved hard to play for Australia's batters. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

That he didn't was not exclusively a matter of Renshaw's dominance but of the rearguard partnerships which have so often saved Australia's bacon in recent times.

Renshaw shared stands of 86 across 32 overs with Pat Cummins and a monumental and possibly series-shaping 134 from 47 overs with Nathan Lyon.

Australia will not be looking too far ahead, but there was a blueprint here, not just of personnel but of general batting philosophy: know your game, make them bowl to you, stick around and wear them down.

Australia's total was the most obvious metric of success, but its innings duration of 137.2 overs will surely please Andrew McDonald and his analysts just as much.

In Australia's 35 Test innings in the two years before this match, they'd batted past the 100-over mark only six times, compared with 13 times in the 42 innings of the two-year period preceding.

That downward trend has, of course, coincided with a proliferation of the result pitches which characterise the World Test Championship era.

Concurrently, it is agreed by most involved in the Australian domestic scene, it has been difficult for Test batting candidates to put their best feet forward, or get in the habit of playing long innings, when the primary bloc of red-ball cricket occurs in spring, when Sheffield Shield pitches sometimes resemble Monty Don's perennial beds.

Without peering too far into the future or wishing disruption on a player who's just delivered something so special, one awkward talking point that will be aired soon enough is if and when Renshaw might move up to his normal position of opener.

The theory going into this game was that in batting down the order, he could blunt the influence of the spinners, which he assuredly did. But he would surely be just as assured against the new ball as he was here against the second new ball.

And yet, who'd be an opener these days? Late on day two, Ryan Rickelton provided a study in contrasts for the Proteas.

Having spent the better part of two days chasing leather in the field, and perhaps daydreaming that he was in Renshaw's shoes, he lasted only three deliveries before chasing Josh Hazlewood outside his off-stump and sending an edge to the cordon.

The more telling image of day two arrived an hour earlier, on the stroke of tea, when an exhausted Renshaw removed his helmet and trudged off for refreshments.

Appearing on the balcony of the player's area, Australian skipper Cummins peered down on the centurion with something like a look of love on his face.

Ray Illingworth once said a captain needs the patience of a saint, the diplomacy of an ambassador, the compassion of a social worker and the skin of a rhino. Colleagues who can bat for eight hours help, too.

World.title: Quick hits: AFL star in the sheds as Aussies go better than Bradman
World.content:
Matt Renshaw and Nathan Lyon outdo Sir Donald Bradman while Gold Coast Suns AFL star Noah Anderson watches on from the stands.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Renshaw's drought-breaking century

Matt Renshaw carried his team. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

It had been over nine years and nine months since Matt Renshaw's last and only Test century.

Opening the batting on January 3, 2017, a then 20-year-old Renshaw peeled off 184 against Pakistan in Sydney, a match in which he lined up alongside the likes of two-Test white-ball specialist Hilton Cartwright and New South Wales great Steve O'Keefe.

A few false dawns, a short-format reinvention and a red-ball renaissance later, and the Queenslander brought up his drought-breaking ton with an immaculately timed clip through mid-wicket for four.

Having lost overnight partner Pat Cummins and number nine Mitch Starc in quick succession after starting the day on 46, Renshaw was almost chanceless in reaching three figures.

It was a classic Test dig by Matt Renshaw. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

It was a richly deserved milestone for a player, who, at 30, still has plenty of good years ahead of him.

And Renshaw just kept going.

And going.

He received much more than able support from Nathan Lyon as he passed 150, before kicking on with number 11 Josh Hazlewood to set a new Test best of 190, falling just short of a maiden double ton as he nicked off after tea.

2. Better than Bradman

The first innings appeared not long for this world when the best betters in the tail, Cummins and Starc, departed.

But Lyon picked up the mantle to knuckle under with Renshaw, albeit in slightly less expressive fashion. At least so it seemed.

After helping Renshaw to triple figures, there was no loss of application from the Aussie batters out in the middle and when Lyon clipped Anrich Nortje off his hip for four in the 108th over, they passed some pretty big names.

In the 124-year history of Tests against South Africa, no Australian ninth-wicket partnership had ever surpassed 78 runs until day two in Durban.

And the two pairings who had reached that mark included some all-time greats: Ian Meckiff and Ken McKay in Johannesburg in 1958, and Sir Donald Bradman with Bill O'Reilly in Adelaide Oval way back in 1932.

Renshaw and Lyon heaped the pain on South Africa. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

And the records kept tumbling as the runs kept coming, with the pair ticking past two Steve Waugh specials, the first a 130-run stand with Geoff Lawson in 1989, and the second a 133-run effort in tandem with Jason Gillespie in 2001.

By the time Lyon was eventually dismissed for a 92-ball 27 and the stand was over on 134, there was only one greater ninth-wicket partnership in the history of Australian cricket — and that had come in the 19th century.

3. Australia's best recovery in over a century

Given the shakiness of Australia's top order over the past decade or so, there have been plenty of opportunities for inspired rearguard actions.

And we certainly have been treated to some remarkable recoveries — think Steve Smith's partnerships with Peter Siddle and Nathan Lyon that took Australia from 8-122 to 284 at Edgbaston in 2019, or Lyon and Cummins combining for a 55-run stand to guide Australia home during the 2023 Ashes.

But not for over 100 years have we seen an Australian comeback as dramatic as the one we were treated to on day two.

Per ABC Sport statistician Ric Finlay, Australia's recovery from 6-124 to 390 was the country's best rebuild since 1925, when an unbeaten double century to number seven Jack Ryder took Australia from 6-119 to 489.

4. Another selection shock for the Aussies?!

With the Australian rearguard action showing no signs of abating, the broadcast camera panned to the tourists' dugout, where it found an unexpected but familiar face for Aussie sports fan.

Dressed in full training kit and looking slightly surprised to be there himself, there he was, Gold Coast Suns AFL star Noah Anderson.

Loading Instagram content

Anderson has travelled with the Australians to South Africa as part of a leadership fact-finding mission, according to Fox commentator Mark Howard.

As the cameras focused in on Anderson, a Sherrin suddenly appeared in the hands of Marnus Labuschagne, sitting alongside the Suns star.

Marnus Labuschagne (second from left) got out the Sherrin to make Noah Anderson (left) feel at home. (Supplied: Fox Cricket)

5. Lyon walks off despite review

Nathan Lyon enjoyed a gutsy, record-breaking dig alongside Matt Renshaw, but when it was over it was pretty obvious.

Marco Jansen's return to the attack brought with it a short-pitched barrage that seemed to rattle the Aussies out of their methodical tactics of Renshaw seeing off the first four balls before giving Lyon a look.

After being twisted up by a bouncer, Renshaw scurried off strike and left Lyon with three balls to negotiate, but it only took Jansen one as he surprised the number 10 with a full one that smashed into his pads.

Nathan Lyon knew he was out but reviewed anyway. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Jansen, the rest of South Africa's fielders and umpire Chris Gaffaney all knew it was out, and so did Lyon, despite deciding to review.

He made an immediate "T" sign before just as quickly walking off the field before the replays were finished.

By the time his dismissal was confirmed he was already halfway up the stairs.

Tech.title: Vurt wants you to look at vertical videos as a genre of their own
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

From Disney Plus to HBO Max, almost every major established streaming service is experimenting with ways to get into vertical content. It’s clear that these companies see video-focused social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram as existential threats. In this arms race for viewers’ attention, it has often felt like everyone is trying to find new ways to exist on people’s phones. But a new startup thinks that the next step in vertical series’ evolution is going to take place on our wide-screen televisions.

Unlike most vertical microdrama / series streaming platforms on the market that have focused on mobile viewing experiences, Vurt has been making a pivot into smart TVs. The company recently launched dedicated apps for Apple TV and Android TV that give users access to 3,500 episodes across more than 100 different shows. Since launching in March, Vurt’s userbase has grown from 10,000 to 675,000 users.

Vurt primarily features the kind of soapy, melodramatic microdramas that have made rival services like DramaBox and ReelShort popular. But whereas those platforms have become inundated with AI-generated slop, the vast majority of Vurt’s series are produced with human casts and crews. And because Vurt monetizes its content through ad partnerships, viewers can watch all of it for free instead of dealing with convoluted microtransactions.

When I spoke with Vurt cofounder / angel investor Hilmon Sorey this week, he told me that the company’s big push into dedicated TV apps was driven by direct feedback from users. People wanted a way to beam verticals they were already watching via their phones onto bigger screens, but Vurt’s development team thought that they could take things a step further.

“At first, we first developed the ability for folks to cast to smart TVs,” Sorey said. “But we decided that wasn’t the best experience because we could leverage all of the technology in those large-screen devices to bring features like HD / 4K video, and the ability to do really high-quality audio.”

To build out its library, Vurt signs licensing agreements with production studios and creators that gives them a 50/50 revenue split. Independent creators can directly submit their projects for distribution on the platform, and once approved, it can be available to stream in just a few days. Sorey said that being fair to creators and taking cues from them are core tenets of Vurt’s corporate philosophy. He also pointed to Vurt’s decision to rely on a “free-to-finish” model as the main way it works to be fair to its users.

“If you are a platform that’s doing your own original content and you don’t have creators to pay, then ‘give us $20 and we’ll give you 500 coffee beans’ kind of gamification is intentional,” Sorey insisted. “It’s a ruse that they can use to boggle your mind because they control that entire content ecosystem.”

Vurt’s foray onto televisions is coming at a time when more established vertical-focused platforms have been looking into ways to exist beyond people’s phones. This past June, Instagram beefed up its TV app to include Reels, disappearing Stories, and horizontally oriented videos — all of which felt like attempts at keeping pace with YouTube. Vurt told me that the company is staying focused on vertical content, but is currently developing new kinds of programming like original series and livestreamed sporting events.

“You’ve got to have your hook to begin and at the tail end of that, you’ve got to thrust them into the next episode by virtue of a cliffhanger.”

In the buildup to launching its TV apps, Vurt consulted content creators about how they like to watch films and TV shows. Many reported preferring viewing things in movie theaters or on big screens because of how immersive those experiences felt. But according to Sorey, the creators also insisted that vertical microdramas can feel just as engaging whether they’re watched on a phone with earbuds in or on a television screen.

“You can have a different kind of immersive experience — even on a wide screen in vertical format — because verticals tell their stories in a very different way,” Sorey said. “You’ve got to have your hook to begin and at the tail end of that, you’ve got to thrust them into the next episode by virtue of a cliffhanger.”

Sorey believes that the stylistic elements vertical microdramas have become known for — formulaic plots, questionable acting, and exceedingly short episodes — make them a specific kind of entertainment that’s distinct from traditional TV shows and films. Those qualities are what tend to make some people see vertical content as unwatchable, but they also seem to be part of what’s keeping Vurt’s users engaged. Sorey says that Vurt has seen overall engagement time increase for viewers using the company’s TV apps. That’s likely because those viewers have a convenient way to consume Vurt’s content without having to pick up their phones.

Though a service like Vurt might make sense for people already hooked on microdramas, what’s far less clear is whether there’s really a broader appetite for vertical videos flanked by blank spaces. With so many other platforms experimenting with ways to turn everything into endless feeds of vertical videos, though, Vurt may be on to something.

Tech.title: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Welcome Home’ event
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

We are quickly coming up on Apple’s “Welcome Home” launch event, where we expect a host of smart home-related announcements. We are expecting refreshes to Apple TV and HomePod Mini, as well as a brand new smart home hub. We could also see the debut of a new platform called homeOS, and some partner devices from LG.

What we probably won’t be seeing is the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook, which Cupertino whisperer Mark Gurman says will debut later this month.

“Welcome Home” will officially kick off in New York on October 13th at 9AM ET. Here’s more about what to expect.

A proper smart home hub

Until now, Apple has primarily relied on the Home app to control all the various bits and bobs that make up your smart home. But it’s a market niche that the company has been eager to tackle more fully. The new device, which could be called HomePad or HomeView or, more simply, Apple Home Hub, will reportedly feature a 6-inch square touchscreen that can either be mounted on a wall or placed on a table or countertop. According to Mark Gurman, the countertop model will somewhat resemble the iMac G4, with the screen attached to an arm set into a half sphere.

It will also supposedly use voice or facial recognition to identify who is interacting with it, pulling up the relevant contacts, calendar appointments, and more. Apple will offer the option for secondary identification through an iPhone to keep personal data more secure. The whole thing will reportedly run a new software platform called…

homeOS

The company may have registered a trademark for the name through a shell company called Home Operations Suite LLC, a move that Apple has pulled before to quietly secure the rights to names. The platform will supposedly feature a streamlined interface that “looks like a mashup of iOS, tvOS and watchOS,” according to Gurman. The focus, obviously, will be on smart home applications, like controlling thermostats and smart locks, and it will also be capable of making FaceTime calls.

The OS will also include your usual assortment of Apple apps and widgets, including Apple Music, Podcasts, and News, as well as Reminders, Notes, and Siri AI.

HomePod Mini and Apple TV get a minor refresh

Word is that not much is changing with the HomePod Mini or Apple TV. The designs will remain the same, but they’ll get a new processor to help handle the added demand of Siri AI. This will be the first update to the HomePod Mini since it was announced on October 13th of 2020 — exactly six years before Apple’s Welcome Home event. While the company isn’t making any dramatic changes for the Mini’s birthday, it will be offering it in new colors, including green and pink.

This will be the first hardware refresh for the Apple TV since 2022. In addition to supporting Siri AI, the new processor will also speed up navigation, which can get a bit laggy. Both are expected to feature Apple’s N1 chip, which includes support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 6.0.

LG and other partner devices

It’s likely that we’ll get a mention of products that integrate with HomeKit and offer new features built on top of homeOS and whatever Apple’s hardware hub ends up being called. But don’t expect Apple to share too much of the spotlight with its partners. We’ve already seen a leak of LG smart home, including deadbolts, thermostats, and more. They’ll also reportedly include an NFC-based “Proximity Control” that pops up a hint in the iPhone’s Dynamic Island when held near the device, as well as a “tap to set up without power” pairing feature.

Tech.title: Horror is big business
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on how pervasive horror has become, follow Andrew Webster. The Stepback, arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

Resident Evil isn’t alone. Rather, it’s indicative of an ongoing trend. Horror was once seen as largely a niche genre, but now, thanks to a combination of factors — including the rise of YouTube and widespread influence of indie games and viral memes — it has steadily grown into a dominant force. Horror tends to be cheaper to produce than other genres, but now it also has sales numbers that compete with the biggest blockbusters. It’s not that there haven’t been major horror success stories before. 2017’s It remains the top-grossing horror flick of all time, and the Resident Evil 2 remake from 2019 has sold almost 20 million copies. But in 2026 the concentration of horror hits, particularly across multiple mediums, has reached a new level, making it clearer than ever that scaring audiences is a big business.

How it’s going

The most obvious example of this in 2026 is in movies. Obsession and Backrooms — two films helmed by young directors who came up through YouTube — have raked in nearly $1 billion combined at the box office. They out-grossed established franchises like Star Wars and even legendary directors like Steven Spielberg. This despite costing a fraction of what a blockbuster film usually costs; Backrooms was made for an estimated $10 million, while Obsession cost less than $1 million. Before that, Iron Lung, another YouTube-centric horror flick, managed to rake in more than $50 million without the backing of a major studio. Horror movies have always been comparatively cheap to make, but now they’re frequently able to make a huge return on that investment.

Meanwhile, in the world of streaming, October has become something of a battleground. This year basically every major service has a tentpole series meant to lure subscribers during spooky season. Amazon just released a remake of Stephen King’s Carrie on Prime Video, helmed by Mike Flanagan, who made his name with a quintet of limited horror series on Netflix between 2018 and 2023, starting with The Haunting of Hill House. With Flanagan now at Amazon, Netflix’s big release this year is Below, a six-episode sea monster thriller starring Josh Hartnett and Stranger Things’ Charlie Heaton. Elsewhere, Peacock has a Friday the 13th prequel called Crystal Lake starring Linda Cardellini as Jason Voorhees’ mom, and AMC Plus is putting out a spooky detective series called Yaga, which features Carrie-Anne Moss and Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams. Not to be excluded, Disney Plus is currently airing the 13th season of American Horror Story.

The one name missing from this list is Apple TV, but that’s because the service got a jump on things by releasing the horror / comedy hybrid Widow’s Bay back in April. The show then proceeded to win a record number of Emmys, and it remains a fixture on Apple TV’s most-watched list. While streaming viewership data is much harder to come by than box office data, the sheer fact that every major streaming service is investing in horror-related series, with the backing of some major star power, is an indication of just how important it is.

And then there are games. While Resident Evil is the biggest name, there are plenty of other titles and franchises that have been buoyed by the current horror renaissance. Silent Hill has been on a steady run, highlighted by the Scottish spinoff Townfall this year, and the iconic Hellraiser just got its first proper video game adaptation. But it’s not just blockbuster releases. Indie horror games have not only been consistent bestsellers on platforms like Steam, they’ve also been the source material for a number of more moderate theatrical hits, including both Iron Lung and Exit 8. And a lot of that success begins with people watching horror games on Twitch and YouTube; Twitch says that viewers watched 287 million hours of horror content between January and September this year, and that the dedicated “horror” tag saw a 6 percent increase in viewership compared to last year.

What happens next

Obviously not all of these projects will be major hits. Not every spooky meme will become a Backrooms-level success. But studios, streamers, and game publishers are taking the genre more seriously now because that potential exists, and they seem more willing to take risks because the upfront costs aren’t as high. This means that, unlike other genres, the possibility remains that even as it explodes in popularity, horror will continue to remain weird and unexpected. After all, the best way to scare folks is to show them something new.
